SIADH remains a diagnosis of exclusion.","Severe neurologic symptoms require immediate 3% saline boluses regardless of chronicity or cause; the initial goal is a 4–6 mmol/L Na increase, not normalization. [1,2]","For chronic SIADH without severe symptoms, treat the cause and restrict fluid first; urea or increased solute with a loop diuretic may be considered when restriction fails. [1]","The common pitfall is overcorrection after the ADH stimulus disappears. Monitor Na and urine output closely, particularly in patients with Na ≤105 mmol/L, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, or advanced liver disease. [2,4]"],"visual_memory_card":{"top_left":"Persistent V2 signaling inserts collecting-duct AQP2","top_right":"Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia; concentrated urine","bottom_left":"Serum osmolality, Uosm, UNa; exclude mimics","bottom_right":"Fluid restrict; symptomatic cases need 3% saline","center":""},"references":[{"id":1,"source":"Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia","year":2014,"society":"ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA","url":"https://doi.org/10.1530/EJE-13-1020","type":"guideline"},{"id":2,"source":"Diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of hyponatremia: expert panel recommendations","year":2013,"society":"US Expert Panel","url":"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2013.07.006","type":"consensus"},{"id":3,"source":"Tolvaptan, a selective oral vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist, for hyponatremia: SALT-1 and SALT-2","year":2006,"society":"New England Journal of Medicine","url":"https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa065181","type":"landmark_trial"},{"id":4,"source":"Treatment Guidelines for Hyponatremia: Stay the Course","year":2024,"society":"American Society of Nephrology","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10843202/","type":"review"}],"sections":[{"heading":"1. Physiology: Na Is a Water Signal","minutes":"3 min","points":["Serum Na approximates the ratio of exchangeable body Na plus K to total body water; therefore, hyponatremia usually reflects excess water relative to effective body solute—not simply Na depletion.","Hypothalamic osmoreceptors normally suppress ADH when plasma tonicity falls. With low ADH, the collecting duct becomes water-impermeable and generates maximally dilute urine, usually Uosm <100 mOsm/kg.","ADH binds the basolateral V2 receptor on collecting-duct principal cells, activates Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cyclic adenosine monophosphate–protein kinase A signaling, and inserts aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels into the apical membrane. Water then moves through AQP2 and exits through basolateral AQP3/AQP4 channels.","In SIADH—more precisely, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD)—V2 signaling persists despite hypotonicity and absence of an appropriate hemodynamic stimulus. Retained water mildly expands extracellular volume, provoking natriuresis and suppressing renin and aldosterone; this limits edema and produces apparent euvolemia rather than progressive overt hypervolemia.","The brain initially swells as hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into cells. Over approximately 48 hours, astrocytes extrude K, Na, chloride, and organic osmolytes to restore cell volume; this reduces cerebral edema but makes rapid correction dangerous because brain osmolytes cannot be replaced quickly.","Symptoms track acuity and cerebral edema better than the absolute Na: nausea, headache, confusion, gait instability, seizures, coma, and respiratory arrest can occur when Na falls rapidly."],"mechanism":"Persistent collecting-duct AQP2 expression prevents appropriate electrolyte-free water excretion. Chronic cerebral osmolyte loss protects against swelling but creates susceptibility to osmotic demyelination when extracellular tonicity rises too quickly.","teaching_pearl":"A concentrated urine in hypotonic hyponatremia is the physiologic signature that ADH is active; it does not by itself establish SIADH.","board_tip":"Hyponatremia with normal or high measured osmolality is not ordinary hypotonic hyponatremia: consider hyperglycemia, exogenous effective osmoles, or pseudohyponatremia."},{"heading":"2. Workup: Tonicity → ADH Activity → Effective Volume","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["Confirm the result and measure serum osmolality. Hypotonic hyponatremia generally has measured osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; hyperglycemia causes translocational hyponatremia, while severe hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia can cause pseudohyponatremia with indirect ion-selective electrodes.","Check Uosm before therapy when feasible. Uosm ≤100 mOsm/kg indicates appropriately suppressed ADH and suggests primary polydipsia or low-solute intake; Uosm >100 indicates active antidiuresis and requires identification of the stimulus. [1]","Next assess effective arterial blood volume and UNa. Low UNa, commonly ≤30 mmol/L, supports renal Na avidity from true hypovolemia or reduced effective arterial volume in HF or cirrhosis; higher UNa suggests SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, kidney salt loss, or diuretic exposure. [1]","Diagnose SIADH only after documenting hypotonic hyponatremia, inappropriately concentrated urine, usually UNa >30 mmol/L with adequate intake, clinical euvolemia, and no adrenal, thyroid, kidney, or diuretic explanation. [1]","Order BMP, serum osmolality, Uosm, UNa, urine K, glucose, morning cortisol—with ACTH stimulation testing if equivocal—and TSH with free T4 when indicated. Review thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, opioids, chemotherapy, pulmonary disease, central nervous system disease, pain, and nausea.","Interpret urine studies cautiously after diuretics. Hypokalemia suggests thiazide effect or poor intake, while low BUN and uric acid with increased fractional urate excretion support SIADH but are not independently diagnostic.","Search for the cause rather than reflexively ordering extensive imaging: medication review and targeted history/examination first; obtain CXR or chest CT and neuroimaging when pulmonary malignancy, infection, or central nervous system pathology is clinically plausible."],"mechanism":"Uosm directly tests whether the kidney has turned off ADH-mediated water conservation. UNa then tests whether the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system is defending effective circulating volume, although diuretics and kidney disease can disrupt this readout.","teaching_pearl":"Normal saline may worsen SIADH: the kidney can excrete infused NaCl in concentrated urine while retaining a portion of the accompanying water—a process called desalination.","board_tip":"Do not label a patient SIADH before excluding glucocorticoid deficiency; cortisol deficiency increases ADH release and can be clinically indistinguishable from SIADH."},{"heading":"3. Treatment: Symptoms First, Then Cause and Water Balance","minutes":"3 min","points":["Seizure, coma, marked somnolence, cardiorespiratory distress, or other severe manifestations require immediate hypertonic therapy regardless of presumed chronicity. Per the European 2014 guideline, give 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, recheck Na, and repeat as needed to achieve about a 5 mmol/L initial rise; the US expert panel uses 100 mL over 10 minutes, repeatable up to three times. [1,2]","The therapeutic endpoint of emergency treatment is neurologic improvement or an initial 4–6 mmol/L rise—not a normal Na. A small increase in tonicity substantially reduces cerebral edema while limiting subsequent osmotic demyelination risk. [1,2]","For chronic SIADH without severe symptoms, stop reversible triggers and treat the underlying pulmonary, neurologic, malignant, or medication cause. Guideline-recommended first-line therapy is fluid restriction, often approximately 500 mL/day below urine output, with adequate dietary protein and salt. [1]","Fluid restriction is unlikely to work when Uosm is very high or the urine electrolyte ratio, (UNa + urine K)/serum Na, exceeds 1 because the kidney is producing little or no electrolyte-free water. Increase solute-driven water excretion rather than tightening restriction indefinitely.","The European 2014 guideline suggests oral urea or low-dose loop diuretic plus oral NaCl as equal second-line options for moderate or profound SIADH; this is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Urea increases osmole excretion and obligate urine water loss, while loop diuretics reduce the medullary gradient and impair urine concentration. [1]","Tolvaptan blocks the V2 receptor and produces aquaresis. SALT-1 and SALT-2 showed improved Na in euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia, but not improved survival or neurologic outcomes; the European guideline recommends against vaptans in moderate or profound hyponatremia because of overcorrection and safety concerns, whereas US recommendations permit selected use. [1-3]","Avoid routine isotonic saline for established euvolemic SIADH and avoid demeclocycline or lithium because their nephrotoxicity is not justified. Do not use fluid restriction alone when severe symptoms require rapid hypertonic therapy. [1]"],"mechanism":"Hypertonic saline raises extracellular tonicity and rapidly draws water out of swollen brain cells. Fluid restriction reduces water input; urea increases renal osmole clearance; loop diuretics impair medullary concentration; and tolvaptan directly blocks ADH-mediated AQP2 insertion.","teaching_pearl":"If hypovolemic hyponatremia is suspected, isotonic saline removes the baroreceptor stimulus for ADH—but this can trigger sudden water diuresis and rapid Na correction once volume is restored.","board_tip":"Potassium repletion raises serum Na because K is an effective body cation; count aggressive K replacement as part of the correction strategy."},{"heading":"4. Safety, Complications & Prognosis","minutes":"1-2 min","points":["For chronic or duration-unknown hyponatremia, the European guideline limits correction to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L during each subsequent 24 hours. The US expert panel recommends a stricter maximum of 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours for patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). [1,2]","Major ODS risk factors are initial Na ≤105 mmol/L, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and advanced liver disease. In these patients, target only a 4–6 mmol/L/day increase and regard 8 mmol/L/day as a hard upper limit. [2,4]","Check serum Na every 2–4 hours during active correction and track urine output closely. Abrupt polyuria with falling Uosm signals loss of the ADH effect and impending autocorrection.","If correction is accelerating, stop active therapy and consider desmopressin to halt free-water excretion. If the limit has already been exceeded, desmopressin plus IV dextrose 5% in water can relower Na toward the safe boundary; this is established expert practice supported mainly by observational evidence rather than randomized outcome trials. [2,4]","ODS classically causes delayed dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis, behavioral change, movement disorders, or locked-in syndrome several days after overcorrection. MRI abnormalities may lag behind symptoms, so an initially normal MRI does not exclude it.","Conversely, undertreated acute severe hyponatremia can cause seizures, respiratory arrest, herniation, and death. Safe management balances the immediate danger of cerebral edema against the delayed danger of excessive correction."],"mechanism":"After chronic adaptation, rapid extracellular tonicity restoration draws water from osmolyte-depleted glial cells, injuring oligodendrocytes and disrupting myelin. Desmopressin re-establishes V2-mediated antidiuresis, while dextrose water replaces urinary free-water losses.","teaching_pearl":"The most dangerous correction often occurs after treatment appears successful: resolution of pain, nausea, hypovolemia, cortisol deficiency, or thiazide exposure can abruptly unleash a dilute water diuresis.","board_tip":"Na correction limits are ceilings, not goals. Severe symptoms justify a controlled 4–6 mmol/L initial rise, followed by active prevention of further unintended correction. [2,4]"}]}

talk.subtitle: A physiology-first approach to tonicity, diagnosis, safe correction, and inappropriate antidiuresis
guideline_sources: European Society of Endocrinology/European Society of Intensive Care Medicine/ERA-EDTA Clinical Practice Guideline on Hyponatraemia (2014)
US Expert Panel Recommendations on Hyponatremia (2013)
The supplied KDIGO reference context does not contain a dedicated hyponatremia or SIADH guideline.
summary_points: Hyponatremia is usually a water-balance disorder: persistent ADH activity lowers serum Na by retaining electrolyte-free water, while cerebral osmolyte adaptation determines symptoms.
First confirm hypotonicity, then use urine osmolality (Uosm) to ask whether ADH is active and urine Na (UNa) plus clinical context to identify the stimulus. SIADH remains a diagnosis of exclusion.
Severe neurologic symptoms require immediate 3% saline boluses regardless of chronicity or cause; the initial goal is a 4–6 mmol/L Na increase, not normalization. [1,2]
For chronic SIADH without severe symptoms, treat the cause and restrict fluid first; urea or increased solute with a loop diuretic may be considered when restriction fails. [1]

The common pitfall is overcorrection after the ADH stimulus disappears. Monitor Na and urine output closely, particularly in patients with Na ≤105 mmol/L, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, or advanced liver disease. [2,4]

sections.heading: 1. Physiology: Na Is a Water Signal
points: Serum Na approximates the ratio of exchangeable body Na plus K to total body water; therefore, hyponatremia usually reflects excess water relative to effective body solute—not simply Na depletion.

Hypothalamic osmoreceptors normally suppress ADH when plasma tonicity falls. With low ADH, the collecting duct becomes water-impermeable and generates maximally dilute urine, usually Uosm <100 mOsm/kg.

ADH binds the basolateral V2 receptor on collecting-duct principal cells, activates Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cyclic adenosine monophosphate–protein kinase A signaling, and inserts aquaporin-2 (AQP2) channels into the apical membrane. Water then moves through AQP2 and exits through basolateral AQP3/AQP4 channels.

In SIADH—more precisely, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD)—V2 signaling persists despite hypotonicity and absence of an appropriate hemodynamic stimulus. Retained water mildly expands extracellular volume, provoking natriuresis and suppressing renin and aldosterone; this limits edema and produces apparent euvolemia rather than progressive overt hypervolemia.

The brain initially swells as hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into cells. Over approximately 48 hours, astrocytes extrude K, Na, chloride, and organic osmolytes to restore cell volume; this reduces cerebral edema but makes rapid correction dangerous because brain osmolytes cannot be replaced quickly.
Symptoms track acuity and cerebral edema better than the absolute Na: nausea, headache, confusion, gait instability, seizures, coma, and respiratory arrest can occur when Na falls rapidly.
sections.mechanism: Persistent collecting-duct AQP2 expression prevents appropriate electrolyte-free water excretion. Chronic cerebral osmolyte loss protects against swelling but creates susceptibility to osmotic demyelination when extracellular tonicity rises too quickly.
sections.teaching_pearl: A concentrated urine in hypotonic hyponatremia is the physiologic signature that ADH is active; it does not by itself establish SIADH.
sections.board_tip: Hyponatremia with normal or high measured osmolality is not ordinary hypotonic hyponatremia: consider hyperglycemia, exogenous effective osmoles, or pseudohyponatremia.

sections.heading: 2. Workup: Tonicity → ADH Activity → Effective Volume
points: Confirm the result and measure serum osmolality. Hypotonic hyponatremia generally has measured osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; hyperglycemia causes translocational hyponatremia, while severe hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia can cause pseudohyponatremia with indirect ion-selective electrodes.

Check Uosm before therapy when feasible. Uosm ≤100 mOsm/kg indicates appropriately suppressed ADH and suggests primary polydipsia or low-solute intake; Uosm >100 indicates active antidiuresis and requires identification of the stimulus. [1]

Next assess effective arterial blood volume and UNa. Low UNa, commonly ≤30 mmol/L, supports renal Na avidity from true hypovolemia or reduced effective arterial volume in HF or cirrhosis; higher UNa suggests SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, kidney salt loss, or diuretic exposure. [1]

Diagnose SIADH only after documenting hypotonic hyponatremia, inappropriately concentrated urine, usually UNa >30 mmol/L with adequate intake, clinical euvolemia, and no adrenal, thyroid, kidney, or diuretic explanation. [1]

Order BMP, serum osmolality, Uosm, UNa, urine K, glucose, morning cortisol—with ACTH stimulation testing if equivocal—and TSH with free T4 when indicated. Review thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, opioids, chemotherapy, pulmonary disease, central nervous system disease, pain, and nausea.

Interpret urine studies cautiously after diuretics. Hypokalemia suggests thiazide effect or poor intake, while low BUN and uric acid with increased fractional urate excretion support SIADH but are not independently diagnostic.

Search for the cause rather than reflexively ordering extensive imaging: medication review and targeted history/examination first; obtain CXR or chest CT and neuroimaging when pulmonary malignancy, infection, or central nervous system pathology is clinically plausible.
sections.mechanism: Uosm directly tests whether the kidney has turned off ADH-mediated water conservation. UNa then tests whether the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system is defending effective circulating volume, although diuretics and kidney disease can disrupt this readout.
sections.teaching_pearl: Normal saline may worsen SIADH: the kidney can excrete infused NaCl in concentrated urine while retaining a portion of the accompanying water—a process called desalination.
sections.board_tip: Do not label a patient SIADH before excluding glucocorticoid deficiency; cortisol deficiency increases ADH release and can be clinically indistinguishable from SIADH.

sections.heading: 3. Treatment: Symptoms First, Then Cause and Water Balance
points: Seizure, coma, marked somnolence, cardiorespiratory distress, or other severe manifestations require immediate hypertonic therapy regardless of presumed chronicity. Per the European 2014 guideline, give 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes, recheck Na, and repeat as needed to achieve about a 5 mmol/L initial rise; the US expert panel uses 100 mL over 10 minutes, repeatable up to three times. [1,2]

The therapeutic endpoint of emergency treatment is neurologic improvement or an initial 4–6 mmol/L rise—not a normal Na. A small increase in tonicity substantially reduces cerebral edema while limiting subsequent osmotic demyelination risk. [1,2]

For chronic SIADH without severe symptoms, stop reversible triggers and treat the underlying pulmonary, neurologic, malignant, or medication cause. Guideline-recommended first-line therapy is fluid restriction, often approximately 500 mL/day below urine output, with adequate dietary protein and salt. [1]

Fluid restriction is unlikely to work when Uosm is very high or the urine electrolyte ratio, (UNa + urine K)/serum Na, exceeds 1 because the kidney is producing little or no electrolyte-free water. Increase solute-driven water excretion rather than tightening restriction indefinitely.

The European 2014 guideline suggests oral urea or low-dose loop diuretic plus oral NaCl as equal second-line options for moderate or profound SIADH; this is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence. Urea increases osmole excretion and obligate urine water loss, while loop diuretics reduce the medullary gradient and impair urine concentration. [1]

Tolvaptan blocks the V2 receptor and produces aquaresis. SALT-1 and SALT-2 showed improved Na in euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia, but not improved survival or neurologic outcomes; the European guideline recommends against vaptans in moderate or profound hyponatremia because of overcorrection and safety concerns, whereas US recommendations permit selected use. [1-3]

Avoid routine isotonic saline for established euvolemic SIADH and avoid demeclocycline or lithium because their nephrotoxicity is not justified. Do not use fluid restriction alone when severe symptoms require rapid hypertonic therapy. [1]
sections.mechanism: Hypertonic saline raises extracellular tonicity and rapidly draws water out of swollen brain cells. Fluid restriction reduces water input; urea increases renal osmole clearance; loop diuretics impair medullary concentration; and tolvaptan directly blocks ADH-mediated AQP2 insertion.
sections.teaching_pearl: If hypovolemic hyponatremia is suspected, isotonic saline removes the baroreceptor stimulus for ADH—but this can trigger sudden water diuresis and rapid Na correction once volume is restored.
sections.board_tip: Potassium repletion raises serum Na because K is an effective body cation; count aggressive K replacement as part of the correction strategy.

sections.heading: 4. Safety, Complications & Prognosis
points: For chronic or duration-unknown hyponatremia, the European guideline limits correction to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L during each subsequent 24 hours. The US expert panel recommends a stricter maximum of 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours for patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). [1,2]

Major ODS risk factors are initial Na ≤105 mmol/L, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and advanced liver disease. In these patients, target only a 4–6 mmol/L/day increase and regard 8 mmol/L/day as a hard upper limit. [2,4]
Check serum Na every 2–4 hours during active correction and track urine output closely. Abrupt polyuria with falling Uosm signals loss of the ADH effect and impending autocorrection.

If correction is accelerating, stop active therapy and consider desmopressin to halt free-water excretion. If the limit has already been exceeded, desmopressin plus IV dextrose 5% in water can relower Na toward the safe boundary; this is established expert practice supported mainly by observational evidence rather than randomized outcome trials. [2,4]

ODS classically causes delayed dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis, behavioral change, movement disorders, or locked-in syndrome several days after overcorrection. MRI abnormalities may lag behind symptoms, so an initially normal MRI does not exclude it.

Conversely, undertreated acute severe hyponatremia can cause seizures, respiratory arrest, herniation, and death. Safe management balances the immediate danger of cerebral edema against the delayed danger of excessive correction.
sections.mechanism: After chronic adaptation, rapid extracellular tonicity restoration draws water from osmolyte-depleted glial cells, injuring oligodendrocytes and disrupting myelin. Desmopressin re-establishes V2-mediated antidiuresis, while dextrose water replaces urinary free-water losses.
sections.teaching_pearl: The most dangerous correction often occurs after treatment appears successful: resolution of pain, nausea, hypovolemia, cortisol deficiency, or thiazide exposure can abruptly unleash a dilute water diuresis.
sections.board_tip: Na correction limits are ceilings, not goals. Severe symptoms justify a controlled 4–6 mmol/L initial rise, followed by active prevention of further unintended correction. [2,4]

Serum sodium tells you about tonicity, not total body sodium.","Three labs sort out nearly every case: serum osmolality (is it truly hypotonic?), urine osmolality (is ADH on? >100 mOsm/kg = yes), and urine sodium (>30-40 mEq/L with euvolemia = SIADH; <20-30 = hypovolemia or an effective arterial volume problem).","SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring hypotonic hyponatremia, urine osm >100, urine Na >30, clinical euvolemia, and normal thyroid and adrenal function. Low serum uric acid with a fractional excretion of urate >12% strongly supports it.","Symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, obtundation, vomiting) is treated with 3% saline 100-150 mL boluses targeting a 4-6 mEq/L rise — enough to reverse cerebral edema — regardless of chronicity [1,2].","Correction speed, not the nadir sodium, causes osmotic demyelination: cap the rise at 8-10 mEq/L per 24 h, and 8 mEq/L or less in high-risk patients (Na <105, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease) [1,2].","Chronic SIADH is treated by targeting the water: fluid restriction first, then increasing solute load (salt tablets + loop diuretic, or urea). Clin J Am Soc Nephrol","year":2012,"society":"Cohort study","url":"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22246281/","type":"study"}],"sections":[{"heading":"Physiology: How the Kidney Normally Defends Tonicity","minutes":"3 min","points":["Sodium concentration is a ratio, not a quantity: [Na] ≈ (exchangeable Na + K) / total body water. Because water crosses cell membranes freely and Na is the dominant effective extracellular osmole, [Na] is the clinical readout of TONICITY — the force that shrinks or swells brain cells. It says nothing about total body sodium: a patient in florid HF is sodium-overloaded and hyponatremic simultaneously.","Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense as little as a 1-2% rise in tonicity and trigger ADH release from the posterior pituitary. Below a plasma osmolality of ~275-280 mOsm/kg, ADH should be fully suppressed and the kidney should dump maximally dilute urine (osm 50-100 mOsm/kg), clearing up to ~15-20 L/day of free water.","ADH binds the V2 receptor on the basolateral principal cell → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation and exocytic trafficking of aquaporin-2 vesicles into the APICAL membrane. AQP3/AQP4 sit constitutively on the basolateral side, so inserting AQP2 completes a transcellular water pathway. No AQP2 in the apical membrane = no water reabsorption in the collecting duct, no matter how concentrated the interstitium.","Diluting urine requires two things: (1) generation of solute-free water by the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, where NKCC2 strips NaCl out of tubular fluid and builds the medullary gradient, and (2) adequate distal delivery of filtrate. Loop diuretics abolish the gradient (so they impair concentrating ability and are therapeutically useful); thiazides block NaCl reabsorption in the water-impermeable distal convoluted tubule WITHOUT touching the medullary gradient, which is exactly why thiazides — not loops — are the classic drug cause of hyponatremia.","Excretion also requires SOLUTE. Urine volume = solute excretion ÷ urine osmolality. A patient eating almost no protein or salt (beer potomania, tea-and-toast) may excrete only 200-250 mOsm/day; even at a maximally dilute 50 mOsm/kg that caps free water clearance at ~4-5 L/day. Exceed it and you become hyponatremic with ADH fully off.","Brain adaptation is the reason chronicity matters more than the number. Within minutes astrocytes extrude Na, K, and Cl; over 24-48 h they export organic osmolytes (myo-inositol, taurine, glutamate, glutamine) via transporters and channels. This normalizes brain volume — patients tolerate a Na of 115 while ambulatory — but it also strips the brain of the osmolytes it needs to re-swell, and osmolyte re-accumulation takes days. Rapid correction of an adapted brain shrinks cells and demyelinates."],"mechanism":"Every hypotonic hyponatremia is a failure of renal free-water excretion. Mechanistically that means either (a) ADH is being secreted non-osmotically (V2 → cAMP → apical AQP2 → water retention), or (b) rarely, ADH is off but solute delivery is too low to carry the water out. Fixing hyponatremia therefore means removing the ADH stimulus, blocking the V2 receptor, or giving solute — not giving sodium per se.","teaching_pearl":"Ask the mechanistic question first: 'Is ADH on or off?' The urine osmolality answers it in one number. Urine osm <100 mOsm/kg means ADH is appropriately suppressed and the problem is water intake or solute deficiency (primary polydipsia, beer potomania, low-solute diet). Urine osm >100 means ADH is acting when it shouldn't be — now you only need to decide whether that ADH is appropriate (volume depletion, HF, cirrhosis) or inappropriate (SIADH).","board_tip":"Check osmolality before you commit: hyperglycemia, mannitol, and glycine cause TRANSLOCATIONAL (truly hypotonic-appearing but hypertonic) hyponatremia, while severe hypertriglyceridemia or paraproteinemia cause PSEUDOhyponatremia with a normal measured osmolality and normal tonicity."},{"heading":"Pathophysiology of SIADH and the Differential It Sits In","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["SIADH = non-osmotic ADH release (or a gain-of-function V2 receptor in nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis). Water is retained → volume expands modestly → ANP/BNP rise and aldosterone falls → the kidney NATRIURESES to restore volume. That is why SIADH patients are clinically euvolemic with a high urine sodium: they reach a new steady state where water is retained but sodium is not. Weight gain is typically only 2-3 L — no edema, because the retained water distributes across total body water.","Because volume is expanded rather than depleted, proximal tubular reabsorption is decreased. This produces the SIADH fingerprint: LOW serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL) and a fractional excretion of urate >12%, plus a low-normal BUN. Hypovolemic hyponatremia does the opposite — high urate, BUN/Cr ratio >20.","Diagnostic criteria (Schwartz-Bartter, as codified in the 2014 European guideline): serum osm <275, urine osm >100, urine Na >30 mEq/L, clinical euvolemia, no diuretic use, and normal adrenal and thyroid function. It is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION — you must rule out hypothyroidism and hypocortisolism, both of which impair water excretion [1].","Etiologies, grouped by mechanism: (1) CNS — stroke, hemorrhage, meningitis, trauma (loss of tonic inhibition of ADH release); (2) pulmonary — pneumonia, TB, positive-pressure ventilation (reduced left atrial filling misread as hypovolemia); (3) ECTOPIC production — small cell lung cancer above all, also head/neck squamous cell; (4) drugs — SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, antipsychotics, MDMA, desmopressin, NSAIDs (potentiate ADH action by removing prostaglandin antagonism of AQP2); (5) pain, nausea, and the postoperative state — extremely potent non-osmotic ADH stimuli and the reason a young postoperative patient given hypotonic fluid can seize.","Two mimics worth naming. RESET OSMOSTAT: ADH regulation is intact but the threshold is shifted down — a stable Na of 125-130 that both dilutes and concentrates appropriately with water loading; it needs no treatment. CEREBRAL/RENAL SALT WASTING: after subarachnoid hemorrhage, true natriuresis with volume DEPLETION; the labs overlap heavily with SIADH but the patient is hypovolemic, so treatment (saline) is the opposite of water restriction. Urate stays low in both, which is why volume assessment is the discriminator.","Do not forget hypovolemic hyponatremia with a HIGH urine sodium: diuretics (especially thiazides), adrenal insufficiency, and salt-wasting nephropathy break the urine-Na rule. And thiazide hyponatremia is often a multi-hit event — impaired dilution plus increased thirst plus low body mass in older women."],"mechanism":"In SIADH the V2/AQP2 axis is switched on regardless of tonicity, so ingested water is retained. The secondary natriuresis (ANP up, aldosterone down) is a normal volume-defense response to that water retention — it makes the patient look euvolemic with a high urine Na, and it is why simply giving isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen the sodium when urine osmolality exceeds the infusate osmolality: the kidney keeps the water and excretes the salt.","teaching_pearl":"Isotonic saline (154 mEq/L Na, 308 mOsm/kg) in a patient whose urine osmolality is 600 mOsm/kg is a hyponatremia-generating maneuver: the kidney excretes the 308 mOsm of solute in ~500 mL of urine and retains ~500 mL of free water. If a fluid challenge fails to raise the Na, you have both diagnosed SIADH and worsened it — stop the saline.","board_tip":"A new SIADH in an older smoker mandates chest imaging for small cell lung cancer. In a young person, ask about MDMA/ecstasy plus water loading, marathon running with hypotonic fluid replacement, and SSRI initiation within the last 2-4 weeks."},{"heading":"Workup: Three Numbers and a Volume Exam","minutes":"2 min","points":["Step 1 — Confirm hypotonicity: measured serum osmolality. If normal or high, you are dealing with pseudohyponatremia or translocational hyponatremia and the entire treatment algorithm changes.","Step 2 — Urine osmolality: <100 = ADH off (polydipsia, low solute intake, beer potomania); >100 = ADH acting.","Step 3 — Urine sodium (on a spot sample, before diuretics or saline): <20-30 mEq/L → hypovolemia or effective arterial underfilling (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome); >30-40 mEq/L with euvolemia → SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, diuretics, or salt wasting [1].","Step 4 — Rule out the endocrine mimics and confirm the SIADH signature: TSH, morning cortisol (or cosyntropin stimulation if suspicious), serum uric acid and fractional excretion of urate, BUN/Cr, potassium, glucose, and a medication review. Add a CXR and consider CT chest/head based on the clinical picture.","Assess volume status deliberately and admit its imprecision — orthostatics, JVP, mucous membranes, skin turgor, and axillary sweat are all only moderately reliable. When genuinely uncertain between hypovolemia and SIADH, a 500 mL-1 L isotonic saline challenge with a repeat Na in 4-6 h is diagnostic: the Na rises in hypovolemia and stays flat or falls in SIADH.","Grade the severity by BOTH biochemistry and symptoms, because they drive different urgency: the 2014 European guideline splits into moderate (125-129), profound (<125), and — the decision that matters — 'moderately severe' (nausea, confusion, headache) versus 'severe' (vomiting, seizure, somnolence, coma, cardiorespiratory distress) symptoms [1]. Also establish DURATION: <48 h documented is acute; otherwise treat as chronic."],"teaching_pearl":"Potassium is a co-solute in the tonicity equation. Repleting a hypokalemic patient shifts K intracellularly in exchange for Na moving out — the serum sodium rises without a drop of hypertonic saline. Count that anticipated rise in your 24-hour correction budget or you will overshoot.","board_tip":"Urine sodium <20 mEq/L in a hyponatremic patient with ascites and a low urate points to cirrhosis with effective arterial underfilling and secondary ADH excess — not SIADH. Treat the splanchnic vasodilation/volume problem; water restriction and albumin, not saline."},{"heading":"Treatment: Match the Intervention to the Mechanism","minutes":"3 min","points":["SEVERE SYMPTOMS (seizure, coma, vomiting, respiratory compromise) — treat as a neurologic emergency regardless of chronicity: 3% hypertonic saline 100-150 mL IV over 10-20 min, repeat up to 2-3 times, targeting a prompt 4-6 mEq/L rise. That magnitude is chosen physiologically — it is roughly what is needed to reverse cerebral edema and abort seizures, and it is far below the osmotic demyelination threshold. Both the 2014 European guideline and the US expert panel endorse the bolus strategy [1,2].","SALSA (JAMA Intern Med 2021) randomized rapid intermittent bolus versus slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline in symptomatic hyponatremia: efficacy was equivalent, and boluses required fewer therapeutic relowering interventions with less overcorrection. Boluses are also faster to administer and do not need central access [3].","CORRECTION LIMITS — the number to memorize: no more than 8-10 mEq/L in the first 24 h and 18 mEq/L in 48 h; drop the 24-h cap to ≤8 mEq/L (many experts say 4-6) in patients at high osmotic demyelination syndrome risk — serum Na <105, hypokalemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, advanced liver disease, or pregnancy [1,2]. Recheck sodium every 2-4 h during active correction.","BEWARE THE AUTOCORRECTION TRAP: when the ADH stimulus is removed — volume repletion in hypovolemia, stopping a thiazide or SSRI, treating adrenal insufficiency, resolving nausea — ADH shuts off and the patient produces liters of maximally dilute urine, self-correcting far faster than any infusion. A brisk urine output with urine osm falling below 100 mOsm/kg is your warning. Rescue with free water (oral or D5W) and/or desmopressin 1-2 mcg IV to re-clamp ADH.","CHRONIC SIADH, stepwise: (1) fluid restriction, usually <800-1000 mL/day and always less than urine output; it fails when the urine-to-serum electrolyte ratio is high (urine Na + K ≥ serum Na) or urine osm >500. (2) Increase solute: oral sodium chloride tablets combined with a loop diuretic — the loop dismantles the medullary gradient so the collecting duct cannot concentrate, converting the AQP2 pathway into a dead end. (3) Urea 15-30 g/day, an osmotic diuretic that drives free water excretion; it is effective, cheap, and safe in long-term SIADH cohorts, though palatability limits it [1,5].","VAPTANS — know the discordance. Tolvaptan is a selective oral V2 antagonist that blocks AQP2 trafficking and produces pure aquaresis; SALT-1 and SALT-2 (NEJM 2006) showed significant sodium increases at day 4 and day 30 versus placebo, and it is FDA-approved for euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia [4]. But the 2014 European guideline recommends AGAINST vaptans (no demonstrated mortality or symptom benefit, overcorrection risk, cost), whereas the US expert panel endorses use in selected patients [1,2]. If used: start inpatient with no fluid restriction for the first 24-48 h, monitor sodium every 6-8 h, and observe the FDA limits — ≤30 days and avoid in liver disease because of hepatotoxicity signals from the ADPKD program. Do not use vaptans in hypovolemic hyponatremia.","Demeclocycline (induces a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by interfering with collecting-duct cAMP generation) is now largely historical — nephrotoxicity, photosensitivity, and unpredictable response.","Prevention is undervalued: avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids in postoperative patients and anyone with a non-osmotic ADH stimulus, and review the medication list for thiazides, SSRIs, and carbamazepine before reaching for a drug to treat the consequence."],"mechanism":"3% saline works because it raises extracellular tonicity, pulling water out of swollen astrocytes and lowering intracranial pressure — it treats cerebral edema, not the sodium number. Chronic therapies each attack a different node: fluid restriction reduces the water input, salt tablets plus a loop increase the solute output while crippling the countercurrent gradient, urea obligates osmotic water loss, and tolvaptan blocks V2 directly so AQP2 never reaches the apical membrane.","teaching_pearl":"The DDAVP clamp is the elegant approach for high-risk profound hyponatremia: give desmopressin to fix the urine output at a maximally concentrated state, then raise the sodium with 3% saline at a rate you fully control. talk.title: Hyponatremia & SIADH: Water, Not Salt
talk.subtitle: From aquaporin trafficking to the 3% saline bolus — a mechanistic approach to the most common electrolyte disorder in the hospital
guideline_sources: European Society of Endocrinology / ESICM / ERA-EDTA Clinical Practice Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Hyponatraemia (2014)
US Expert Panel Recommendations on Hyponatremia (Verbalis et al., Am J Med 2013)
Landmark trials: SALT-1/SALT-2 (tolvaptan, NEJM 2006), SALSA (JAMA Intern Med 2021)
summary_points: Hyponatremia is a disorder of WATER, not sodium: the defect is an inability to excrete free water, almost always because ADH is present when it should be off. Serum sodium tells you about tonicity, not total body sodium.

Three labs sort out nearly every case: serum osmolality (is it truly hypotonic?), urine osmolality (is ADH on? >100 mOsm/kg = yes), and urine sodium (>30-40 mEq/L with euvolemia = SIADH; <20-30 = hypovolemia or an effective arterial volume problem).

SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring hypotonic hyponatremia, urine osm >100, urine Na >30, clinical euvolemia, and normal thyroid and adrenal function. Low serum uric acid with a fractional excretion of urate >12% strongly supports it.
Symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, obtundation, vomiting) is treated with 3% saline 100-150 mL boluses targeting a 4-6 mEq/L rise — enough to reverse cerebral edema — regardless of chronicity [1,2].

Correction speed, not the nadir sodium, causes osmotic demyelination: cap the rise at 8-10 mEq/L per 24 h, and 8 mEq/L or less in high-risk patients (Na <105, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease) [1,2].

Chronic SIADH is treated by targeting the water: fluid restriction first, then increasing solute load (salt tablets + loop diuretic, or urea). Tolvaptan works mechanistically but the 2014 European guideline recommends against vaptans while the US expert panel supports selected use — an explicit guideline discordance [1,2,4].

sections.heading: Physiology: How the Kidney Normally Defends Tonicity
points: Sodium concentration is a ratio, not a quantity: [Na] ≈ (exchangeable Na + K) / total body water. Because water crosses cell membranes freely and Na is the dominant effective extracellular osmole, [Na] is the clinical readout of TONICITY — the force that shrinks or swells brain cells. It says nothing about total body sodium: a patient in florid HF is sodium-overloaded and hyponatremic simultaneously.

Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense as little as a 1-2% rise in tonicity and trigger ADH release from the posterior pituitary. Below a plasma osmolality of ~275-280 mOsm/kg, ADH should be fully suppressed and the kidney should dump maximally dilute urine (osm 50-100 mOsm/kg), clearing up to ~15-20 L/day of free water.

ADH binds the V2 receptor on the basolateral principal cell → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation and exocytic trafficking of aquaporin-2 vesicles into the APICAL membrane. AQP3/AQP4 sit constitutively on the basolateral side, so inserting AQP2 completes a transcellular water pathway. No AQP2 in the apical membrane = no water reabsorption in the collecting duct, no matter how concentrated the interstitium.

Diluting urine requires two things: (1) generation of solute-free water by the water-impermeable thick ascending limb, where NKCC2 strips NaCl out of tubular fluid and builds the medullary gradient, and (2) adequate distal delivery of filtrate. Loop diuretics abolish the gradient (so they impair concentrating ability and are therapeutically useful); thiazides block NaCl reabsorption in the water-impermeable distal convoluted tubule WITHOUT touching the medullary gradient, which is exactly why thiazides — not loops — are the classic drug cause of hyponatremia.

Excretion also requires SOLUTE. Urine volume = solute excretion ÷ urine osmolality. A patient eating almost no protein or salt (beer potomania, tea-and-toast) may excrete only 200-250 mOsm/day; even at a maximally dilute 50 mOsm/kg that caps free water clearance at ~4-5 L/day. Exceed it and you become hyponatremic with ADH fully off.

Brain adaptation is the reason chronicity matters more than the number. Within minutes astrocytes extrude Na, K, and Cl; over 24-48 h they export organic osmolytes (myo-inositol, taurine, glutamate, glutamine) via transporters and channels. This normalizes brain volume — patients tolerate a Na of 115 while ambulatory — but it also strips the brain of the osmolytes it needs to re-swell, and osmolyte re-accumulation takes days. Rapid correction of an adapted brain shrinks cells and demyelinates.
sections.mechanism: Every hypotonic hyponatremia is a failure of renal free-water excretion. Mechanistically that means either (a) ADH is being secreted non-osmotically (V2 → cAMP → apical AQP2 → water retention), or (b) rarely, ADH is off but solute delivery is too low to carry the water out. Fixing hyponatremia therefore means removing the ADH stimulus, blocking the V2 receptor, or giving solute — not giving sodium per se.
sections.teaching_pearl: Ask the mechanistic question first: 'Is ADH on or off?' The urine osmolality answers it in one number. Urine osm <100 mOsm/kg means ADH is appropriately suppressed and the problem is water intake or solute deficiency (primary polydipsia, beer potomania, low-solute diet). Urine osm >100 means ADH is acting when it shouldn't be — now you only need to decide whether that ADH is appropriate (volume depletion, HF, cirrhosis) or inappropriate (SIADH).
sections.board_tip: Check osmolality before you commit: hyperglycemia, mannitol, and glycine cause TRANSLOCATIONAL (truly hypotonic-appearing but hypertonic) hyponatremia, while severe hypertriglyceridemia or paraproteinemia cause PSEUDOhyponatremia with a normal measured osmolality and normal tonicity.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology of SIADH and the Differential It Sits In
points: SIADH = non-osmotic ADH release (or a gain-of-function V2 receptor in nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis). Water is retained → volume expands modestly → ANP/BNP rise and aldosterone falls → the kidney NATRIURESES to restore volume. That is why SIADH patients are clinically euvolemic with a high urine sodium: they reach a new steady state where water is retained but sodium is not. Weight gain is typically only 2-3 L — no edema, because the retained water distributes across total body water.

Because volume is expanded rather than depleted, proximal tubular reabsorption is decreased. This produces the SIADH fingerprint: LOW serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL) and a fractional excretion of urate >12%, plus a low-normal BUN. Hypovolemic hyponatremia does the opposite — high urate, BUN/Cr ratio >20.

Diagnostic criteria (Schwartz-Bartter, as codified in the 2014 European guideline): serum osm <275, urine osm >100, urine Na >30 mEq/L, clinical euvolemia, no diuretic use, and normal adrenal and thyroid function. It is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION — you must rule out hypothyroidism and hypocortisolism, both of which impair water excretion [1].

Etiologies, grouped by mechanism: (1) CNS — stroke, hemorrhage, meningitis, trauma (loss of tonic inhibition of ADH release); (2) pulmonary — pneumonia, TB, positive-pressure ventilation (reduced left atrial filling misread as hypovolemia); (3) ECTOPIC production — small cell lung cancer above all, also head/neck squamous cell; (4) drugs — SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, antipsychotics, MDMA, desmopressin, NSAIDs (potentiate ADH action by removing prostaglandin antagonism of AQP2); (5) pain, nausea, and the postoperative state — extremely potent non-osmotic ADH stimuli and the reason a young postoperative patient given hypotonic fluid can seize.

Two mimics worth naming. RESET OSMOSTAT: ADH regulation is intact but the threshold is shifted down — a stable Na of 125-130 that both dilutes and concentrates appropriately with water loading; it needs no treatment. CEREBRAL/RENAL SALT WASTING: after subarachnoid hemorrhage, true natriuresis with volume DEPLETION; the labs overlap heavily with SIADH but the patient is hypovolemic, so treatment (saline) is the opposite of water restriction. Urate stays low in both, which is why volume assessment is the discriminator.

Do not forget hypovolemic hyponatremia with a HIGH urine sodium: diuretics (especially thiazides), adrenal insufficiency, and salt-wasting nephropathy break the urine-Na rule. And thiazide hyponatremia is often a multi-hit event — impaired dilution plus increased thirst plus low body mass in older women.
sections.mechanism: In SIADH the V2/AQP2 axis is switched on regardless of tonicity, so ingested water is retained. The secondary natriuresis (ANP up, aldosterone down) is a normal volume-defense response to that water retention — it makes the patient look euvolemic with a high urine Na, and it is why simply giving isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen the sodium when urine osmolality exceeds the infusate osmolality: the kidney keeps the water and excretes the salt.
sections.teaching_pearl: Isotonic saline (154 mEq/L Na, 308 mOsm/kg) in a patient whose urine osmolality is 600 mOsm/kg is a hyponatremia-generating maneuver: the kidney excretes the 308 mOsm of solute in ~500 mL of urine and retains ~500 mL of free water. If a fluid challenge fails to raise the Na, you have both diagnosed SIADH and worsened it — stop the saline.
sections.board_tip: A new SIADH in an older smoker mandates chest imaging for small cell lung cancer. In a young person, ask about MDMA/ecstasy plus water loading, marathon running with hypotonic fluid replacement, and SSRI initiation within the last 2-4 weeks.

sections.heading: Workup: Three Numbers and a Volume Exam
points: Step 1 — Confirm hypotonicity: measured serum osmolality. If normal or high, you are dealing with pseudohyponatremia or translocational hyponatremia and the entire treatment algorithm changes.
Step 2 — Urine osmolality: <100 = ADH off (polydipsia, low solute intake, beer potomania); >100 = ADH acting.

Step 3 — Urine sodium (on a spot sample, before diuretics or saline): <20-30 mEq/L → hypovolemia or effective arterial underfilling (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome); >30-40 mEq/L with euvolemia → SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, diuretics, or salt wasting [1].

Step 4 — Rule out the endocrine mimics and confirm the SIADH signature: TSH, morning cortisol (or cosyntropin stimulation if suspicious), serum uric acid and fractional excretion of urate, BUN/Cr, potassium, glucose, and a medication review. Add a CXR and consider CT chest/head based on the clinical picture.

Assess volume status deliberately and admit its imprecision — orthostatics, JVP, mucous membranes, skin turgor, and axillary sweat are all only moderately reliable. When genuinely uncertain between hypovolemia and SIADH, a 500 mL-1 L isotonic saline challenge with a repeat Na in 4-6 h is diagnostic: the Na rises in hypovolemia and stays flat or falls in SIADH.

Grade the severity by BOTH biochemistry and symptoms, because they drive different urgency: the 2014 European guideline splits into moderate (125-129), profound (<125), and — the decision that matters — 'moderately severe' (nausea, confusion, headache) versus 'severe' (vomiting, seizure, somnolence, coma, cardiorespiratory distress) symptoms [1]. Also establish DURATION: <48 h documented is acute; otherwise treat as chronic.
sections.teaching_pearl: Potassium is a co-solute in the tonicity equation. Repleting a hypokalemic patient shifts K intracellularly in exchange for Na moving out — the serum sodium rises without a drop of hypertonic saline. Count that anticipated rise in your 24-hour correction budget or you will overshoot.
sections.board_tip: Urine sodium <20 mEq/L in a hyponatremic patient with ascites and a low urate points to cirrhosis with effective arterial underfilling and secondary ADH excess — not SIADH. Treat the splanchnic vasodilation/volume problem; water restriction and albumin, not saline.

sections.heading: Treatment: Match the Intervention to the Mechanism
points: SEVERE SYMPTOMS (seizure, coma, vomiting, respiratory compromise) — treat as a neurologic emergency regardless of chronicity: 3% hypertonic saline 100-150 mL IV over 10-20 min, repeat up to 2-3 times, targeting a prompt 4-6 mEq/L rise. That magnitude is chosen physiologically — it is roughly what is needed to reverse cerebral edema and abort seizures, and it is far below the osmotic demyelination threshold. Both the 2014 European guideline and the US expert panel endorse the bolus strategy [1,2].

SALSA (JAMA Intern Med 2021) randomized rapid intermittent bolus versus slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline in symptomatic hyponatremia: efficacy was equivalent, and boluses required fewer therapeutic relowering interventions with less overcorrection. Boluses are also faster to administer and do not need central access [3].

CORRECTION LIMITS — the number to memorize: no more than 8-10 mEq/L in the first 24 h and 18 mEq/L in 48 h; drop the 24-h cap to ≤8 mEq/L (many experts say 4-6) in patients at high osmotic demyelination syndrome risk — serum Na <105, hypokalemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, advanced liver disease, or pregnancy [1,2]. Recheck sodium every 2-4 h during active correction.

BEWARE THE AUTOCORRECTION TRAP: when the ADH stimulus is removed — volume repletion in hypovolemia, stopping a thiazide or SSRI, treating adrenal insufficiency, resolving nausea — ADH shuts off and the patient produces liters of maximally dilute urine, self-correcting far faster than any infusion. A brisk urine output with urine osm falling below 100 mOsm/kg is your warning. Rescue with free water (oral or D5W) and/or desmopressin 1-2 mcg IV to re-clamp ADH.

CHRONIC SIADH, stepwise: (1) fluid restriction, usually <800-1000 mL/day and always less than urine output; it fails when the urine-to-serum electrolyte ratio is high (urine Na + K ≥ serum Na) or urine osm >500. (2) Increase solute: oral sodium chloride tablets combined with a loop diuretic — the loop dismantles the medullary gradient so the collecting duct cannot concentrate, converting the AQP2 pathway into a dead end. (3) Urea 15-30 g/day, an osmotic diuretic that drives free water excretion; it is effective, cheap, and safe in long-term SIADH cohorts, though palatability limits it [1,5].

VAPTANS — know the discordance. Tolvaptan is a selective oral V2 antagonist that blocks AQP2 trafficking and produces pure aquaresis; SALT-1 and SALT-2 (NEJM 2006) showed significant sodium increases at day 4 and day 30 versus placebo, and it is FDA-approved for euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia [4]. But the 2014 European guideline recommends AGAINST vaptans (no demonstrated mortality or symptom benefit, overcorrection risk, cost), whereas the US expert panel endorses use in selected patients [1,2]. If used: start inpatient with no fluid restriction for the first 24-48 h, monitor sodium every 6-8 h, and observe the FDA limits — ≤30 days and avoid in liver disease because of hepatotoxicity signals from the ADPKD program. Do not use vaptans in hypovolemic hyponatremia.
Demeclocycline (induces a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by interfering with collecting-duct cAMP generation) is now largely historical — nephrotoxicity, photosensitivity, and unpredictable response.

Prevention is undervalued: avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids in postoperative patients and anyone with a non-osmotic ADH stimulus, and review the medication list for thiazides, SSRIs, and carbamazepine before reaching for a drug to treat the consequence.
sections.mechanism: 3% saline works because it raises extracellular tonicity, pulling water out of swollen astrocytes and lowering intracranial pressure — it treats cerebral edema, not the sodium number. Chronic therapies each attack a different node: fluid restriction reduces the water input, salt tablets plus a loop increase the solute output while crippling the countercurrent gradient, urea obligates osmotic water loss, and tolvaptan blocks V2 directly so AQP2 never reaches the apical membrane.
sections.teaching_pearl: The DDAVP clamp is the elegant approach for high-risk profound hyponatremia: give desmopressin to fix the urine output at a maximally concentrated state, then raise the sodium with 3% saline at a rate you fully control. This converts an unpredictable renal variable into a pure arithmetic problem and prevents the sudden aquaresis that causes most overcorrection.
sections.board_tip: Osmotic demyelination presents 2-6 days AFTER correction — a patient who improved now develops dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, pseudobulbar affect, or locked-in syndrome, with MRI changes lagging behind the clinical picture. If you discover you have overshot within the first 24 h, actively RELOWER with D5W ± desmopressin; that is a recognized rescue maneuver [1,2].

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Hyponatremia is the most common electrolyte abnormality in hospitalized patients, present in roughly 15-30% depending on the threshold used, and is independently associated with longer length of stay, higher readmission rates, and increased in-hospital and long-term mortality across HF, cirrhosis, pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism cohorts.

Interpret that mortality signal carefully: most of it reflects severity of the underlying disease (the sodium is a barometer of neurohormonal activation), and no trial has shown that correcting the sodium reduces mortality — which is precisely the argument the 2014 European guideline makes against reflexive pharmacologic correction with vaptans [1,4].

'Asymptomatic' chronic hyponatremia is not benign at the patient level: mild chronic hyponatremia is associated with gait instability, attentional deficits, falls, osteoporosis and fracture, and these gait and cognitive deficits improve with correction — a meaningful outcome even without a mortality signal [2].

Osmotic demyelination syndrome is rare (well under 1% of hyponatremia admissions) but devastating: outcomes range from full recovery to permanent quadriparesis or death, with roughly half of survivors left with significant deficits. Its risk is driven by the RATE of correction plus the host factors (Na <105, hypokalemia, malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, liver disease) — meaning it is largely iatrogenic and largely preventable [1,2].

In SIADH, prognosis tracks the cause: drug-induced and pain/nausea/postoperative SIADH resolve completely with removal of the stimulus; SIADH from small cell lung cancer improves with chemotherapy and recurs with relapse, functioning as a tumor marker; CNS-related SIADH is usually transient over days to weeks.

Practical bottom line: the two things that change patient-level outcomes are (1) recognizing and rapidly treating true symptomatic cerebral edema, and (2) not correcting too fast. Everything else is mechanism-directed management of the underlying disease.
sections.teaching_pearl: Two errors kill or maim in this disease, and they are opposites: failing to give 3% saline to the seizing patient with acute water intoxication, and giving too much sodium too fast to the chronically adapted patient. Sorting acute from chronic — and symptomatic from asymptomatic — is the single highest-yield decision in the entire algorithm.
sections.board_tip: If a stem gives you a Na of 118 in a patient who is alert, ambulatory, and asymptomatic, the answer is almost never hypertonic saline — it is identify and remove the ADH stimulus plus fluid restriction, with a deliberate correction cap of 8-10 mEq/L per 24 h.

claude_errors: Overstates SALSA (2021): the trial's primary outcome (overcorrection: 17.2% rapid bolus vs 24.2% slow infusion) was NOT statistically significant; only the need for therapeutic relowering differed. Stating boluses produced 'less overcorrection' misrepresents the result.

Lists pregnancy among osmotic demyelination risk factors — not an established ODS risk factor in either the 2014 ESE guideline or the 2013 US panel (recognized factors are Na ≤105, hypokalemia, alcoholism, malnutrition, advanced liver disease).
Minor overstatement: maximal free-water clearance of '15–20 L/day' is above the usually cited ~10–15 L/day ceiling.

The common trap is choosing fluid restriction because SIADH is present; a seizure makes emergency hypertonic saline—not chronic SIADH therapy—the immediate priority. [1]
teaching_points: Neurologic symptom severity, rather than the presumed duration or cause of hyponatremia, determines the need for emergency hypertonic saline. [1]
After initial improvement, limit correction to no more than 10 mEq/L during the first 24 hours and 8 mEq/L during each subsequent 24-hour period. [1]
Fluid restriction and oral urea are therapies for stable SIADH, not substitutes for hypertonic saline during a hyponatremic seizure. [1]
summary_points: Seizure plus confirmed hypotonic hyponatremia mandates immediate bolus 3% saline; diagnostic evaluation and longer-term SIADH therapy follow stabilization. [1]

question.stem:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for 3 days of progressive nausea, gait instability, and confusion. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and a recently discovered hilar mass awaiting biopsy. He takes amlodipine but no diuretics. At urgent care, he received 1 L of 0.9% saline; 4 hours later, his serum sodium had decreased. His daughter reports a 1-minute generalized seizure during transport.

Temperature 36.8 C, BP 136/78 mm Hg, HR 82/min, RR 16/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. He is somnolent but arousable. Mucous membranes are moist, jugular venous pressure is normal, and edema is absent.

Sodium is 116 mEq/L, decreased from 119 mEq/L; glucose 96 mg/dL, serum osmolality 244 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 78 mEq/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, and morning cortisol 18 mcg/dL.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation:
The 2014 European hyponatremia guideline strongly recommends, despite low-certainty evidence (grade 1D), immediate IV administration of 150 mL of 3% saline over 20 minutes for hyponatremia with severe neurologic symptoms. The bolus may be repeated while checking serum sodium until an increase of approximately 5 mEq/L is achieved or symptoms improve.

This patient has a hyponatremic seizure and therefore requires emergency hypertonic saline regardless of whether the hyponatremia is acute or chronic. Low serum osmolality confirms hypotonic hyponatremia. Euvolemia, concentrated urine, elevated urine sodium, normal thyroid and adrenal testing, and a possible pulmonary malignancy support SIADH.

His sodium decreased after isotonic saline because persistent ADH activity caused retention of water while infused sodium was excreted in highly concentrated urine, sometimes termed desalination. Once neurologic symptoms improve, hypertonic saline should be stopped and serum sodium monitored frequently to avoid osmotic demyelination from overcorrection. Evaluation and chronic treatment of the underlying SIADH follow stabilization.

wrong_explanations.why: Conivaptan can increase free-water excretion but is not appropriate for emergency reversal of cerebral edema. Vasopressin antagonists also risk uncontrolled overcorrection in profound hyponatremia.
Fluid restriction is guideline-suggested first-line therapy for stable moderate or profound SIADH, but it acts too slowly for a patient with a hyponatremic seizure.
Isotonic saline treats hypovolemic hyponatremia. In SIADH with highly concentrated urine, sodium may be excreted while water is retained, causing the serum sodium to fall further.
Oral urea promotes osmotic water excretion and is a guideline-suggested second-line option for stable SIADH. It does not provide sufficiently rapid correction during severe neurologic symptoms.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must confirm hypotonic SIADH, recognize paradoxical worsening with isotonic saline, and allow severe neurologic symptoms to override chronic SIADH treatment choices.
reasoning_steps: Confirm true hypotonic hyponatremia from the low serum sodium and measured serum osmolality.
Identify SIADH from euvolemia, concentrated urine, elevated urine sodium, normal thyroid and adrenal function, and the pulmonary mass.
Recognize the generalized seizure as a severe manifestation of hyponatremic cerebral edema requiring immediate correction.
Select bolus hypertonic saline and reject isotonic saline, fluid restriction, urea, and conivaptan as inadequate or potentially harmful in the emergency phase.

talk.title: Worsening Hyponatremia on Isotonic Saline: Recognizing SIADH Physiology
talk.subtitle: Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with concentrated urine in a smoker with a hilar mass
guideline_sources: 2014 European (ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA) Clinical Practice Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Hyponatraemia
US Hyponatremia Expert Panel Recommendations (Verbalis et al, Am J Med 2013)
talk.key_point: In SIADH, isotonic saline can lower serum sodium further when urine osmolality exceeds infusate osmolality; fluid restriction is first-line therapy for chronic, minimally symptomatic hyponatremia.

abim_classification.specific_topic: SIADH: desalination effect of isotonic saline; fluid restriction and Furst ratio

board_pearls: When urine osmolality (640 mOsm/kg) exceeds the osmolality of 0.9% NaCl (~308 mOsm/kg), the kidney excretes the infused sodium in a smaller volume of concentrated urine and retains free water — 'desalination' — so serum sodium falls further. [1,4]

The 2014 European hyponatraemia guideline recommends fluid restriction as first-line treatment for moderate/profound chronic hyponatremia from SIADH, and recommends AGAINST vasopressin receptor antagonists and demeclocycline. [1]

Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms (seizures, obtundation, vomiting with altered mentation); mild nausea and fatigue in chronic hyponatremia do not qualify — the discriminator between 3% saline and fluid restriction is symptom severity, not the sodium number. [1]

The Furst ratio ((urine Na + urine K)/serum Na) predicts failure of fluid restriction when >1; here (70+25)/120 = 0.79, so fluid restriction alone is expected to work. Ratios >1 warrant oral urea, salt plus loop diuretic, or a vaptan. [3]

Common trap: escalating or continuing isotonic saline because the sodium 'has not corrected.' In SIADH with concentrated urine this predictably worsens hyponatremia; isotonic saline is diagnostic-therapeutic only for hypovolemic hyponatremia. [1,4]
teaching_points: SIADH diagnosis requires hypotonic hyponatremia (serum osm <275), urine osm >100 mOsm/kg, urine Na >30 mEq/L, clinical euvolemia, and exclusion of hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and diuretics; low BUN and low uric acid support it.
Small cell lung cancer is the classic paraneoplastic cause of SIADH; a hilar mass in a heavy smoker with new hyponatremia mandates tissue diagnosis and staging alongside sodium management.

Correction limits: raise serum sodium no more than 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours (4-6 mEq/L if high risk for osmotic demyelination) — chronic hyponatremia, malnutrition, alcohol use, hypokalemia, and liver disease raise ODS risk.

Second-line options when fluid restriction fails or is not tolerated: oral urea 15-30 g/day, sodium chloride tablets with a loop diuretic, or tolvaptan (US expert panel supports vaptans; the 2014 European guideline recommends against them — an explicit transatlantic divergence).
summary_points: Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with urine osm 640 mOsm/kg and urine Na 70 mEq/L in a smoker with a hilar mass is paraneoplastic SIADH. [1]
Isotonic saline worsens SIADH when urine osmolality exceeds ~308 mOsm/kg; stop it. [1,4]
Fluid restriction (~800 mL/day, less than urine output) is first-line for chronic, minimally symptomatic SIADH. [1]
Hypertonic saline is for severe neurologic symptoms only; tolvaptan and demeclocycline are not first-line. [1,2]

question.stem:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated in the hospital for persistent hyponatremia. He was admitted 24 hours ago after 3 weeks of fatigue, anorexia, and 5-kg weight loss. He reports mild nausea but no headache, confusion, or seizures. He has a 45-pack-year smoking history and takes no diuretics or antidepressants. Admission serum sodium was 124 mEq/L, and 0.9% NaCl at 100 mL/h was started.

Temperature 36.7 C, BP 126/78 mm Hg, HR 74/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on room air. He is alert and fully oriented. Mucous membranes are moist, jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no edema. Breath sounds are decreased at the right apex.

Sodium 120 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, BUN 8 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, glucose 96 mg/dL, uric acid 2.4 mg/dL, TSH normal, 8 AM cortisol 18 µg/dL. Serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg; urine sodium 70 mEq/L; urine potassium 25 mEq/L. CXR shows a right hilar mass.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Stop saline and restrict fluid to 800 mL/day

question.explanation: This is SIADH: hypotonic hyponatremia (serum osm 250 mOsm/kg), inappropriately concentrated urine (640 mOsm/kg), urine sodium >30 mEq/L, clinical euvolemia, low BUN and uric acid, with normal TSH and cortisol — most likely paraneoplastic from the right hilar mass in a heavy smoker. The 2014 European (ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA) hyponatraemia guideline recommends fluid restriction as FIRST-LINE treatment for moderate or profound chronic hyponatraemia due to SIADH, and specifically advises restricting intake below urine output. It equally explains why the sodium fell on 0.9% NaCl: when urine osmolality (640 mOsm/kg) exceeds the osmolality of the infusate (~308 mOsm/kg), the infused sodium is excreted in a smaller volume of concentrated urine while free water is retained — the 'desalination' effect — so isotonic saline predictably worsens hyponatremia in SIADH. Isotonic saline is appropriate only when hypovolemia is suspected (not here: euvolemic exam, urine Na 70 mEq/L). Hypertonic saline is reserved by the same guideline for moderately severe or severe symptoms (vomiting with obtundation, seizures, coma); this patient is alert and oriented with only mild nausea, so a 3% saline bolus is not indicated. The Furst ratio, (urine Na + urine K)/serum Na = (70+25)/120 = 0.79, is <1, predicting that fluid restriction will succeed; a ratio >1 would signal likely failure and prompt oral urea, salt tablets plus a loop diuretic, or a vaptan. Concurrent oncologic evaluation for suspected small cell lung cancer should proceed, since treating the tumor treats the SIADH.

wrong_explanations.why: Hypertonic saline is reserved for moderately severe/severe symptoms — seizures, obtundation, coma, or vomiting with altered mentation. This alert, oriented patient with mild nausea and chronic hyponatremia does not meet that threshold, and unnecessary 3% saline risks overcorrection and osmotic demyelination.

This is the central trap. With urine osmolality 640 mOsm/kg exceeding the ~308 mOsm/kg of 0.9% NaCl, the kidney excretes the sodium load in concentrated urine and retains free water, lowering serum sodium further — exactly what happened over the first 24 hours.

Vaptans are second-line at best; the 2014 European guideline recommends against vasopressin receptor antagonists in SIADH, and the US expert panel positions them after fluid restriction fails. With a Furst ratio of 0.79, restriction has not yet been tried and is likely to work.

Demeclocycline is recommended against by the 2014 European guideline because of nephrotoxicity, photosensitivity, and unpredictable onset. It is a historical agent, not an appropriate next step before an adequate trial of fluid restriction.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must recognize SIADH, explain why sodium fell on isotonic saline using the urine-versus-infusate osmolality relationship, judge symptom severity to exclude hypertonic saline, and apply the guideline hierarchy that places fluid restriction ahead of vaptans and demeclocycline.
reasoning_steps: Classify the hyponatremia: serum osm 250 with urine osm 640, urine Na 70, euvolemic exam, low BUN/uric acid, normal TSH and cortisol — SIADH, likely paraneoplastic from the hilar mass.
Explain the paradoxical drop: urine osmolality 640 > isotonic saline 308 mOsm/kg, so saline administration causes net free-water retention (desalination) — isotonic saline must be stopped.
Grade symptom severity: alert, oriented, mild nausea only in chronic hyponatremia — does not meet criteria for hypertonic saline.
Apply the Furst ratio: (70+25)/120 = 0.79 (<1), predicting fluid restriction will be effective.
Apply guideline hierarchy: fluid restriction is first-line for chronic SIADH, while vaptans and demeclocycline are not, so restrict free water to 800 mL/day and pursue tumor workup.

claude_errors: Furst ratio applied loosely: a (UNa+UK)/SNa of 0.79 falls in the 0.5–1.0 intermediate band, which per the original Furst data predicts need for restriction to <500 mL/day, not the 800 mL/day prescribed/endorsed as 'expected to work'; stating that a ratio <1 predicts success of fluid restriction overstates the rule (the validated cut-off for likely failure is >1, but 0.5–1.0 predicts only partial response)

Teaching point states ODS-risk correction limit as '8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours' as a general ceiling; the 2014 European guideline limit it cites is 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and 8 mmol/L per 24 h thereafter (US panel: 6–8/day, hard limit 10–12), so the composite figure blurs two different society thresholds
judge.why: Both artifacts are medically sound, correctly identify paraneoplastic SIADH, and correctly cite the 2014 ESICM/ESE/ERA-EDTA guideline including the 150 mL 3% saline bolus (grade 1D), the 10/8 mEq/L correction ceilings, and the guideline's recommendations against vaptans and demeclocycline. Artifact A is flawless but narrower: it teaches a single reflex (severe symptoms → hypertonic saline) and its distractor explanations are thin. Artifact B teaches the harder, more board-discriminating concept (symptom severity, not the sodium number, drives therapy; desalination physiology quantified against infusate osmolality; the explicit US-vs-European divergence on vaptans; ancillary low BUN/uric acid), with accurate, verifiable citations (Verbalis 2013 Am J Med, Sterns NEJM 2015, Furst Am J Med Sci 2000) and no misattributed claims. B's only flaws are a slightly over-permissive application of the Furst ratio and a blended correction-limit figure — minor relative to its substantially greater teaching value for an IM resident.

talk.title: Acute COPD Exacerbation Management
talk.subtitle: Mechanism-driven stabilization, selective antibiotics, ventilatory support, and recurrence prevention
guideline_sources: GOLD 2025 COPD Strategy
summary_points: A COPD exacerbation acutely increases airway inflammation, mucus, and bronchoconstriction, worsening expiratory flow limitation, dynamic hyperinflation, V/Q mismatch, and respiratory muscle load.

Target SpO2 88-92%; excessive oxygen can worsen hypercapnia through increased V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect, not simply by suppressing respiratory drive. Reassess with an ABG after oxygen initiation when hypercapnia is possible.[1]

GOLD 2025 recommends a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA), with or without a short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA), plus prednisone-equivalent 40 mg daily for 5 days in moderate or severe exacerbations.[1,2]

Give antibiotics for increased sputum purulence plus increased dyspnea or sputum volume, all three cardinal symptoms, or a need for invasive or noninvasive ventilation; antibiotics are not routine for every exacerbation.[1,3]

Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is first-line ventilatory support for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis unless contraindicated; do not delay intubation when NIV is failing.[1,4,5]
The common pitfall is anchoring on COPD: pneumonia, HF, PE, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, and acute coronary syndrome can mimic or precipitate an exacerbation and must be actively assessed.

visual_memory_card.top_left: Inflammation narrows airways, causing dynamic hyperinflation
visual_memory_card.top_right: Worsened dyspnea, cough, sputum within 14 days
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: ABG plus CXR identify failure and mimics
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Bronchodilators, prednisone, controlled oxygen; NIV if acidotic
