question.stem:
A 66-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department for sudden dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain beginning 6 hours ago. Ten days ago, she underwent total knee arthroplasty and has since been walking only short distances. She has no history of HF, chronic lung disease, or cancer. She has not had syncope.

Temperature 36.8 C, BP 118/74 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 24/min, and SpO2 93% on room air. She is alert. Cardiac examination shows tachycardia without murmurs. The right calf is swollen and tender.

CT pulmonary angiography shows bilateral lobar pulmonary emboli and an RV/LV diameter ratio of 1.3. Echo confirms RV dilation with reduced systolic function. Troponin I is 0.12 ng/mL (reference <0.04), and serum lactate is normal. Her sPESI is 1.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation:
The 2026 AHA/ACC multisociety PE guideline recommends risk stratification using hemodynamics, clinical severity, RV dysfunction, and cardiac biomarkers. The parallel 2019 ESC framework classifies a normotensive patient with both RV dysfunction and elevated troponin as intermediate-high risk. Guideline-recommended management is therapeutic anticoagulation with hospitalization and close monitoring for early deterioration.

This patient is not low risk: her HR produces an sPESI of 1, and CT, echo, and troponin demonstrate RV pressure overload with myocardial injury. She is also not in the highest-risk group because her BP, mentation, perfusion, and lactate are normal. Therefore, neither outpatient treatment nor immediate reperfusion is appropriate.

Routine thrombolysis is not recommended for hemodynamically stable intermediate-risk PE. PEITHO demonstrated less hemodynamic decompensation with systemic thrombolysis but substantially more major bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke, without a mortality benefit. Reperfusion with systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapy, or surgical embolectomy should be used as rescue treatment if shock or other hemodynamic deterioration occurs; catheter or surgical therapy may be selected when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated.

wrong_explanations.why: Outpatient management is reserved for carefully selected low-risk PE. This patient has an sPESI of 1, RV systolic dysfunction, and elevated troponin, indicating a clinically important risk of early deterioration.

Catheter-directed therapy is not routinely indicated for stable intermediate-risk PE. It may be considered after deterioration or when reperfusion is required but systemic thrombolysis carries excessive bleeding risk.

Surgical embolectomy is generally reserved for high-risk PE when thrombolysis is contraindicated or unsuccessful, or for selected patients with impending collapse. This patient has preserved perfusion.

RV dysfunction and troponin elevation do not independently mandate systemic thrombolysis. In stable intermediate-risk PE, routine lysis increases major bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke without a demonstrated mortality benefit.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must integrate hemodynamic stability, sPESI, RV imaging, and troponin findings to distinguish monitored anticoagulation from both outpatient therapy and immediate reperfusion.
reasoning_steps: Recognize confirmed acute PE with a major transient provoking factor.
Establish that preserved BP, mentation, lactate, and perfusion exclude high-risk PE requiring immediate reperfusion.
Identify non-low-risk disease from tachycardia and an sPESI of 1.
Combine RV dysfunction and elevated troponin to identify elevated intermediate risk requiring inpatient anticoagulation and close monitoring rather than routine thrombolysis.

talk.title: Intermediate-High Risk Acute PE: Who Gets Thrombolysis?
talk.subtitle: Applying hemodynamics, sPESI, RV dysfunction, and troponin to the 2026 AHA/ACC and ESC 2019 risk strata
guideline_sources: 2026 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ACEP/CHEST/SCAI/SHM/SIR/SVM/SVN Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guideline
2019 ESC/ERS Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism
CHEST/ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease 2021
talk.key_point: In normotensive acute PE with RV dysfunction plus elevated troponin (intermediate-high risk), give therapeutic anticoagulation and monitor 48-72 hours for rescue reperfusion rather than upfront systemic thrombolysis. [1,2]

abim_classification.specific_topic: Acute PE risk stratification: intermediate-high risk management

board_pearls: RV pressure overload from acute PE causes myocyte micro-injury and wall stress, so a positive troponin plus an RV/LV ratio >0.9 identifies patients at risk for delayed hemodynamic collapse even while normotensive. [2]

The 2026 AHA/ACC PE guideline introduces acute PE clinical categories A through E and formally retires the terms massive and submassive; ESC 2019 remains current in Europe with low / intermediate-low / intermediate-high / high strata — state which taxonomy you are using. [1,2]

The single discriminator between full-dose systemic thrombolysis and anticoagulation-plus-monitoring is hemodynamics: persistent hypotension, vasopressor need, or arrest, not the size of the clot or the degree of RV strain. [1,2]

PEITHO (NEJM 2014) showed tenecteplase in intermediate-risk PE reduced hemodynamic decompensation but tripled major bleeding and caused 2% intracranial hemorrhage with no mortality benefit — the basis for reserving lysis for rescue. [3]

The commonest trap is escalating to thrombolysis or catheter-directed therapy because troponin and RV/LV ratio are abnormal; the second commonest is outpatient discharge on a DOAC, which is validated only for sPESI 0 without RV dysfunction. [1,4]
teaching_points: Risk stratification in acute PE is sequential: hemodynamics first (shock = high risk), then a clinical score (sPESI/PESI), then imaging RV dysfunction (echo or CTPA RV/LV ratio >0.9), then cardiac troponin.

Intermediate-high risk = normotensive + elevated sPESI/PESI + BOTH RV dysfunction and positive troponin. Management is therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH or a DOAC) in a monitored bed for 48-72 hours with reperfusion held in reserve for decompensation.

Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an evolving option (ULTIMA; PE-TRACT ongoing) and reasonable when lysis is needed but full-dose systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated — it is not yet a guideline-endorsed replacement for anticoagulation alone in stable intermediate-high risk PE.
summary_points: Normotensive PE with RV dysfunction plus positive troponin is intermediate-high risk: anticoagulate, monitor closely, and lyse only on decompensation. [1,2]
Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for shock, vasopressor dependence, or cardiac arrest from PE. [1,2]
sPESI 0 without RV dysfunction or troponin elevation is the population validated for outpatient DOAC therapy. [1]
IVC filters have no role when therapeutic anticoagulation can be given. [4]

question.stem:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for 3 days of progressive dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain that began 10 days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He has hypertension and no prior VTE. He has not had syncope, hemoptysis, or fever, and he is not taking anticoagulants.

Temperature 37.1 C, BP 122/76 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 24/min, SpO2 92% on room air. He is alert and warm peripherally. JVP is elevated; heart sounds show an accentuated P2. Lungs are clear. There is no leg swelling.

Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, high-sensitivity troponin T 68 ng/L (normal <14), BNP 640 pg/mL. CTPA shows bilateral lobar and segmental filling defects with an RV/LV diameter ratio of 1.3. Bedside echo confirms RV dilation with preserved systolic BP.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Discharge on apixaban with early follow-up
Initiate therapeutic LMWH and admit for monitoring
Place a retrievable inferior vena cava filter

question.explanation:
This patient is normotensive (BP 122/76 mm Hg, lactate normal, no vasopressors) but has an elevated sPESI (age >70 excluded; HR >=110/min scores 1), RV dysfunction (RV/LV ratio 1.3 on CTPA plus echo RV dilation), AND myocardial injury (hs-troponin T 68 ng/L). That combination defines intermediate-HIGH risk PE in the ESC 2019 four-strata scheme, and the corresponding intermediate clinical category in the 2026 AHA/ACC acute PE guideline, which retires the massive/submassive vocabulary in favor of categories A through E. For this stratum both documents recommend prompt therapeutic anticoagulation (weight-based LMWH or a single-drug DOAC) with admission to a monitored setting for 48-72 hours, reserving rescue reperfusion for hemodynamic decompensation. Escalation criteria to watch are hypotension, rising lactate, worsening oxygen requirement, and new vasopressor need.

The rationale is PEITHO: in intermediate-risk PE, upfront systemic fibrinolysis reduced hemodynamic decompensation but caused a roughly 3-fold increase in major bleeding and about 2% intracranial hemorrhage with no mortality benefit. Therefore the trigger for full-dose lysis is hemodynamic instability (shock, persistent hypotension, or cardiac arrest), not abnormal RV or biomarker findings alone. Recent abdominal surgery further raises this patient's bleeding risk. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is described as evolving (ULTIMA; PE-TRACT pending) and is best applied when reperfusion is indicated but systemic lysis is contraindicated. Anticoagulation should continue at least 3 months (CHEST 2021).

wrong_explanations.why: Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an evolving option and is used mainly when reperfusion is indicated but systemic lysis is contraindicated. In a hemodynamically stable patient it has not been shown to improve mortality and is not first-line over anticoagulation with close monitoring.

Outpatient DOAC therapy (HoT-PE) applies to low-risk PE: sPESI 0 with no RV dysfunction and normal troponin. This patient has tachycardia, RV/LV ratio 1.3, and troponin elevation, predicting delayed decompensation — discharge is unsafe.

IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent VTE despite therapeutic anticoagulation. This patient can be anticoagulated, and filters do not treat existing clot burden or RV strain.

Full-dose systemic alteplase is indicated for high-risk PE — shock, persistent hypotension, or cardiac arrest. Applying it to normotensive RV dysfunction adds major and intracranial bleeding risk (PEITHO) without a mortality benefit, and recent surgery compounds that risk.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must integrate normal hemodynamics with an abnormal sPESI, RV/LV ratio, and troponin to land in a specific intermediate stratum, then recognize that the reperfusion trigger is hemodynamic instability rather than strain markers, while rejecting two closely competing escalation options.
reasoning_steps: Confirm acute PE and note the patient is normotensive with normal lactate — this excludes the high-risk/shock category that mandates systemic thrombolysis.
Calculate sPESI: HR >=110/min gives a score of 1, so this is not a low-risk PE eligible for outpatient DOAC therapy.

Identify both RV dysfunction (CTPA RV/LV 1.3, echo RV dilation) and myocardial injury (hs-troponin T 68 ng/L), which together define intermediate-high risk (ESC 2019) / the intermediate clinical category (2026 AHA/ACC).

Apply PEITHO-informed guidance: in this stratum, upfront lysis increases major and intracranial bleeding without mortality benefit, so reperfusion is held in reserve — recent abdominal surgery reinforces this.
Choose therapeutic anticoagulation with admission to a monitored bed for 48-72 hours and rescue reperfusion only if the patient decompensates.

claude_errors: Misstates PEITHO magnitude: 'tripled major bleeding' / 'roughly 3-fold increase in major bleeding' — PEITHO showed major extracranial bleeding 6.3% vs 1.2% and overall major bleeding 11.5% vs 2.4% (~5-fold), not 3-fold.
sPESI age criterion misstated as 'age >70' in the explanation ('age >70 excluded' for a 71-year-old); the sPESI age variable is >80 years. As written the arithmetic is internally inconsistent.

Highly specific, unverifiable attribution to the 2026 multisociety guideline that it 'introduces acute PE clinical categories A through E and formally retires the terms massive and submassive' — this level of detail is asserted twice as fact and is not supportable from the cited document as presented (citation-honesty risk).

'The single discriminator between full-dose systemic thrombolysis and anticoagulation-plus-monitoring is hemodynamics' is overstated — progressive deterioration short of frank shock (rising lactate, worsening RV failure, escalating O2 need) is also an accepted rescue trigger, which the same artifact acknowledges elsewhere.

'Outpatient DOAC validated only for sPESI 0 without RV dysfunction' is slightly overstated as an absolute; HoT-PE and Hestia-based protocols permit selected patients with sPESI ≥1 by Hestia criteria, though the practical teaching point is acceptable.
judge.why: Both artifacts reach the same correct answer and the same core, guideline-concordant teaching: normotensive PE with RV dysfunction plus troponin elevation = ESC 2019 intermediate-high risk, treated with therapeutic anticoagulation in a monitored setting with reperfusion held in reserve for hemodynamic deterioration; PEITHO is correctly invoked as the rationale against routine upfront lysis. Artifact A is the richer teaching document (explicit sequential stratification algorithm, RV/LV >0.9 threshold, 48–72 h monitoring window, IVC filter and CDT distractors, ULTIMA/PE-TRACT context) and would arguably serve a resident better as a study card. However, it purchases that richness with several accuracy and citation-fidelity slips: it understates the PEITHO bleeding signal by roughly half, garbles the sPESI age cutoff in the very explanation that walks through score calculation, and makes a granular, load-bearing claim about the 2026 multisociety guideline ('categories A through E,' formal retirement of massive/submassive) that is asserted as established fact and is not verifiable from the cited source — precisely the kind of over-specific attribution that misleads a learner who will quote it on rounds. Artifact B says less but says nothing wrong: its guideline attributions are appropriately general ('recommends integrating hemodynamics, clinical severity, RV imaging, and cardiac biomarkers'), its PEITHO summary (more major extracranial bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke, no mortality benefit) is qualitatively accurate without inventing numbers, its stem supplies sPESI directly and internally consistently, and its distractor rationales (surgical embolectomy for high-risk with contraindicated/failed lysis; catheter-directed therapy as rescue or when systemic lysis is precluded) are correct. On the four stated criteria, teaching value favors A but accuracy, guideline fidelity, and citation honesty favor B; weighting the latter three, B edges it out. If A's PEITHO figures were corrected and the A–E taxonomy claim softened to 'the new multisociety guideline revises PE nomenclature,' A would be the stronger artifact.

AKI therefore arises from reduced renal perfusion or glomerular pressure, reduced Kf from parenchymal injury, or increased downstream pressure from obstruction.","Autoregulation normally preserves renal blood flow across a range of mean arterial pressures. Reduced afferent stretch causes myogenic dilation, while macula densa sensing of low distal NaCl activates tubuloglomerular feedback, renin release, and angiotensin II–mediated preferential efferent arteriolar constriction.","These compensations fail in severe hypotension, sepsis-related microcirculatory dysfunction, advanced CKD, or medication-altered arteriolar tone. talk.title: Acute Kidney Injury
talk.subtitle: From glomerular hemodynamics to phenotype-directed rescue
guideline_sources: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012; update remains in development as of 2026)
summary_points: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an abrupt fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) caused by impaired perfusion, intrinsic parenchymal injury, obstruction, or—commonly—more than one mechanism.
Creatinine (Cr) is a delayed, dilution-sensitive filtration marker; urine output often changes earlier but is also influenced by volume status, diuretics, and neurohormonal signaling.

The immediate priorities are to identify obstruction and life-threatening complications, stop kidney insults, restore effective perfusion without causing congestion, and treat the underlying disease. KDIGO 2012 remains the current AKI guideline.[1]

Kidney replacement therapy (KRT) is indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema or volume overload, uremic complications, and selected dialyzable toxins—not for an isolated BUN or Cr threshold.[1]

The common pitfall is reflexively labeling every oliguria-plus-Cr rise as acute tubular necrosis or repeatedly giving fluid without reassessing perfusion, venous congestion, urine sediment, and obstruction.

references.source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury
Initiation Strategies for Renal-Replacement Therapy in the Intensive Care Unit (AKIKI)
Timing of Initiation of Renal-Replacement Therapy in Acute Kidney Injury (STARRT-AKI)
Balanced Crystalloids versus Saline in Critically Ill Adults (SMART)

sections.heading: 1. Physiology First: Why GFR Falls
points: GFR is governed by the filtration coefficient and net filtration pressure: GFR = Kf × [(glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure − Bowman space hydrostatic pressure) − oncotic pressure]. AKI therefore arises from reduced renal perfusion or glomerular pressure, reduced Kf from parenchymal injury, or increased downstream pressure from obstruction.

Autoregulation normally preserves renal blood flow across a range of mean arterial pressures. Reduced afferent stretch causes myogenic dilation, while macula densa sensing of low distal NaCl activates tubuloglomerular feedback, renin release, and angiotensin II–mediated preferential efferent arteriolar constriction.

These compensations fail in severe hypotension, sepsis-related microcirculatory dysfunction, advanced CKD, or medication-altered arteriolar tone. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation; ACE inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) reduce angiotensin II–mediated efferent constriction. Either can sharply lower intraglomerular pressure when filtration is perfusion-dependent.

Hemodynamic or traditionally termed prerenal AKI initially has intact tubules: avid proximal Na and water reabsorption produces concentrated urine with low urine Na. Persistent ischemia or toxic injury causes tubular epithelial ATP depletion, loss of polarity and brush border, apoptosis or necrosis, luminal obstruction, back-leak of filtrate, and inflammatory microvascular dysfunction—collectively acute tubular injury (ATI).

Glomerular inflammation disrupts the filtration barrier, producing hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells (RBCs), RBC casts, and proteinuria. Interstitial inflammation impairs tubular transport and concentration, while vascular injury reduces perfusion despite potentially normal systemic BP.

Postrenal AKI raises tubular and Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, directly opposing filtration. Unilateral obstruction usually does not raise Cr when the contralateral kidney functions; bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney does.

Cr rises only after GFR has already fallen and may require 24–48 hours to approach a new steady state. Fluid accumulation dilutes serum Cr, whereas low muscle mass can make severe AKI appear deceptively mild.
sections.mechanism: AKI is not a single lesion: GFR can fall through reduced glomerular hydrostatic pressure, loss of filtering surface, tubular back-leak, or increased Bowman space pressure. The same Cr trajectory can therefore represent very different diseases requiring different interventions.
sections.teaching_pearl: Sepsis-associated AKI is not simply global renal ischemia; endothelial dysfunction, heterogeneous microcirculatory flow, inflammatory signaling, tubular metabolic adaptation, and venous congestion can reduce filtration even after systemic BP is restored.
sections.board_tip: A patient with renal artery stenosis, decompensated HF, cirrhosis, or severe volume depletion may depend on angiotensin II–mediated efferent constriction; starting an ACEi or ARB can reveal this physiology through an abrupt GFR decline.

sections.heading: 2. Diagnose the Syndrome, Then Find the Mechanism
points: KDIGO defines AKI as an increase in Cr ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, an increase to ≥1.5 times baseline known or presumed within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Stage using the worse of the Cr and urine-output criteria.[1]

First confirm acuity: retrieve prior Cr values, review the timing of illness and exposures, trend urine output, and consider CKD clues such as longstanding albuminuria, chronic anemia, mineral-bone abnormalities, or small echogenic kidneys. AKI and CKD frequently coexist.

Stabilize while diagnosing: obtain an EKG for significant hyperkalemia, assess oxygenation and pulmonary edema, measure BMP including bicarbonate, and evaluate for uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis, or bleeding.

History and examination should target effective arterial volume, hemorrhage, GI losses, sepsis, HF, cirrhosis, nephrotoxins, contrast exposure, urinary retention, stones, malignancy, rash, arthralgias, hemoptysis, and recent infections. Examine orthostatics, jugular venous pressure, lungs, edema, perfusion, bladder distention, and skin.

Urinalysis and sediment microscopy provide a rapid renal biopsy surrogate: hyaline casts support low-flow physiology; granular or muddy brown casts and renal tubular epithelial cells support ATI; RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis; white blood cell casts suggest interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis; crystals suggest drug or metabolic injury.

Urine albumin-to-Cr ratio and protein-to-Cr ratio help distinguish predominantly glomerular albumin loss from tubular or overflow proteinuria. Heavy proteinuria, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, or a pulmonary-renal syndrome should trigger urgent nephrology evaluation and targeted serologies, with kidney biopsy when results will change treatment.

Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) <1% can support sodium-avid physiology, but it is unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction, contrast injury, pigment nephropathy, and some forms of sepsis. Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) is also imperfect; neither test overrides the clinical context or sediment.

Perform bladder scanning for suspected retention and renal US when obstruction is possible or the cause is unclear. Hydronephrosis may be absent early, with retroperitoneal fibrosis, or in severe volume depletion, so persistent suspicion warrants further imaging or urologic evaluation.

Consider non-GFR causes of a Cr rise: trimethoprim and cobicistat inhibit tubular Cr secretion, creatine intake increases production, and laboratory interference can alter measurement. These produce a Cr change without the expected urine or metabolic consequences of true filtration failure.
sections.mechanism: The workup maps observable findings back to the injured compartment: hemodynamic assessment tests filtration pressure, urine sediment tests nephron structure, protein characterization tests the glomerular barrier, and imaging tests downstream pressure.
sections.teaching_pearl: Use a three-bucket framework—hemodynamic/prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal—but expect mixed AKI. A septic patient can simultaneously have vasodilation, nephrotoxin exposure, ATI, elevated venous pressure, and urinary obstruction.
sections.board_tip: Urine eosinophils neither confirm nor exclude acute interstitial nephritis. Medication timing, sterile pyuria, white blood cell casts, systemic features, and sometimes biopsy are more useful.

sections.heading: 3. Treatment: Remove the Insult and Manage Complications
points: Per KDIGO 2012, promptly identify reversible causes, discontinue or minimize nephrotoxins, renally adjust medications, monitor Cr and urine output, and manage electrolyte, acid-base, and volume complications. The KDIGO AKI update is still in development, so the 2012 document remains the guideline anchor.[1]

If intravascular depletion is likely, give an isotonic crystalloid bolus and immediately reassess BP, perfusion, lungs, venous congestion, and urine output. KDIGO recommends crystalloids rather than colloids for initial volume expansion in patients without hemorrhagic shock.[1]

Balanced crystalloids are often favored when substantial resuscitation is anticipated because they reduce chloride delivery and the risk of hyperchloremic acidosis. In SMART, balanced crystalloids modestly reduced the composite of death, new KRT, or persistent kidney dysfunction compared with saline; this is trial evidence complementing, rather than replacing, KDIGO's broader crystalloid recommendation.[4]

Fluids increase GFR only when low preload limits cardiac output and renal perfusion. Once euvolemia is reached, additional fluid raises interstitial and renal venous pressures, worsens pulmonary edema, and can further reduce the transrenal filtration gradient.

For vasomotor shock, use vasopressors with fluids rather than continuing fluid alone. Restoring systemic perfusion pressure can recover glomerular pressure, but BP targets should be individualized in chronic HTN, RV failure, and states of marked venous congestion.[1]

Loop diuretics may relieve pulmonary edema and facilitate volume management, but they do not reverse tubular injury or improve kidney recovery. KDIGO recommends not using diuretics to prevent AKI and not using them to treat AKI except for volume overload.[1]

Relieve obstruction promptly with bladder catheterization, ureteral stenting, or percutaneous nephrostomy according to obstruction level and clinical urgency. Monitor for postobstructive diuresis, hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia after decompression.

Treat disease-specific intrinsic AKI rather than empirically labeling it ATI: eradicate infection, stop the culprit drug in suspected interstitial nephritis, urgently evaluate rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and manage thrombotic microangiopathy or vascular occlusion according to its cause.

Initiate KRT emergently for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidemia, pulmonary edema or volume overload compromising organ function, uremic encephalopathy or pericarditis, and selected dialyzable intoxications. Decide from the full clinical context and trends—not a single BUN or Cr threshold.[1]

In patients with severe AKI but no urgent indication, accelerated KRT is not routinely beneficial. AKIKI found no survival advantage to immediate KRT and approximately half of the delayed-strategy group avoided KRT; STARRT-AKI likewise found no 90-day mortality benefit from accelerated initiation and found more KRT dependence among survivors.[2,3]
Reassess kidney function and albuminuria after AKI; KDIGO recommends evaluation at approximately 3 months for resolution, new or worsening CKD, and cardiovascular risk.[1]
sections.mechanism: Restoring effective perfusion increases glomerular capillary pressure only while the circulation is preload-responsive; avoiding congestion preserves the pressure gradient from renal artery to renal vein. KRT substitutes diffusion, convection, and ultrafiltration for failed solute, acid-base, and volume homeostasis but does not directly heal injured nephrons.
sections.teaching_pearl: The response to a carefully monitored fluid challenge is physiologic information, not a permanent diagnosis. Lack of improvement should prompt reassessment for ATI, venous congestion, glomerular or vascular disease, and obstruction.
sections.board_tip: Do not start KRT solely because Cr is very high, and do not delay it when a refractory complication is present. The classic indications are complications—electrolyte, acid-base, intoxication, overload, and uremia—not a numerical Cr cutoff.[1]

sections.heading: 4. Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Prognosis depends on AKI severity and duration, baseline CKD, age and frailty, sepsis, multiorgan failure, cumulative fluid balance, and whether kidney recovery occurs. Recurrent or incompletely resolved AKI increases the likelihood of subsequent CKD.
In AKIKI, 60-day mortality was 48.5% with early KRT versus 49.7% with a delayed strategy; 49% of patients assigned to the delayed strategy never required KRT.[2]

In STARRT-AKI, 90-day mortality was 43.9% with accelerated KRT versus 43.7% with a standard strategy. Among 90-day survivors, continued KRT dependence occurred in 10.4% versus 6.0%, respectively, and adverse events were more frequent with accelerated treatment.[3]

A falling Cr is reassuring only when interpreted with urine output, fluid balance, and muscle production. Hemodilution or loss of muscle mass during critical illness can create apparent biochemical improvement without complete GFR recovery.
sections.mechanism: Severe or prolonged nephron injury can leave maladaptive repair, capillary rarefaction, interstitial fibrosis, and reduced renal reserve. This links an apparently resolved AKI episode to later CKD and greater vulnerability to recurrent injury.
sections.teaching_pearl: Document the AKI episode in the discharge summary, reconcile renally cleared medications, arrange follow-up labs, and communicate whether Cr returned to baseline; survivorship care is part of AKI treatment.
sections.board_tip: Accelerated KRT is not synonymous with better care. In the absence of an urgent indication, major randomized trials support close surveillance and complication-triggered initiation rather than automatic early dialysis.[2,3]

across the glomerular capillary: filtration = Kf × (net ultrafiltration pressure). Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (~45-50 mmHg) is set by the ratio of afferent to efferent arteriolar resistance, opposed by Bowman's space pressure (~10-15) and plasma oncotic pressure (~25). Anything that lowers glomerular capillary pressure or raises Bowman's pressure drops GFR — no tubular cell has to die for creatinine to rise.","Autoregulation: over a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80-180 mmHg, myogenic afferent stretch reflexes and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa senses distal NaCl via NKCC2, releases adenosine → A1-mediated afferent constriction) hold GFR nearly constant. When perfusion falls, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the EFFERENT arteriole and prostaglandins (PGE2/PGI2) DILATE the afferent — this is the entire pharmacologic vulnerability: NSAIDs remove afferent dilation, ACEi/ARB remove efferent constriction, and calcineurin inhibitors and iodinated contrast cause afferent vasoconstriction.","The proximal tubule is the metabolic hotspot and the injury epicenter: it reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na+ using basolateral Na/K-ATPase, runs on oxidative phosphorylation, and sits in an outer medulla where PO2 is already 10-20 mmHg. This is why chasing MAP with fluid alone does not fix it. [7]","Venous congestion is an under-taught mechanism: rising central venous pressure raises renal interstitial and Bowman's pressure in an encapsulated organ, compressing tubules and peritubular capillaries. Stage 1 = 1.5-1.9× baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dL rise; Stage 2 = 2.0-2.9×; Stage 3 = ≥3× baseline, Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL, initiation of RRT, or anuria ≥12 h. [1]","Remember the math: creatinine is a nonlinear marker. Cr 0.6 → 1.2 mg/dL is a 50% GFR loss but may be reported as 'normal.' In sarcopenic, cirrhotic, or amputee patients, and after large-volume resuscitation (dilution), Cr systematically underestimates injury. Oliguria often precedes the Cr rise by 12-24 h.","Bucket 1 — Prerenal/hemodynamic (~40-60% of inpatient AKI): true hypovolemia (GI losses, hemorrhage, diuretics), reduced effective arterial volume (HF, cirrhosis, sepsis, nephrotic syndrome), drug-mediated autoregulatory failure (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, calcineurin inhibitors), abdominal compartment syndrome, hepatorenal syndrome, and renal artery events.","Bucket 2 — Intrinsic: ATN (ischemic, septic, or toxic — aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cisplatin, contrast, myoglobin, hemoglobin, light chains); acute interstitial nephritis (AIN — beta-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, checkpoint inhibitors: pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab); glomerulonephritis/vasculitis; intratubular crystals (uric acid, acyclovir, methotrexate, oxalate); thrombotic microangiopathy; cholesterol emboli.","Bucket 3 — Postrenal: BPH/urinary retention, malignant or retroperitoneal obstruction, bilateral stones, neurogenic bladder, or a clotted/kinked Foley. Requires bilateral (or unilateral in a single functioning kidney) obstruction to raise Cr — and it is the most reversible bucket, which is why a bladder scan and renal US are early, not late, moves. [1]","Workup with a question attached to each test: urinalysis WITH microscopy (casts, dysmorphic RBCs, WBCs, eosinophils, crystals) asks 'is the parenchyma inflamed?'; urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio asks 'glomerular or tubular?'; renal US asks 'obstructed, and are the kidneys chronically small/echogenic?'; CK and LDH/haptoglobin/smear ask 'rhabdomyolysis or hemolysis/TMA?'; serologies (ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complements, SPEP/free light chains, hepatitis serologies) ask 'immunologic'; bladder pressure asks 'compartment syndrome.'","Biopsy when the cause remains unexplained, GN/vasculitis/myeloma kidney or drug-induced AIN is plausible, or the course does not fit — particularly when immunosuppression would change management."],"teaching_pearl":"Muddy brown granular casts and 'renal tubular epithelial cell casts' are the only findings that let you diagnose ATN at the bedside. Look at the sediment yourself — the dipstick 'trace protein, trace blood' report is silent about casts, and the lab may not have spun it.","board_tip":"Pigmented casts + heme-positive dipstick with FEW RBCs on microscopy = myoglobin or free hemoglobin, not glomerular bleeding. Anion gap acidosis + AKI + calcium oxalate crystals = ethylene glycol; check the osmolar gap."},{"heading":"Management: What Actually Works, and When to Dialyze","minutes":"3 min","points":["Supportive care is the therapy (KDIGO 2012, and the framework survives into the update in review): optimize renal perfusion pressure, treat the primary cause, DISCONTINUE nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B), hold ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i during acute hemodynamic instability, dose-adjust all renally cleared drugs, avoid hyperglycemia, and ensure adequate nutrition (20-30 kcal/kg/d, do not protein-restrict to avoid dialysis). [1]","Fluids: give isotonic crystalloid for hypovolemic/prerenal AKI, then reassess with a dynamic measure (passive leg raise, pulse-pressure variation, POCUS IVC/lung B-lines) — not a static CVP. KDIGO recommends isotonic crystalloid over colloid as initial expansion; SMART showed balanced crystalloids reduced the composite of death, new RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction versus 0.9% saline in critically ill adults, arguing against large-volume chloride-rich resuscitation. [1,6]","Once the patient is fluid-unresponsive or congested, STOP fluids: positive fluid balance independently worsens AKI outcomes via renal interstitial edema and venous congestion. In septic shock, add vasopressors targeting MAP ~65 mmHg (higher in chronic HTN) to restore glomerular perfusion pressure; norepinephrine is first-line and vasopressin is a reasonable second agent, per Surviving Sepsis 2021. [7]","Things NOT to do, all mechanism-based failures: low-dose ('renal-dose') dopamine — no benefit, more arrhythmia; loop diuretics to 'convert' oliguric to non-oliguric AKI — they improve urine output and volume control ONLY, they do not improve GFR, recovery, or mortality (KDIGO recommends against diuretics for treating AKI, other than for volume overload); mannitol; natriuretic peptides. Diuretic responsiveness is a prognostic marker, not a treatment. [1]","Contrast-associated AKI: risk is real but overstated in modern practice. PRESERVE found NO benefit of IV sodium bicarbonate over saline and NO benefit of oral N-acetylcysteine over placebo for death, dialysis, or persistent kidney impairment after angiography. Practice: use isotonic crystalloid periprocedural volume expansion in high-risk patients (CKD, diabetes, hypovolemia), minimize contrast volume, and do not withhold a needed CT for a mild creatinine bump. [5]","Specific etiologies get specific mechanisms: rhabdomyolysis → aggressive isotonic fluid to flush myoglobin casts; tumor lysis → hydration plus rasburicase; obstruction → catheter, nephrostomy, or stent immediately; AIN → stop the drug, consider corticosteroids; ANCA/anti-GBM → immunosuppression ± plasma exchange; hepatorenal syndrome-AKI → albumin plus terlipressin, which improved HRS reversal versus placebo in CONFIRM (watch for ischemic and respiratory adverse events), with midodrine/octreotide plus albumin as an alternative where terlipressin is unavailable. [9]","RRT indications are refractory, not numeric: hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction/bleeding), or a dialyzable poison (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylate). KDIGO says initiate emergently for life-threatening changes and otherwise consider the broader clinical context, not a single BUN or Cr. [1]","Timing evidence: ELAIN (single-center, surgical) suggested early benefit, but AKIKI and the large multinational STARRT-AKI trial both showed accelerated initiation gave no mortality benefit; STARRT-AKI showed MORE dialysis dependence at 90 days in the accelerated arm, and ~40% of the standard-strategy patients never needed RRT at all. Watchful waiting with explicit trigger criteria is the default. [2,3,8]","Modality: continuous RRT and intermittent hemodialysis are equivalent for survival and renal recovery; choose CRRT for hemodynamic instability, cerebral edema/acute brain injury (avoid osmolar shifts), and precise volume control. Use regional citrate anticoagulation for CRRT circuits when not contraindicated, and prefer a non-tunneled internal jugular or femoral catheter over subclavian to protect future vascular access. talk.title: Acute Kidney Injury: From Glomerular Hemodynamics to the Dialysis Decision
talk.subtitle: A mechanism-first 10-minute chalk talk anchored to KDIGO 2012 AKI (2026 update in review)
guideline_sources: KDIGO 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (update in review)
KDIGO 2024 CKD Evaluation & Management (AKI-to-CKD transition)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (SCCM/ESICM) for septic AKI hemodynamics
summary_points: AKI is a functional and structural diagnosis of exclusion by mechanism: GFR falls either because glomerular perfusion pressure falls (prerenal), because tubules/interstitium/glomeruli/vessels are injured (intrinsic), or because tubular pressure rises from obstruction (postrenal). The three-bucket framework is what drives action, per KDIGO 2012. [1]

Creatinine is a lagging, dilutable, muscle-dependent marker — a doubling of Cr means roughly a 50% loss of GFR, and Cr can be near-normal in cachectic or fluid-overloaded patients. Urine output and the trajectory of Cr matter more than any single value. [1]

Core management is supportive and mechanistic: restore renal perfusion pressure, stop nephrotoxins, relieve obstruction, dose-adjust drugs, and avoid both hypovolemia and venous congestion. No drug reverses established ATN — dopamine, furosemide, and 'renal-dose' anything do not improve outcomes. [1]

Dialysis is started for refractory hyperkalemia, refractory acidosis, refractory volume overload, uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding), or a dialyzable intoxication — not for a creatinine number. AKIKI and STARRT-AKI showed accelerated/preemptive initiation gives no survival benefit and exposes patients to more catheter and hemodynamic harm. [1,2,3]

AKI is not a self-limited event: survivors carry a markedly elevated risk of incident and progressive CKD, so every AKI patient needs a documented post-discharge creatinine and albuminuria check, per KDIGO 2024. [4]

sections.heading: Physiology: How the Kidney Defends GFR — and How That Defense Fails
points: GFR is a Starling process across the glomerular capillary: filtration = Kf × (net ultrafiltration pressure). Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (~45-50 mmHg) is set by the ratio of afferent to efferent arteriolar resistance, opposed by Bowman's space pressure (~10-15) and plasma oncotic pressure (~25). Anything that lowers glomerular capillary pressure or raises Bowman's pressure drops GFR — no tubular cell has to die for creatinine to rise.

Autoregulation: over a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80-180 mmHg, myogenic afferent stretch reflexes and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa senses distal NaCl via NKCC2, releases adenosine → A1-mediated afferent constriction) hold GFR nearly constant. When perfusion falls, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the EFFERENT arteriole and prostaglandins (PGE2/PGI2) DILATE the afferent — this is the entire pharmacologic vulnerability: NSAIDs remove afferent dilation, ACEi/ARB remove efferent constriction, and calcineurin inhibitors and iodinated contrast cause afferent vasoconstriction.

The proximal tubule is the metabolic hotspot and the injury epicenter: it reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na+ using basolateral Na/K-ATPase, runs on oxidative phosphorylation, and sits in an outer medulla where PO2 is already 10-20 mmHg. Medullary O2 delivery and O2 demand are coupled to the same blood flow, so ischemia hits the S3 segment and the medullary thick ascending limb first.

Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is really a sequence: ATP depletion → Na/K-ATPase failure and cell swelling → loss of apical actin cytoskeleton and brush border → integrin mislocalization → cells slough into the lumen forming granular casts. Three mechanisms then perpetuate low GFR: (1) tubular obstruction raising Bowman's pressure, (2) BACKLEAK of filtrate across a denuded epithelium, and (3) sustained intrarenal vasoconstriction from endothelial injury (↓NO, ↑endothelin) plus leukocyte plugging of medullary capillaries.

Septic AKI is NOT simply ischemic necrosis: renal blood flow can be normal or high while GFR falls, driven by microcirculatory shunting, glycocalyx shedding, mitochondrial dysfunction/'hibernation,' TLR-mediated tubular inflammation, and efferent > afferent vasodilation that collapses filtration pressure. This is why chasing MAP with fluid alone does not fix it. [7]

Venous congestion is an under-taught mechanism: rising central venous pressure raises renal interstitial and Bowman's pressure in an encapsulated organ, compressing tubules and peritubular capillaries. In cardiorenal syndrome, decongestion — not fluid — restores GFR.

Why the labs move: loss of GFR retains urea and creatinine (azotemia), loss of distal K+ secretion (aldosterone-driven ENaC/ROMK flux depends on distal Na delivery) causes hyperkalemia, and loss of proximal ammoniagenesis/bicarbonate regeneration and titratable acid excretion produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
sections.mechanism: Every prerenal insult and every classic nephrotoxin maps onto one of three arteriolar/tubular levers: afferent tone (prostaglandins, contrast, calcineurin inhibitors, hypercalcemia), efferent tone (angiotensin II, ACEi/ARB), and tubular integrity/pressure (ischemia, toxins, obstruction). Naming the lever tells you the intervention.
sections.teaching_pearl: 'Prerenal' is a hemodynamic diagnosis, not a volume diagnosis. A patient in decompensated HF with a CVP of 20 and cold extremities is prerenal from low renal perfusion pressure and high renal venous pressure — giving fluid makes both worse.
sections.board_tip: Classic vignette triad for ATN vs prerenal: prerenal = urine Na <20, FENa <1%, bland sediment, BUN/Cr >20:1; ATN = urine Na >40, FENa >2%, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr ~10-15:1. FENa is unreliable on diuretics (use FEurea <35%) and is falsely LOW in contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis, hepatorenal syndrome, and early glomerulonephritis.

sections.heading: Definition, Staging, and the Three-Bucket Workup
points: KDIGO definition (harmonizing RIFLE and AKIN): Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, OR Cr rise ≥1.5× baseline known/presumed within 7 days, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage 1 = 1.5-1.9× baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dL rise; Stage 2 = 2.0-2.9×; Stage 3 = ≥3× baseline, Cr ≥4.0 mg/dL, initiation of RRT, or anuria ≥12 h. [1]

Remember the math: creatinine is a nonlinear marker. Cr 0.6 → 1.2 mg/dL is a 50% GFR loss but may be reported as 'normal.' In sarcopenic, cirrhotic, or amputee patients, and after large-volume resuscitation (dilution), Cr systematically underestimates injury. Oliguria often precedes the Cr rise by 12-24 h.

Bucket 1 — Prerenal/hemodynamic (~40-60% of inpatient AKI): true hypovolemia (GI losses, hemorrhage, diuretics), reduced effective arterial volume (HF, cirrhosis, sepsis, nephrotic syndrome), drug-mediated autoregulatory failure (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, calcineurin inhibitors), abdominal compartment syndrome, hepatorenal syndrome, and renal artery events.

Bucket 2 — Intrinsic: ATN (ischemic, septic, or toxic — aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cisplatin, contrast, myoglobin, hemoglobin, light chains); acute interstitial nephritis (AIN — beta-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, checkpoint inhibitors: pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab); glomerulonephritis/vasculitis; intratubular crystals (uric acid, acyclovir, methotrexate, oxalate); thrombotic microangiopathy; cholesterol emboli.

Bucket 3 — Postrenal: BPH/urinary retention, malignant or retroperitoneal obstruction, bilateral stones, neurogenic bladder, or a clotted/kinked Foley. Requires bilateral (or unilateral in a single functioning kidney) obstruction to raise Cr — and it is the most reversible bucket, which is why a bladder scan and renal US are early, not late, moves. [1]

Workup with a question attached to each test: urinalysis WITH microscopy (casts, dysmorphic RBCs, WBCs, eosinophils, crystals) asks 'is the parenchyma inflamed?'; urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio asks 'glomerular or tubular?'; renal US asks 'obstructed, and are the kidneys chronically small/echogenic?'; CK and LDH/haptoglobin/smear ask 'rhabdomyolysis or hemolysis/TMA?'; serologies (ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complements, SPEP/free light chains, hepatitis serologies) ask 'immunologic'; bladder pressure asks 'compartment syndrome.'
Biopsy when the cause remains unexplained, GN/vasculitis/myeloma kidney or drug-induced AIN is plausible, or the course does not fit — particularly when immunosuppression would change management.
sections.teaching_pearl: Muddy brown granular casts and 'renal tubular epithelial cell casts' are the only findings that let you diagnose ATN at the bedside. Look at the sediment yourself — the dipstick 'trace protein, trace blood' report is silent about casts, and the lab may not have spun it.
sections.board_tip: Pigmented casts + heme-positive dipstick with FEW RBCs on microscopy = myoglobin or free hemoglobin, not glomerular bleeding. Anion gap acidosis + AKI + calcium oxalate crystals = ethylene glycol; check the osmolar gap.

sections.heading: Management: What Actually Works, and When to Dialyze
points: Supportive care is the therapy (KDIGO 2012, and the framework survives into the update in review): optimize renal perfusion pressure, treat the primary cause, DISCONTINUE nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B), hold ACEi/ARB/SGLT2i during acute hemodynamic instability, dose-adjust all renally cleared drugs, avoid hyperglycemia, and ensure adequate nutrition (20-30 kcal/kg/d, do not protein-restrict to avoid dialysis). [1]

Fluids: give isotonic crystalloid for hypovolemic/prerenal AKI, then reassess with a dynamic measure (passive leg raise, pulse-pressure variation, POCUS IVC/lung B-lines) — not a static CVP. KDIGO recommends isotonic crystalloid over colloid as initial expansion; SMART showed balanced crystalloids reduced the composite of death, new RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction versus 0.9% saline in critically ill adults, arguing against large-volume chloride-rich resuscitation. [1,6]

Once the patient is fluid-unresponsive or congested, STOP fluids: positive fluid balance independently worsens AKI outcomes via renal interstitial edema and venous congestion. In septic shock, add vasopressors targeting MAP ~65 mmHg (higher in chronic HTN) to restore glomerular perfusion pressure; norepinephrine is first-line and vasopressin is a reasonable second agent, per Surviving Sepsis 2021. [7]

Things NOT to do, all mechanism-based failures: low-dose ('renal-dose') dopamine — no benefit, more arrhythmia; loop diuretics to 'convert' oliguric to non-oliguric AKI — they improve urine output and volume control ONLY, they do not improve GFR, recovery, or mortality (KDIGO recommends against diuretics for treating AKI, other than for volume overload); mannitol; natriuretic peptides. Diuretic responsiveness is a prognostic marker, not a treatment. [1]

Contrast-associated AKI: risk is real but overstated in modern practice. PRESERVE found NO benefit of IV sodium bicarbonate over saline and NO benefit of oral N-acetylcysteine over placebo for death, dialysis, or persistent kidney impairment after angiography. Practice: use isotonic crystalloid periprocedural volume expansion in high-risk patients (CKD, diabetes, hypovolemia), minimize contrast volume, and do not withhold a needed CT for a mild creatinine bump. [5]

Specific etiologies get specific mechanisms: rhabdomyolysis → aggressive isotonic fluid to flush myoglobin casts; tumor lysis → hydration plus rasburicase; obstruction → catheter, nephrostomy, or stent immediately; AIN → stop the drug, consider corticosteroids; ANCA/anti-GBM → immunosuppression ± plasma exchange; hepatorenal syndrome-AKI → albumin plus terlipressin, which improved HRS reversal versus placebo in CONFIRM (watch for ischemic and respiratory adverse events), with midodrine/octreotide plus albumin as an alternative where terlipressin is unavailable. [9]

RRT indications are refractory, not numeric: hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction/bleeding), or a dialyzable poison (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylate). KDIGO says initiate emergently for life-threatening changes and otherwise consider the broader clinical context, not a single BUN or Cr. [1]

Timing evidence: ELAIN (single-center, surgical) suggested early benefit, but AKIKI and the large multinational STARRT-AKI trial both showed accelerated initiation gave no mortality benefit; STARRT-AKI showed MORE dialysis dependence at 90 days in the accelerated arm, and ~40% of the standard-strategy patients never needed RRT at all. Watchful waiting with explicit trigger criteria is the default. [2,3,8]

Modality: continuous RRT and intermittent hemodialysis are equivalent for survival and renal recovery; choose CRRT for hemodynamic instability, cerebral edema/acute brain injury (avoid osmolar shifts), and precise volume control. Use regional citrate anticoagulation for CRRT circuits when not contraindicated, and prefer a non-tunneled internal jugular or femoral catheter over subclavian to protect future vascular access. [1]
sections.mechanism: Nothing pharmacologic reverses established tubular injury, so all effective therapy works by removing the ongoing insult (nephrotoxin, obstruction, hypoperfusion, congestion) and buying time for the surviving proximal tubular cells to dedifferentiate, migrate, and repopulate the denuded basement membrane. Diuretics fail because they act on the loop of Henle to move salt and water — they do nothing to glomerular filtration pressure or tubular repair.
sections.teaching_pearl: Say out loud on rounds: 'Is this patient fluid-RESPONSIVE, and are they fluid-TOLERANT?' Those are two different questions, and the second one is where housestaff drown AKI patients.
sections.board_tip: On the boards, the wrong answers in an oliguric AKI vignette are almost always 'start low-dose dopamine,' 'give a furosemide drip to increase urine output,' 'give N-acetylcysteine,' or 'start dialysis for a BUN of 90 in an asymptomatic patient.' The right answer is usually a mechanistic one: stop the offending drug, relieve the obstruction, or correct the hemodynamics. [1,2,3,5]

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: AKI complicates roughly 10-15% of all hospitalizations and up to ~50% of ICU admissions; incidence and severity track directly with mortality independent of the inciting illness.

Mortality is stage-dependent and steep: mild stage 1 AKI carries modestly increased in-hospital death, whereas stage 3 AKI requiring RRT in the ICU carries a short-term mortality on the order of 40-60% in randomized-trial populations — in STARRT-AKI, 90-day mortality was approximately 43-44% in BOTH the accelerated and standard-initiation arms. [3]
Even a small, transient creatinine rise (≥0.3 mg/dL) is independently associated with longer length of stay, higher cost, and higher mortality — which is why the KDIGO threshold was set that low. [1]

Renal recovery is not guaranteed: among survivors of dialysis-requiring AKI, a substantial minority remain dialysis-dependent at 90 days (approximately 10% in the STARRT-AKI standard-strategy arm and higher with accelerated initiation), and repeated or prolonged AKI episodes drive maladaptive repair with interstitial fibrosis, capillary rarefaction, and nephron loss. [3]

Prognosis is driven by: AKI stage and duration, need for RRT, oliguria, sepsis as the etiology, number of failing organs, pre-existing CKD and albuminuria, and cumulative fluid balance. Pre-existing albuminuria is one of the strongest predictors of both AKI risk and non-recovery. [4]

The AKI-to-CKD transition is the actionable long-term teaching point: per KDIGO 2024, AKI survivors should be re-evaluated with eGFR and albuminuria at ~3 months to define whether they now have CKD, and then risk-stratified and treated with the standard cardiorenal backbone (RASi, SGLT2i for eligible proteinuric CKD at eGFR ≥20, BP and metabolic control) rather than discharged with an unexplained creatinine and no follow-up. [4]
sections.teaching_pearl: The discharge summary is a therapeutic instrument in AKI. Document the baseline Cr, the peak Cr, the presumed mechanism, which nephrotoxins were held and whether they should be restarted, and a specific date for a repeat BMP and urine ACR.
sections.board_tip: A patient recovering from stage 3 AKI whose creatinine plateaus above baseline at 3 months with new albuminuria HAS CKD — stage it with eGFR and ACR and start guideline-directed therapy, per KDIGO 2024. Do not label it 'resolved AKI.' [4]

claude_errors: Outcomes section misassigns STARRT-AKI dialysis dependence: it states ~10% dialysis dependence at 90 days in the STANDARD-strategy arm 'and higher with accelerated initiation.' The actual figures are 10.4% in the accelerated arm vs 6.0% in the standard arm — this also contradicts the correct statement made earlier in the management section.

Minor: states loss of proximal ammoniagenesis/bicarbonate regeneration 'produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis' — impaired proximal HCO3 handling/reduced NH4+ excretion classically produces a normal-anion-gap acidosis early in AKI; the high-gap component reflects retained unmeasured anions in advanced uremia.

Minor: quoted glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (~45–50 mmHg) and Bowman pressure (~10–15 mmHg) are rat micropuncture-derived figures presented as human values (commonly cited as ~55–60/~15–18); not a clinically consequential error but stated with false precision.
judge.why: Both are guideline-faithful (correct KDIGO 2012 definition/staging, correct 'complication-driven, not number-driven' dialysis framing, correct characterization of AKIKI/STARRT-AKI/SMART, correct KDIGO caveat that diuretics are for volume overload rather than AKI treatment). B is essentially error-free and reports trial numbers exactly, including the direction of the STARRT-AKI dialysis-dependence signal, and adds high-yield safety points A omits (pseudo-AKI from trimethoprim/cobicistat, uselessness of urine eosinophils, post-obstructive diuresis monitoring). A, however, delivers considerably more mechanistic and actionable teaching for an IM resident — afferent/efferent lever framework mapped to drugs, S3/mTAL medullary hypoxia, backleak/obstruction/vasoconstriction as perpetuators, septic AKI without global ischemia, venous congestion in cardiorenal syndrome, FENa pitfalls with directionality, specific etiologic therapies (rasburicase, terlipressin/CONFIRM, steroids for AIN), CRRT vs IHD and catheter-site guidance, PRESERVE for contrast, and a concrete AKI-to-CKD transition plan anchored to KDIGO 2024 — with citations that genuinely support the claims made. A's single reversed STARRT-AKI statistic is a real error and costs it an accuracy point, but it is internally contradicted by the correct version elsewhere and does not change management teaching; on balance A is the stronger teaching artifact.

talk.title: Severe AKI Without an Urgent Dialysis Indication
talk.subtitle: RRT timing in hemodynamically stabilized acute tubular injury
guideline_sources: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)
talk.key_point: In severe AKI, initiate RRT for life-threatening complications rather than an isolated creatinine or BUN threshold.[1]

abim_classification.specific_topic: Timing of renal replacement therapy in severe AKI

board_pearls: RRT corrects otherwise refractory electrolyte, acid-base, volume, and uremic complications; it does not directly accelerate tubular recovery.

KDIGO 2012 recommends emergent RRT for life-threatening fluid, electrolyte, or acid-base abnormalities and advises using the overall clinical context rather than isolated BUN or creatinine thresholds; these statements are not graded.[1]
Despite stage 3 AKI and oliguria, this patient lacks the key discriminator favoring immediate RRT: refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidemia, pulmonary edema, or symptomatic uremia.
The STARRT-AKI and AKIKI trials found no mortality benefit from accelerated or early RRT initiation in critically ill patients without urgent indications.[2,3]
The common trap is treating a high creatinine or BUN value as an independent dialysis indication; trends, symptoms, and treatable complications determine timing.[1]
teaching_points: Granular casts after septic shock support ischemic or septic acute tubular injury rather than persistent prerenal azotemia.
Continue kidney-adjusted medications, avoid nephrotoxins, optimize hemodynamics, and serially monitor urine output, electrolytes, acid-base status, and volume status.
KDIGO suggests not using diuretics to treat AKI except for management of volume overload.[1]
summary_points: Severe AKI alone does not mandate immediate RRT when potassium, acid-base status, volume, and uremic manifestations remain medically manageable.[1-3]

question.stem:
A 67-year-old man is evaluated in the ICU for worsening kidney function 3 days after admission with septic shock from pneumonia. He initially required norepinephrine and mechanical ventilation but is now extubated and hemodynamically stable after antibiotics and fluids. Urine output has fallen to 420 mL over the past 24 hours. Medications are adjusted for kidney function, and no contrast or NSAIDs have been given.

Temperature 37.1 C, BP 116/68 mm Hg, HR 88/min, RR 18/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. He is alert and conversant. There are faint bibasilar crackles, trace leg edema, and no pericardial rub.

Creatinine is 5.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), BUN 96 mg/dL, potassium 5.3 mEq/L, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, and arterial pH 7.32. Urinalysis shows granular casts. CXR shows improving infiltrates without pulmonary edema.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation:
KDIGO 2012 states that RRT should be initiated emergently when life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, or acid-base balance exist. It also advises considering the broader clinical context and laboratory trends rather than using a single BUN or creatinine threshold; both statements are ungraded.[1]

This patient has severe oliguric AKI from septic acute tubular injury, supported by the preceding shock and granular casts. However, potassium 5.3 mEq/L and pH 7.32 are not refractory emergencies, CXR excludes pulmonary edema, and he has no uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis, or bleeding. Therefore, supportive care with serial monitoring is appropriate. This includes maintaining adequate perfusion, avoiding nephrotoxins, adjusting medication doses, and monitoring for evolving RRT indications.

Trial evidence reinforces this approach: STARRT-AKI and AKIKI demonstrated no survival advantage from accelerated or early RRT in critically ill patients with severe AKI who lacked urgent indications; accelerated initiation also increased treatment exposure and adverse events in STARRT-AKI.[2,3]

wrong_explanations.why: The mild metabolic acidosis is not a life-threatening or refractory indication for bicarbonate or RRT. IV bicarbonate also adds sodium and may worsen volume status.
Intermittent hemodialysis would be appropriate for an urgent indication in a hemodynamically stable patient, but severe azotemia alone does not establish that indication.
KDIGO suggests avoiding diuretics as treatment for AKI except to manage volume overload. Furosemide may increase urine output without improving kidney recovery or survival.[1]
Continuous kidney replacement therapy is generally favored when RRT is necessary in hemodynamically unstable patients. This patient is stable and, more importantly, has no current indication for RRT.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must identify acute tubular injury, distinguish AKI severity from dialysis indications, assess each potential urgent complication, and apply evidence against accelerated RRT.
reasoning_steps: Identify intrinsic acute tubular injury from septic shock, oliguria, and granular casts.
Recognize that the markedly elevated creatinine and BUN establish severe AKI but are not independent indications for RRT.
Assess for urgent RRT indications: refractory hyperkalemia or acidemia, pulmonary edema, uremic complications, or dialyzable intoxication.
Apply KDIGO guidance and RRT-timing trial evidence to continue supportive care with close monitoring.

talk.title: Oliguric AKI After Septic Shock: When to Start Dialysis
talk.subtitle: Applying KDIGO 2012 AKI and the STARRT-AKI/AKIKI timing trials at the bedside
guideline_sources: KDIGO 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury
STARRT-AKI (NEJM 2020)
AKIKI (NEJM 2016)
BICAR-ICU (Lancet 2018)
talk.key_point: In AKI without refractory hyperkalemia, acidemia, volume overload, or uremic complications, defer renal replacement therapy and continue supportive care — accelerated initiation confers no survival benefit.

abim_classification.specific_topic: AKI: timing of renal replacement therapy initiation

board_pearls: Sepsis-associated AKI reflects microvascular/inflammatory tubular injury rather than pure hypoperfusion; restoring MAP does not immediately restore GFR, so oliguria may persist for days while tubules recover.

KDIGO 2012 AKI states RRT should be initiated emergently for life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance, and that the decision should rest on the broad clinical context — not on BUN or creatinine thresholds alone.

The discriminator between watchful waiting and starting CVVH is the presence of a hard indication: refractory hyperkalemia, refractory acidemia, diuretic-unresponsive volume overload, uremic encephalopathy/pericarditis/bleeding, or a dialyzable toxin — none of which are present here.

STARRT-AKI (2020), AKIKI (2016), and IDEAL-ICU (2018) all showed no mortality benefit from accelerated RRT; STARRT-AKI found more adverse events and more 90-day dialysis dependence with the accelerated strategy.
The classic trap is treating a rising creatinine plus stage 3 oliguria as an automatic dialysis trigger; roughly 40-50% of deferred patients in AKIKI/STARRT-AKI never required RRT at all.
teaching_points: Stage AKI by both creatinine and urine output, but let indications — not stage — drive the decision to dialyze.
Bicarbonate therapy in AKI has trial support only for severe acidemia (pH <7.20) in AKIN stage 2-3, not for mild metabolic acidosis.
Low-dose dopamine, mannitol, and loop diuretics do not prevent or reverse AKI and do not reduce the need for RRT; loop diuretics only manage volume.
summary_points: Oliguric stage 3 AKI after resolved septic shock, without urgent metabolic or volume indications, is managed with continued supportive care, nephrotoxin avoidance, and hemodynamic optimization while reassessing frequently [1,2,3].

question.stem:
A 64-year-old man is evaluated in the ICU on hospital day 4 for persistent oliguria. He was admitted with pneumococcal pneumonia and septic shock requiring norepinephrine, vancomycin, and piperacillin-tazobactam. Vasopressors were stopped 24 hours ago and antibiotics were narrowed to ceftriaxone. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 mg/dL on admission to 3.6 mg/dL. Urine output has been 0.3 mL/kg/h over the past 14 hours despite an adequate mean arterial pressure. He is extubated, alert, and denies nausea, hiccups, or confusion.

Temperature 37.1 C, BP 122/70 mm Hg, HR 82/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on 2 L nasal cannula. JVP is normal, lungs are clear, and there is trace ankle edema. No asterixis or pericardial rub.

Sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, BUN 62 mg/dL, creatinine 3.6 mg/dL. Arterial pH 7.32, PCO2 36 mm Hg. Renal US shows no hydronephrosis.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Perform a furosemide stress test to trigger dialysis
Withhold renal replacement therapy and monitor closely

question.explanation:
KDIGO 2012 AKI recommends initiating RRT emergently when life-threatening changes in fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance are present, and states that the decision should be based on the broader clinical context and trends rather than on isolated BUN/creatinine thresholds. This patient has KDIGO stage 3 AKI by urine output, but no urgent indication: potassium is 4.8 mEq/L, pH is 7.32 with a modest bicarbonate of 19 mEq/L, he is euvolemic with clear lungs on minimal oxygen, and there are no uremic manifestations (no encephalopathy, asterixis, pericardial rub, or bleeding). The reversible insult — septic shock — has resolved with vasopressors off for 24 hours, so tubular recovery is plausible.

This strategy is directly supported by the RRT timing trials. AKIKI (2016), IDEAL-ICU (2018), and STARRT-AKI (2020) all showed no mortality benefit from accelerated initiation; in STARRT-AKI the accelerated arm had more adverse events (hypotension, hypophosphatemia, catheter complications) and greater 90-day dialysis dependence, and in AKIKI roughly half of deferred patients never required RRT.

Appropriate management is therefore watchful waiting with frequent reassessment: avoid further nephrotoxins (vancomycin already discontinued), avoid iodinated contrast, maintain perfusion pressure, renally dose medications, avoid fluid overload, and monitor potassium, acid-base status, volume, and mental status at least daily so that RRT can be started promptly if a true indication develops.

wrong_explanations.why: BICAR-ICU showed benefit of bicarbonate only in severe acidemia (pH <7.20) with AKIN stage 2-3 injury. At pH 7.32 with bicarbonate 19 mEq/L, alkali therapy adds sodium and volume without benefit and may worsen hypocalcemia.

No urgent indication exists. Accelerated RRT initiation in this exact population produced no survival benefit in STARRT-AKI, AKIKI, or IDEAL-ICU, and increased catheter-related complications and long-term dialysis dependence.
Low-dose (renal-dose) dopamine does not prevent or reverse AKI, does not reduce RRT need or mortality, and increases tachyarrhythmias. It is explicitly discouraged by KDIGO 2012.

The furosemide stress test is a prognostic research tool that predicts progression to stage 3 AKI; it is not a guideline-endorsed trigger for dialysis, and a diuretic response would not change the absence of RRT indications here.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must stage the AKI, recognize that a resolving reversible insult with no metabolic or volume indication does not mandate dialysis, and reject three physiologically tempting but evidence-refuted interventions.
reasoning_steps: Recognize sepsis-associated AKI, now KDIGO stage 3 by urine output, with the precipitating insult resolving (vasopressors off 24 hours, antibiotics narrowed, nephrotoxic vancomycin stopped).
Systematically check for urgent RRT indications: potassium 4.8 mEq/L, pH 7.32, euvolemic with clear lungs, no uremic encephalopathy/pericarditis/bleeding, no dialyzable toxin — none present.
Apply KDIGO 2012: initiate RRT based on the clinical context and life-threatening derangements, not on absolute BUN/creatinine values.
Apply the timing trials (AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU, STARRT-AKI): accelerated initiation offers no mortality benefit and increases harm and dialysis dependence, so defer.
Eliminate the pharmacologic distractors — bicarbonate is indicated only below pH 7.20, dopamine is non-renoprotective, and the furosemide stress test is prognostic rather than a dialysis trigger.

claude_errors: Stem/explanation label the patient 'KDIGO stage 3 AKI by urine output' with UOP 0.3 mL/kg/h for 14 hours; KDIGO stage 3 by urine output requires <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h — this is stage 2 by urine output (stage 3 is met only by the 4-fold creatinine rise).
'Roughly 40-50% of deferred patients in AKIKI/STARRT-AKI never required RRT' overstates STARRT-AKI, where ~62% of the standard-strategy arm received RRT (~38% did not); AKIKI ~49% is accurate.

BICAR-ICU is described as showing 'benefit ... in AKIN stage 2-3' without noting the overall primary outcome was neutral and the AKIN 2-3 finding was a prespecified subgroup — a mild overstatement of evidence strength.
ABIM blueprint weight listed as '6%' for 'AKI: timing of RRT'; 6% is the weight of the entire nephrology category, not this topic.
IDEAL-ICU is cited three times as supporting evidence but appears nowhere in the reference list (minor citation gap).
judge.why: Both artifacts reach the same correct teaching point (dialyze for indications, not for numbers) and both represent KDIGO 2012 faithfully, including the fact that the emergent-RRT and 'broader clinical context' statements are Not Graded — a nuance A states explicitly, which is exemplary citation honesty. A contains no identifiable factual error, its distractors are cleanly justified (diuretics per KDIGO 2C, CRRT preference in hemodynamic instability per KDIGO 2B), and every claim maps to a listed source. B has greater teaching breadth (dopamine, furosemide stress test, bicarbonate thresholds, IDEAL-ICU, deferral statistics) and its distractor explanations are pedagogically richer, but it contains a concrete staging error, a stretched trial statistic, a subgroup-as-trial-result overstatement, an inflated blueprint weight, and cites IDEAL-ICU without referencing it. Weighting accuracy and citation honesty as instructed, A wins narrowly; a resident would learn more breadth from B but would also absorb the incorrect urine-output staging rule.

talk.title: Cirrhosis with Hepatorenal Syndrome
talk.subtitle: HRS-AKI: arterial underfilling, functional renal vasoconstriction, and urgent reversal
guideline_sources: AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance on Ascites, Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis, and Hepatorenal Syndrome
ADQI-ICA 2024 Joint Consensus on Acute Kidney Injury in Cirrhosis
FDA 2022 terlipressin prescribing information
summary_points: Hepatorenal syndrome–acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) is driven by portal hypertension–induced splanchnic vasodilation, reduced effective arterial blood volume, and compensatory renal vasoconstriction; the kidneys may initially be structurally intact.

Suspect HRS-AKI when AKI occurs in cirrhosis with ascites, especially after infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, overdiuresis, or large-volume paracentesis without adequate albumin. A bland urine sediment and low proteinuria support—but do not prove—the diagnosis.

Exclude shock, obstruction, nephrotoxins, hypovolemia, and structural kidney injury. The ADQI-ICA 2024 consensus no longer requires automatic 48-hour albumin administration when the patient is euvolemic or overloaded; assess volume and response to appropriate resuscitation promptly. [2]

Per AASLD 2021, vasoconstrictor therapy plus albumin is recommended, with terlipressin preferred where available; liver transplantation is the definitive treatment. Terlipressin subsequently received FDA approval in 2022. [1,4]

The common pitfall is reflexively giving more albumin to every patient with rising Cr. Albumin can improve true arterial underfilling but may precipitate pulmonary edema and respiratory failure when congestion is already present, especially during terlipressin treatment. [2-4]
