sections.heading: 1. Physiology First: Why the Kidney Fails
points: Portal hypertension increases shear stress and bacterial-product signaling in the splanchnic circulation. Endothelial nitric oxide, carbon monoxide, and vasodilatory peptides lower splanchnic vascular resistance, sequestering blood outside the effective arterial compartment despite normal or increased total body water.

Arterial underfilling unloads carotid and renal baroreceptors, activating the sympathetic nervous system, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and nonosmotic ADH release. Angiotensin II and sympathetic tone constrict renal vessels; aldosterone and ADH retain sodium and water, producing ascites, edema, and dilutional hyponatremia.

Early cirrhosis is compensated by increased cardiac output. With progression, vasodilation intensifies while cirrhotic cardiomyopathy limits contractile reserve; mean arterial pressure and renal perfusion pressure fall, particularly during infection, bleeding, diuresis, or anesthesia.

Intrarenal vasoconstriction lowers renal blood flow and GFR. Increased proximal sodium reabsorption leaves little sodium for the distal nephron, so urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) are often low—but these indices are not diagnostic because advanced cirrhosis and diuretics distort them.

Systemic inflammation, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and bile acids can also injure tubular and endothelial cells. HRS-AKI therefore exists on a continuum with acute tubular injury rather than as a perfectly pure, reversible prerenal state.

The older terms HRS type 1 and type 2 have been replaced by HRS-AKI and non-AKI phenotypes such as HRS-AKD or HRS-CKD, emphasizing the tempo of Cr change rather than an arbitrary terminal Cr threshold. [2]
sections.mechanism: The central lesion is not total-body volume depletion but severe arterial underfilling. Neurohormonal compensation preserves systemic pressure at the cost of intense renal vasoconstriction, while sodium and water retention worsen ascites without adequately restoring effective arterial volume.
sections.teaching_pearl: A patient can be edematous, have tense ascites, and still have inadequate effective arterial filling; total-body fluid and arterial perfusion are different variables.
sections.board_tip: HRS-AKI is a functional hemodynamic diagnosis, but prolonged vasoconstriction and inflammation can evolve into structural tubular injury.

sections.heading: 2. Recognition and Workup: HRS Is a Diagnosis of Exclusion
points: Recognize AKI as an increase in serum Cr of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or at least 50% from baseline within 7 days. In cirrhosis, a seemingly modest rise is important because low muscle mass and reduced hepatic creatine production cause Cr to overestimate kidney function. [2]

Look immediately for precipitants: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) or another infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, diarrhea, vomiting, excessive diuresis, recent large-volume paracentesis, iodinated contrast, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, aminoglycosides, or shock.

Perform diagnostic paracentesis in hospitalized patients with cirrhosis and ascites. An ascitic polymorphonuclear leukocyte count of at least 250 cells/mm3 establishes SBP and should trigger immediate antibiotics plus albumin. [1]

Order BMP/CMP, CBC, urinalysis with microscopy, urine protein quantification, cultures as indicated, and renal US when obstruction is plausible. Granular casts, substantial proteinuria or hematuria, nephrotic-range protein loss, or abnormal kidney morphology should redirect the differential toward structural disease.

Assess volume using history, orthostatic findings, perfusion, pulmonary examination, urine output, bedside US/echo when available, and response to carefully selected fluid. Exclude untreated shock and stop nephrotoxins and diuretics during the initial evaluation.

AASLD 2021 uses diuretic withdrawal and an albumin challenge—1 g/kg/day, maximum 100 g/day, for up to 2 days—when AKI does not resolve with initial risk-factor management. The newer ADQI-ICA 2024 consensus advises against making 48 hours of albumin mandatory: if intravascular depletion is present, resuscitate and assess response within approximately 24 hours; if euvolemic or overloaded, avoid reflex albumin loading. [1,2]

HRS-AKI is favored by cirrhosis with ascites, qualifying AKI, failure to improve after adequate volume restoration when indicated, and absence of a stronger explanation such as shock, obstruction, glomerulonephritis, drug-induced injury, or acute tubular injury. [2]
sections.mechanism: Each test separates potentially reversible arterial underfilling from structural or obstructive kidney disease. Albumin is informative only when reduced central blood volume is plausible; failure to respond suggests that persistent vasodilation and renal vasoconstriction—not simple fluid loss—are maintaining the AKI.
sections.teaching_pearl: Urine sodium, FENa, and fractional excretion of urea may support the hemodynamic picture, but none can distinguish HRS-AKI reliably from other causes on its own.
sections.board_tip: Do not diagnose HRS merely because a patient has cirrhosis and low urine sodium; septic acute tubular injury is common and can coexist with HRS physiology.

sections.heading: 3. Treatment: Reverse Vasodilation, Protect the Lungs, Bridge to Transplant
points: Treat the precipitant immediately: control bleeding, obtain cultures and treat infection, stop NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins, hold diuretics during active AKI, and correct true hypovolemia. For SBP, give an appropriate third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3; this strategy reduces renal impairment and mortality. [1,5]

GUIDELINE-RECOMMENDED: Per AASLD 2021, use a vasoconstrictor plus albumin for HRS-AKI, with terlipressin preferred where available. The guidance predates US approval, but terlipressin received FDA approval in 2022 for adults with HRS and rapidly declining kidney function. [1,4]

Terlipressin is a vasopressin analogue whose active metabolite stimulates V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle. Splanchnic vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance, improves effective arterial filling and mean arterial pressure, suppresses maladaptive RAAS/sympathetic activation, and thereby improves renal perfusion.

Give concentrated albumin alongside vasoconstrictor therapy, commonly 20–40 g/day after initial resuscitation, but individualize to hemodynamics and congestion. Albumin expands plasma volume and binds inflammatory mediators, yet excessive dosing increases pulmonary hydrostatic pressure.

In CONFIRM, verified HRS reversal occurred in 32% with terlipressin versus 17% with placebo, establishing efficacy for renal reversal; however, it did not demonstrate a clear 90-day survival advantage and produced more serious respiratory complications. [3]

Before and during terlipressin, assess oxygen saturation and volume status. Do not initiate it in hypoxemia, and discontinue it for worsening hypoxia or ischemic complications; ongoing coronary, peripheral, or mesenteric ischemia is a contraindication. Benefit is less likely and toxicity greater with very advanced acute-on-chronic liver failure or markedly elevated Cr. [3,4]

If terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated, norepinephrine plus albumin is the preferred ICU alternative and requires continuous monitoring. Midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin is an AASLD-listed fallback when neither terlipressin nor norepinephrine can be used, but its efficacy is substantially lower. [1]

Start liver transplant evaluation at diagnosis because pharmacologic reversal is a bridge, not definitive therapy. Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is reserved for standard indications—refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary edema, or uremic complications—and is most appropriate as a bridge to transplant or recovery from a reversible insult. [1]

For large-volume paracentesis greater than 5 L, give albumin 6–8 g per liter removed to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, which otherwise intensifies arterial underfilling and may precipitate HRS-AKI. [1]
sections.mechanism: Terlipressin addresses the upstream hemodynamic lesion by constricting the pathologically dilated splanchnic vascular bed; albumin supports central plasma volume. Together they redirect blood toward the effective arterial circulation, but excessive afterload or intravascular expansion can cause ischemia and pulmonary edema.
sections.teaching_pearl: A rising mean arterial pressure during vasoconstrictor therapy is a mechanistic sign that effective arterial filling is improving; follow Cr and urine output to determine whether the kidney responds.
sections.board_tip: Terlipressin reverses HRS-AKI in some patients but is not a substitute for transplantation and should never be continued through worsening hypoxemia. [3,4]

sections.heading: 4. Outcomes & Prognosis
points: HRS-AKI signals advanced circulatory failure and carries high short-term mortality, especially when accompanied by infection, shock, severe acute-on-chronic liver failure, progressive bilirubin or international normalized ratio elevation, or failure of Cr to improve.

Response is more likely when therapy begins before severe kidney dysfunction develops and when vasoconstrictors produce a meaningful rise in mean arterial pressure. High baseline Cr, minimal hemodynamic response, and multiorgan failure predict nonresponse.
CONFIRM demonstrated improved HRS reversal but no clear improvement in 90-day survival, underscoring that correcting renal hemodynamics does not reverse the underlying hepatic failure. [3]

Liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment. Kidney function may recover after liver transplantation when injury is predominantly functional, whereas prolonged AKI, preexisting CKD, or substantial tubular injury increases the probability of persistent kidney dysfunction and possible need for simultaneous liver-kidney transplantation. [1]
sections.mechanism: Vasoconstrictors can temporarily correct renal perfusion, but portal hypertension, hepatic failure, systemic inflammation, and cirrhotic cardiomyopathy persist. Prognosis therefore depends on hepatic recovery or transplantation, not Cr reversal alone.
sections.teaching_pearl: Successful HRS reversal is clinically valuable as a bridge to transplantation, but it is a surrogate renal endpoint—not proof that the patient's underlying mortality risk has resolved.
sections.board_tip: Evaluate transplant candidacy early rather than waiting to see whether terlipressin normalizes Cr.

Failure to raise MAP on vasoconstrictors predicts non-response.","Recurrence after successful reversal is common, which reinforces that vasoconstrictor therapy buys time — the durable outcome comes from liver transplantation, after which most patients recover kidney function, though pre-transplant AKI duration predicts persistent CKD.","Practical implications: refer early for transplant evaluation (an AKI episode is itself an indication to escalate listing urgency), avoid iatrogenic precipitants, and integrate palliative care discussions when a patient with recurrent HRS is not a transplant candidate — that population has a prognosis comparable to advanced malignancy."],"teaching_pearl":"HRS-AKI is not really a kidney prognosis — it is a marker of end-stage hepatic hemodynamics. Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion: cirrhosis with ascites, KDIGO-defined AKI, NO improvement after 2 days off diuretics plus albumin 1 g/kg/day, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and a bland urine (protein <500 mg/day, <50 RBC/hpf, normal renal US). FENa <0.2% and urine Na <10 mEq/L support it but do not define it.
Always hunt the precipitant: SBP or other infection, GI bleed, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, overdiuresis, or NSAIDs. Treating the trigger is as important as the vasoconstrictor.

First-line therapy per AASLD 2021 is terlipressin plus albumin — a V1 agonist that constricts the splanchnic bed, refills the effective arterial volume, and switches off the renal vasoconstrictor reflex. Norepinephrine + albumin is the ICU alternative; midodrine/octreotide/albumin is the weakest option.
Terlipressin carries an FDA boxed warning for serious/fatal respiratory failure (CONFIRM: 11% vs 2%) — do not start it in hypoxemic or volume-overloaded patients, and give albumin judiciously.

Liver transplantation is the only definitive cure. Untreated HRS-AKI carries very high short-term mortality, and need for prolonged dialysis pre-transplant should trigger consideration of simultaneous liver-kidney transplant.

sections.heading: The Physiology: Why a Normal Kidney Stops Working
points: Start at the sinusoid. Fibrosis plus activated stellate cells raise intrahepatic resistance → portal hypertension. Increased portal pressure and shear stress upregulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase in the SPLANCHNIC arterial bed, and bacterial translocation from a leaky gut delivers PAMPs (LPS) that drive further NO, carbon monoxide, prostacyclin, and endocannabinoid release.

The result is progressive splanchnic ARTERIAL vasodilation. Blood pools in a dilated mesenteric bed, so despite total body sodium and water OVERLOAD (ascites, edema), the EFFECTIVE arterial blood volume falls. This is the central paradox of cirrhosis: the patient is volume-overloaded and simultaneously arterially underfilled.

Carotid and aortic baroreceptors sense the low effective volume and unleash three neurohormonal systems: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (angiotensin II), sympathetic nervous system (norepinephrine), and non-osmotic ADH release. Aldosterone drives avid distal sodium retention (urine Na often <10 mEq/L); ADH drives free-water retention → dilutional hyponatremia, a marker of how activated the axis is.

Early cirrhosis compensates by raising cardiac output. Late cirrhosis cannot: CIRRHOTIC CARDIOMYOPATHY (blunted beta-adrenergic responsiveness, impaired contractile reserve, QT prolongation) means cardiac output plateaus or falls just as vasodilation worsens. Mean arterial pressure drops, and renal perfusion pressure becomes critically dependent on the vasoconstrictor reflex.

At the kidney: angiotensin II, norepinephrine, and endothelin-1 constrict the afferent arteriole; renal blood flow falls and the autoregulatory curve is shifted rightward, so GFR becomes pressure-dependent. Compensatory intrarenal vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) are the last line of defense — which is exactly why an NSAID can convert compensated cirrhosis into HRS overnight.

Modern framing adds a second hit: SYSTEMIC INFLAMMATION. Circulating PAMPs/DAMPs and cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6) cause direct renal microvascular dysfunction and tubular stress, which is why infection — especially SBP — is the classic precipitant and why HRS and acute tubular injury frequently coexist on a spectrum rather than as clean silos.

Bottom line: in HRS the nephron is histologically normal. Kidneys from HRS patients transplanted into others work. The lesion lives in the circulation, not the kidney — and that dictates the entire treatment strategy.
sections.mechanism: Portal hypertension → NO/prostacyclin-mediated splanchnic vasodilation → reduced effective arterial volume → baroreceptor-driven RAAS/SNS/ADH activation → intense renal afferent vasoconstriction with preserved renal histology. Fix the arterial circulation and the GFR returns.
sections.teaching_pearl: HRS is 'the right kidney in the wrong circulation.' If you find yourself reaching for a kidney biopsy, you are usually solving the wrong problem — look at the splanchnic bed and the mean arterial pressure instead.
sections.board_tip: Hyponatremia, low urine sodium, refractory ascites, and a rising creatinine in a cirrhotic patient = maximally activated RAAS/ADH. That constellation identifies the patient at highest risk of HRS BEFORE the creatinine climbs.

sections.heading: Making the Diagnosis: AKI in Cirrhosis Is a Three-Way Fork
points: Frame every cirrhotic AKI as one of three things: (1) hypovolemic/prerenal AKI (overdiuresis, GI bleed, diarrhea from lactulose) — responds to volume; (2) acute tubular injury (shock, sepsis, contrast, aminoglycosides, bile-acid nephrosis) — granular casts, higher urine sodium; (3) HRS-AKI — functional, volume-unresponsive vasoconstriction. Post-renal obstruction and intrinsic glomerular disease (IgA in alcohol-related liver disease, membranoproliferative pattern in HCV) round out the differential [5].

AASLD 2021 / ICA criteria for HRS-AKI: cirrhosis with ascites; AKI by KDIGO staging (Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥50% from baseline within 7 days); NO response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal PLUS albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day); absence of shock; no current or recent nephrotoxins; and no evidence of structural injury — proteinuria <500 mg/day, <50 RBC/hpf, normal renal ultrasound [1,2].

Note what the modern definition DROPPED: the old fixed creatinine threshold of 2.5 mg/dL and the rigid 'type 1 vs type 2' labels. We now say HRS-AKI (rapidly progressive, the old type 1) and HRS-NAKI (HRS-CKD/AKD, the old type 2 with refractory ascites), because waiting for Cr 2.5 delayed therapy and worsened outcomes [2].

Serum creatinine systematically OVERESTIMATES GFR in cirrhosis: sarcopenia lowers creatinine generation, hyperbilirubinemia interferes with the Jaffe assay, and urea synthesis is impaired so BUN is low. A 'normal' Cr of 1.0 in a cachectic cirrhotic may represent a GFR of 40. Trend the creatinine from the patient's own best recent baseline, not from the lab's reference range.

Supportive labs: FENa <0.2%, urine Na <10 mEq/L, urine osmolality > serum, bland sediment, oliguria. These are typical but NOT diagnostic — and diuretics or prior ATN will muddy them. Urinary NGAL, where available, is markedly higher in ATN than HRS and can help, though it is not required by guideline.

Practical step: hold diuretics and beta blockers, hold ALL NSAIDs, culture blood/urine and do a DIAGNOSTIC PARACENTESIS on every cirrhotic with AKI. Ascitic PMN ≥250/mm3 defines SBP — the single most common HRS precipitant, and treating it changes everything [1].
sections.mechanism: The albumin challenge is a physiologic test, not just resuscitation: albumin expands the effective arterial volume and binds inflammatory mediators/NO. If the AKI corrects, the lesion was true hypovolemia; if it persists despite a filled circulation, the vasoconstrictor reflex is autonomous — that is HRS.
sections.teaching_pearl: HRS-AKI is a diagnosis of exclusion that you should be able to defend in four sentences: filled the tank, stopped the diuretics, no shock, no nephrotoxins, clean urine and normal ultrasound. If any of those four is unmet, you have not made the diagnosis yet.
sections.board_tip: Classic vignette: cirrhotic admitted with SBP, given cefotaxime but NOT albumin, creatinine doubles on day 3. Answer: HRS-AKI precipitated by SBP — and the omitted albumin is the testable error [4].

sections.heading: Treatment: Refill the Arterial Circulation
points: FIRST-LINE per AASLD 2021: TERLIPRESSIN plus ALBUMIN. Terlipressin is a synthetic vasopressin analogue with relative V1-receptor selectivity — it constricts the dilated splanchnic bed, redistributes blood back into the central arterial compartment, raises mean arterial pressure, and thereby withdraws the RAAS/SNS/endothelin drive on the afferent arteriole. FDA-approved September 2022 [1,3].

Dosing: terlipressin 1 mg IV q6h (bolus) — or continuous infusion 2 mg/day where available — escalating to 2 mg q6h if creatinine has not fallen ≥25% by day 3; albumin roughly 1 g/kg on day 1 then 20–40 g/day. Response is judged by creatinine, not urine output alone; typical course up to 14 days [1].

CONFIRM (NEJM 2021) is the pivotal trial: HRS reversal 32% with terlipressin vs 17% with placebo, but serious respiratory failure occurred in 11% vs 2% and 90-day mortality was not significantly improved. This produced an FDA BOXED WARNING for serious or fatal respiratory failure [3]. Do not start terlipressin if SpO2 <90%, in significant volume overload, or in ACLF grade 3 with high baseline Cr — screen oxygenation before and during therapy, and be disciplined about total albumin volume.

ALTERNATIVES, in descending order of evidence: NOREPINEPHRINE plus albumin (continuous infusion, titrated to raise MAP ~10 mmHg; requires central access/ICU but head-to-head trials show comparable HRS reversal to terlipressin) [7]; then MIDODRINE (oral alpha-1 agonist) plus OCTREOTIDE (splanchnic vasoconstrictor via inhibition of vasodilatory peptides) plus albumin, which AASLD reserves for when terlipressin is unavailable and which is the least effective regimen [1].

Simultaneously: stop diuretics, stop non-selective beta blockers (they blunt the compensatory cardiac output and lower MAP in this setting), stop NSAIDs/ACEi/ARBs, treat infection with appropriate antibiotics, and control any GI bleed. Avoid further large-volume paracentesis unless tense ascites is compromising respiration — and if you tap, replace albumin 6–8 g per liter removed [1].

SALVAGE and definitive care: renal replacement therapy is a BRIDGE, not a treatment — indicated for the standard KDIGO indications (refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, uremic complications) in a patient who is a transplant candidate or expected to recover [5]. TIPS can improve renal function by lowering portal pressure but risks precipitating hepatic encephalopathy and worsening ACLF; it is a selected-patient option, not routine [1]. LIVER TRANSPLANTATION is the only definitive cure; prolonged pre-transplant dialysis (generally >4–6 weeks) should prompt evaluation for simultaneous liver-kidney transplant.

PREVENTION is where the biggest wins are and each has trial support: albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 with SBP reduces HRS and mortality (Sort, NEJM 1999) [4]; albumin 6–8 g/L for paracentesis >5 L prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction; secondary antibiotic prophylaxis (norfloxacin or ciprofloxacin) after an SBP episode; and never an NSAID in a cirrhotic with ascites [1].
sections.mechanism: Every effective therapy targets the SAME lever: splanchnic arterial tone. Terlipressin (V1), norepinephrine (alpha-1), midodrine (alpha-1), and octreotide all constrict the mesenteric bed; albumin expands the plasma volume and scavenges NO and inflammatory mediators. Raising effective arterial volume and MAP switches off angiotensin II/norepinephrine-mediated afferent constriction and restores GFR in a structurally intact kidney — which is also why TIPS (lowering the upstream portal pressure) and transplant (removing the cause entirely) work.
sections.teaching_pearl: Track the mean arterial pressure as your pharmacodynamic readout. A rise of ~10–15 mmHg in MAP is the physiologic signal that you have actually recruited the splanchnic reservoir — if MAP has not budged, your dose is too low, not your diagnosis wrong.
sections.board_tip: Two high-yield facts about terlipressin: it is a V1 agonist (so ischemic complications — digital, mesenteric, cardiac — plus hyponatremia from residual V2 effect), and it carries a boxed warning for respiratory failure. The board answer to 'cirrhotic with HRS-AKI, first-line therapy?' is terlipressin + albumin [1,3].

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Untreated HRS-AKI (the old type 1) is among the most lethal complications of cirrhosis — historical median survival is on the order of weeks, and short-term mortality without liver transplant or vasoconstrictor therapy exceeds 50% at one month. HRS-NAKI (old type 2, with refractory ascites) is more indolent, with median survival typically measured in several months.

Even with modern therapy, only about a third of patients achieve HRS reversal with terlipressin plus albumin (32% in CONFIRM), and reversal did not translate into a statistically significant 90-day survival benefit in that trial — the improvement is in renal recovery, dialysis avoidance, and transplant bridging rather than a large mortality shift [3,6].

Prognosis is driven by the LIVER, not the kidney: MELD/MELD 3.0 score, ACLF grade and number of failing organs, baseline creatinine at treatment initiation (lower Cr predicts response), bilirubin, and whether the precipitant is reversible. Failure to raise MAP on vasoconstrictors predicts non-response.

Recurrence after successful reversal is common, which reinforces that vasoconstrictor therapy buys time — the durable outcome comes from liver transplantation, after which most patients recover kidney function, though pre-transplant AKI duration predicts persistent CKD.

Practical implications: refer early for transplant evaluation (an AKI episode is itself an indication to escalate listing urgency), avoid iatrogenic precipitants, and integrate palliative care discussions when a patient with recurrent HRS is not a transplant candidate — that population has a prognosis comparable to advanced malignancy.
sections.teaching_pearl: HRS-AKI is not really a kidney prognosis — it is a marker of end-stage hepatic hemodynamics. The creatinine tells you how sick the liver is, and the treatment plan should always include the question: 'Is this patient a transplant candidate, and if not, what does goals-of-care look like?'
sections.board_tip: An episode of HRS-AKI in a cirrhotic patient should trigger transplant evaluation, not just vasoconstrictor therapy. And prolonged dialysis dependence before transplant is the trigger to consider simultaneous liver-kidney transplantation.

board_pearls: HRS-AKI results from severe splanchnic vasodilation, reduced effective arterial volume, and compensatory renal vasoconstriction despite total-body volume overload.
The 2021 AASLD Practice Guidance recommends albumin plus a vasoconstrictor for HRS-AKI and identifies terlipressin as the preferred vasoconstrictor where available. [1]
Norepinephrine is a reasonable alternative but generally requires continuous infusion and ICU monitoring; terlipressin is preferred when available and not contraindicated. [1]
In CONFIRM, terlipressin plus albumin produced more verified HRS reversal than placebo plus albumin but increased serious respiratory adverse events. [2]

Do not choose midodrine plus octreotide merely because it is easier to administer; AASLD reserves this less effective regimen for situations in which terlipressin and norepinephrine are unavailable. [1]
teaching_points: HRS-AKI is supported by cirrhosis with ascites, dynamic AKI, failure to improve after diuretic withdrawal and albumin, and absence of shock, nephrotoxins, obstruction, or structural kidney injury.
Albumin alone addresses reduced effective arterial volume but does not reverse the marked splanchnic vasodilation driving established HRS-AKI.
Terlipressin is FDA-approved for HRS with rapid reduction in kidney function, but it can cause serious respiratory failure; assess oxygenation and volume status before and during treatment. [3]
summary_points: This patient has HRS-AKI rather than persistent hypovolemia or structural AKI and should receive terlipressin with albumin, with close respiratory monitoring. [1,3]

question.stem:
A 59-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis is evaluated for rising creatinine during hospitalization for tense ascites. On admission, creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL. After 4 days, it is 3.2 mg/dL despite stopping furosemide and spironolactone and administering albumin 1 g/kg daily for 2 days. He has had no bleeding, diarrhea, recent contrast exposure, or NSAID use. Diagnostic paracentesis shows 80 PMNs/mm3 and negative culture.

Temperature 36.8 C, BP 102/64 mm Hg, HR 82/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert with tense ascites and peripheral edema. His lungs are clear, and there is no JVD.

Sodium is 128 mEq/L and BUN is 52 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, or casts. Renal US shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation:
The 2021 AASLD Practice Guidance recommends a vasoconstrictor plus albumin for HRS-AKI and identifies terlipressin as the preferred vasoconstrictor where available. Norepinephrine is the second choice, whereas midodrine plus octreotide is reserved for situations in which neither preferred option can be administered. This guideline recommendation predates the 2022 US FDA approval of terlipressin.

This patient has cirrhosis with ascites and rapidly progressive AKI that did not improve after diuretic withdrawal and albumin expansion. Negative ascitic studies, stable hemodynamics, absent nephrotoxin exposure, bland urine sediment, and normal renal US argue against SBP-associated AKI, shock, acute tubular injury, glomerular disease, and obstruction. He therefore has HRS-AKI caused by marked splanchnic vasodilation and secondary renal vasoconstriction.

Terlipressin constricts the splanchnic circulation, increases effective arterial volume, and improves renal perfusion. Albumin is continued with treatment. His normal oxygenation and clear lungs provide no immediate respiratory contraindication, although oxygenation and volume status require close monitoring because terlipressin can cause serious respiratory failure.

wrong_explanations.why: Albumin alone has already failed to improve kidney function. Established HRS-AKI requires vasoconstrictor therapy in addition to albumin.
Dialysis is reserved for standard urgent indications or as a bridge to transplantation. This patient has no refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, pulmonary edema, or uremic complication.
Midodrine plus octreotide has lower efficacy and is a fallback when terlipressin and norepinephrine cannot be administered; no such limitation is present.
Norepinephrine plus albumin is an effective alternative but generally requires ICU monitoring and is second-line when guideline-preferred terlipressin is available and not contraindicated.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must distinguish functional HRS-AKI from volume-responsive and structural AKI, then apply the guideline hierarchy among several plausible vasoconstrictor regimens.
reasoning_steps: Identify a dynamic AKI in a patient with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites.
Use albumin nonresponse and diuretic withdrawal to exclude persistent volume-responsive prerenal AKI.
Use the bland urine sediment, normal renal US, stable hemodynamics, and absent infection or nephrotoxin exposure to support HRS-AKI over structural or postrenal disease.
Apply the AASLD vasoconstrictor hierarchy and confirm that no hypoxemia or pulmonary findings contraindicate the preferred therapy.

talk.title: Rising Creatinine After SBP in Decompensated Cirrhosis
talk.subtitle: Diagnosing HRS-AKI and selecting first-line vasoconstrictor therapy (AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance)
guideline_sources: AASLD Ascites, SBP and Hepatorenal Syndrome 2021 Practice Guidance (Biggins et al, Hepatology 2021;74:1014)
KDIGO 2012 AKI Guideline
CONFIRM trial (terlipressin plus albumin, NEJM 2021)
talk.key_point: In HRS-AKI, after stopping diuretics and failing a 48-hour albumin challenge with a bland urinalysis, terlipressin plus albumin is first-line; midodrine-octreotide is a substitute only when terlipressin is unavailable.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Hepatorenal syndrome-AKI: diagnosis and vasoconstrictor therapy

board_pearls: HRS-AKI is functional, not structural: splanchnic arterial vasodilation from portal hypertension reduces effective arterial volume, activating renin-angiotensin and sympathetic systems, causing intense renal vasoconstriction with a bland urinalysis and urine sodium typically under 10 mEq/L. Terlipressin, a V1 agonist, reverses splanchnic vasodilation and restores renal perfusion. [1,2]

AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance states terlipressin plus albumin is first-line for HRS-AKI, with midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin reserved for settings where terlipressin (FDA-approved September 2022) is unavailable. [1]

The discriminator from midodrine-octreotide is availability, not efficacy: terlipressin achieved significantly higher HRS reversal than placebo in CONFIRM, whereas midodrine-octreotide has weak, largely uncontrolled data and is explicitly the alternative regimen. [1,2]

Diagnosis of HRS-AKI requires no improvement after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg/day, absence of shock, no nephrotoxins, and no structural kidney injury (no significant proteinuria, hematuria, or abnormal imaging). [1]

The classic trap is resuming diuretics or ordering dialysis: diuretics worsen effective arterial hypovolemia, and renal replacement therapy is reserved for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or uremia, or as a bridge to transplant - not as initial HRS therapy. [1,3]
teaching_points: Albumin infusion (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) with antibiotics at SBP diagnosis prevents HRS-AKI and reduces mortality; omitting it, as in this patient, is a common precipitant.

Terlipressin carries a boxed warning for serious or fatal respiratory failure; avoid it with hypoxia or volume overload, and AASLD advises caution when serum creatinine exceeds 5 mg/dL or with ACLF grade 3 because of low response rates and high adverse-event risk.
Liver transplantation is the only definitive therapy for HRS-AKI; vasoconstrictor plus albumin is a bridge, and every patient should be assessed for transplant candidacy concurrently.
summary_points: Cirrhosis, ascites, AKI unresponsive to albumin and diuretic withdrawal, with bland urine and normal kidney imaging, equals HRS-AKI. [1]
Start terlipressin plus albumin as first-line; substitute midodrine-octreotide-albumin (or norepinephrine in the ICU) only if terlipressin is unavailable. [1]
Give albumin with antibiotics for every episode of SBP to prevent HRS-AKI. [1]

question.stem:
A 58-year-old man is evaluated in the hospital for rising creatinine. He was admitted 5 days ago with fever and abdominal pain; diagnostic paracentesis showed 620 PMNs/mm3, and ceftriaxone was started, though albumin was not administered at diagnosis. He has alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites, previously managed with furosemide and spironolactone, both held on admission. He has received albumin 1 g/kg daily for the past 48 hours. He has received no NSAIDs, contrast, or aminoglycosides.

Temperature 36.9 C, BP 96/58 mm Hg, HR 92/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air. He has moderate ascites without tenderness. There is no asterixis and no peripheral edema.

Creatinine has risen from 0.9 mg/dL on admission to 2.4 mg/dL. Sodium 129 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL, INR 1.7. Urine sodium 7 mEq/L; urinalysis shows no protein, blood, or casts. Renal US is normal. Repeat ascitic PMN count is 80/mm3.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: This patient meets criteria for HRS-AKI: cirrhosis with ascites, doubling of creatinine, no shock or nephrotoxin exposure, urine sodium under 10 mEq/L with bland urinalysis and normal kidney imaging (excluding ATN and glomerular disease), and no improvement after 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg/day. The SBP has responded microbiologically (PMN 80/mm3), but SBP treated without albumin is a classic HRS precipitant. Per the AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance on ascites, SBP, and hepatorenal syndrome, terlipressin plus albumin is FIRST-LINE therapy for HRS-AKI; midodrine plus octreotide plus albumin is recommended only when terlipressin is unavailable, and norepinephrine plus albumin is an ICU alternative. Terlipressin, a vasopressin V1 receptor agonist, reverses the splanchnic arterial vasodilation that drives effective arterial underfilling and reflex renal vasoconstriction, restoring renal perfusion. Terlipressin was FDA-approved in September 2022 on the basis of CONFIRM, which showed superior HRS reversal versus placebo. Before starting, confirm the absence of hypoxia or volume overload because of the boxed warning for respiratory failure; this patient's SpO2 is 97% on room air. AASLD also advises caution when creatinine exceeds 5 mg/dL or with ACLF grade 3 - neither applies here. Concurrent liver transplant evaluation is essential, since transplantation remains the only definitive therapy.

wrong_explanations.why: Per KDIGO, renal replacement therapy is indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or uremic complications, or as a transplant bridge. This patient has none; potassium and bicarbonate are acceptable. Dialysis before a trial of vasoconstrictor plus albumin skips proven, potentially reversal-inducing therapy.

TIPS is an option for refractory ascites and has only limited, non-guideline-endorsed data in HRS. In a patient with bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL and INR 1.7, TIPS risks worsening encephalopathy and hepatic decompensation, and it is not the initial treatment for HRS-AKI.

Diuretics must be withheld in HRS-AKI. Restarting them worsens effective arterial hypovolemia and renal vasoconstriction. The very low urine sodium and lack of edema indicate avid sodium retention from underfilling, not diuretic-responsive volume overload.

This is the correct regimen only when terlipressin is unavailable. AASLD 2021 designates terlipressin plus albumin as first-line; midodrine-octreotide has weaker, largely uncontrolled evidence and lower HRS reversal rates. Choosing it here reflects pre-2022 practice, before FDA approval of terlipressin.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must confirm HRS-AKI by excluding ATN, prerenal azotemia, and persistent SBP, then choose between two vasoconstrictor regimens that differ only by guideline hierarchy and drug availability.
reasoning_steps: Recognize that creatinine doubled in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites shortly after SBP that was treated without albumin.
Exclude structural injury and obstruction: bland urinalysis without protein, blood, or casts; urine sodium 7 mEq/L; normal renal US - arguing against ATN or glomerular disease.
Confirm the diagnostic requirement is met: no response after 48 hours off diuretics with albumin 1 g/kg/day, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and resolving ascitic PMN count.
Apply AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance: terlipressin plus albumin is first-line for HRS-AKI; midodrine-octreotide is only the substitute when terlipressin is unavailable.
Verify no contraindication to terlipressin (SpO2 97%, no volume overload, creatinine under 5 mg/dL, no ACLF grade 3) before selecting it.

claude_errors: States 'The discriminator from midodrine-octreotide is availability, not efficacy' — AASLD 2021 explicitly describes midodrine/octreotide as substantially LESS EFFECTIVE, and the artifact contradicts itself two lines later ('lower HRS reversal rates'); efficacy is a discriminator.

Misstates the AASLD hierarchy: midodrine+octreotide is presented as the substitute 'only when terlipressin is unavailable,' with norepinephrine demoted to a mere 'ICU alternative.' AASLD 2021 ranks norepinephrine above midodrine/octreotide, reserving midodrine/octreotide for when neither terlipressin nor norepinephrine can be given.

Attributes to AASLD 2021 the specific cautions 'serum creatinine exceeds 5 mg/dL or ACLF grade 3' — these thresholds derive from the terlipressin FDA label/CONFIRM post-hoc analyses (2022), which postdate the 2021 guidance; citation overreach.
Cites KDIGO 2012 as the source for a discrete list of RRT indications including 'transplant bridge'; KDIGO gives no such enumerated list and says nothing about bridging to liver transplant.

Boxed-warning statement is overstated as an absolute ('avoid it with hypoxia or volume overload') without noting it is a relative safety caution requiring oxygenation assessment; also frames it as guideline-derived.
judge.why: Both artifacts reach the correct answer (terlipressin + albumin) and correctly frame HRS-AKI pathophysiology and diagnostic criteria. A is more faithful to the AASLD 2021 hierarchy (terlipressin preferred > norepinephrine > midodrine/octreotide), correctly notes that the 2021 guidance predates the 2022 FDA approval, cites CONFIRM's respiratory adverse-event signal accurately, and — importantly for teaching value — includes norepinephrine as a distractor so the resident must reason through the full hierarchy. B contains a self-contradictory and guideline-inaccurate pearl ('the discriminator is availability, not efficacy'), collapses the vasoconstrictor hierarchy by relegating norepinephrine, and attributes label-derived cautions and RRT indication lists to sources that do not support them. B's richer clinical vignette (SBP without albumin as precipitant, urine sodium, TIPS distractor) is a teaching strength, but the guideline-fidelity and citation-honesty errors are decisive.

  "title": "Community-Acquired Pneumonia",
  "subtitle": "From alveolar host defense and shunt physiology to severity-based antibiotics and the contested ATS 2025 update",
  "guideline_sources": [

  "summary_points": [
    "Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) causes neutrophil-rich alveolar exudate, surfactant dysfunction, reduced compliance, and low-ventilation/perfused lung units; true intrapulmonary shunt explains why severe hypoxemia may respond incompletely to supplemental oxygen.",
    "Diagnose CAP by a compatible acute syndrome plus a new infiltrate on chest imaging. Use the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) to support disposition, then use the ATS major/minor criteria to identify severe CAP requiring ICU-level assessment.[2,3]",
    "Guideline-recommended empiric therapy remains amoxicillin or doxycycline for otherwise healthy outpatients and a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone for most hospitalized adults. Add methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or Pseudomonas coverage only for validated individual risk factors.[1,2]",
    "ATS 2025 conditionally suggests systemic corticosteroids for severe CAP, except influenza pneumonia, with low-quality evidence—a reversal from ATS/IDSA 2019. The CAPE COD trial found lower 28-day mortality with early hydrocortisone in selected ICU patients with severe CAP.[1,4]",
    "ATS 2025 conditionally permits a 3- to 5-day course, with a minimum of 3 days, for clinically stable outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP.   "sections": [
    {
      "heading": "1. Physiology First: Why an Alveolar Infection Causes Hypoxemia",
      "minutes": "2-3 min",
      "points": [
        "Normal distal airways use mucociliary clearance, cough, secretory immunoglobulin, antimicrobial peptides, surfactant proteins, alveolar macrophages, and recruited neutrophils to keep the alveolar space nearly sterile. CAP develops when inoculum and microbial virulence overwhelm these defenses or when aspiration, impaired consciousness, smoking, age, or chronic cardiopulmonary disease weakens them.",
        "Alveolar macrophages recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns through Toll-like and NOD-like receptors. Nuclear factor-kappa B and inflammasome activation release tumor necrosis factor, IL-1, IL-6, and neutrophil chemokines; systemic IL-1 and IL-6 produce fever and acute-phase responses, while tumor necrosis factor contributes to vasodilation, capillary leak, and shock in severe infection.",
        "Endothelial and epithelial permeability rises, allowing protein-rich fluid, fibrin, erythrocytes, and neutrophils to fill alveoli. This exudate produces air bronchograms and lobar or multifocal opacities; neutrophil enzymes, reactive oxygen species, and microbial toxins may injure type I pneumocytes and the alveolar-capillary barrier.",
        "Type II pneumocyte dysfunction reduces surfactant, increasing surface tension and promoting dependent alveolar collapse. Consolidated and atelectatic units become stiff, so lung compliance falls and the work of breathing rises, producing tachypnea and pleuritic splinting.",
        "Perfusion continues through poorly ventilated or nonventilated alveoli, creating low ventilation/perfusion ratios and true intrapulmonary shunt. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction partly redirects blood, but inflammation blunts this compensation; severe shunt therefore responds less completely to oxygen than simple ventilation/perfusion mismatch.",
        "Early tachypnea usually lowers PaCO2 and produces respiratory alkalosis. A normalizing or rising PaCO2 in a severely tachypneic patient may indicate respiratory muscle fatigue, worsening dead space, or impending ventilatory failure rather than improvement."
      ],
      "mechanism": "Innate immune signaling is necessary for microbial clearance but also fills the gas-exchanging unit with inflammatory exudate. The resulting shunt, surfactant loss, and low compliance connect the molecular response directly to hypoxemia, crackles, tachypnea, and respiratory failure.",
      "teaching_pearl": "Oxygen corrects low ventilation/perfusion mismatch better than true shunt; persistent hypoxemia despite increasing oxygen should trigger reassessment for extensive consolidation, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), empyema, or another diagnosis.",
      "board_tip": "Pneumonia classically produces an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, whereas pure hypoventilation produces hypoxemia with a relatively normal gradient."
    },
    {
      "heading": "2. Recognition, Severity, and a Question-Driven Workup",
      "minutes": "2-3 min",
      "points": [
        "Establish the syndrome: acute cough, sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, fever or hypothermia, tachypnea, focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, or hypoxemia plus a new infiltrate. Older adults may instead present with delirium, falls, anorexia, or functional decline.",
        "Confirm parenchymal disease with a chest X-ray (CXR). Lung ultrasound can rapidly identify subpleural consolidation, dynamic air bronchograms, or a parapneumonic effusion and is addressed as a diagnostic modality in ATS 2025; CT is useful when suspicion remains high despite nondiagnostic initial imaging or when obstruction, abscess, embolism, or another mimic is plausible.[1]",
        "Ask whether the patient can go home: ATS/IDSA 2019 prefers the validated PSI over unstructured judgment or CURB-65, but disposition must also account for oxygen requirement, hemodynamics, oral intake, cognition, mobility, adherence, and home support.[2,3]",
        "Identify severe CAP using either one major criterion—vasopressor-dependent shock or invasive mechanical ventilation—or at least three minor criteria: respiratory rate at least 30/min, PaO2/FiO2 at most 250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN at least 20 mg/dL, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, or hypotension requiring aggressive fluids.[2]",
        "For uncomplicated outpatient CAP, routine cultures are low yield. Obtain blood cultures and a high-quality lower respiratory specimen in severe CAP or when empirically covering MRSA or Pseudomonas because microbiology can justify narrowing or stopping that coverage.[2]",
        "Order influenza and other respiratory viral nucleic acid amplification testing when circulating or epidemiologically plausible. Legionella urinary antigen is most useful in severe CAP or an outbreak/travel exposure; pneumococcal urinary antigen can assist selected severe cases.[2]",
        "Do not use a low procalcitonin level to withhold initial antibiotics when the clinical and radiographic diagnosis of CAP is established: early or localized bacterial infection may not generate a high value. Serial trends may support de-escalation only when integrated with clinical improvement and microbiology.[2]",
        "If hypotension, altered mentation, oliguria, or marked hypoxemia suggests sepsis, obtain CBC, CMP, lactate, blood cultures, and an ABG or venous blood gas as appropriate. Each test should answer a question: organ dysfunction, perfusion failure, pathogen identification, or ventilatory reserve."
      ],
      "mechanism": "Severity tools quantify the consequences of failed pulmonary and systemic compensation: shunt causes hypoxemia, inflammation causes confusion and cytopenias, renal hypoperfusion raises BUN, and vasoplegia produces hypotension.",
      "teaching_pearl": "The PSI estimates mortality and supports admission decisions, whereas the ATS severe-CAP criteria ask a different question: who needs ICU-level monitoring or organ support.[2,3]",
      "board_tip": "Healthcare-associated pneumonia is no longer a treatment category. Prior healthcare exposure alone does not justify vancomycin or antipseudomonal therapy; look for validated, patient-specific resistance risks.[2]"
    },
    {
      "heading": "3. Treatment: Match Spectrum and Duration to Risk",
      "minutes": "3 min",
      "points": [
        "Otherwise healthy outpatient without resistant-pathogen risk: guideline-recommended options are amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Azithromycin monotherapy is acceptable only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%.[1,2]",
        "Outpatient with comorbid heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease; diabetes; alcoholism; malignancy; or asplenia: use amoxicillin-clavulanate or an oral cephalosporin plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy with levofloxacin or moxifloxacin after weighing adverse effects.[1,2]",
        "Non-severe inpatient CAP: use a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Severe CAP: use a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a beta-lactam plus levofloxacin or moxifloxacin; avoid beta-lactam monotherapy.[1,2]",
        "Add MRSA coverage with vancomycin or linezolid when there is prior respiratory isolation of MRSA or locally validated risk, particularly recent hospitalization with parenteral antibiotics. Add antipseudomonal therapy such as cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem for analogous Pseudomonas risk, then de-escalate promptly if cultures and rapid tests are negative.[2]",
        "Do not routinely add anaerobic coverage for suspected aspiration pneumonia. Anaerobes become a treatment target when aspiration is complicated by lung abscess, necrotizing infection, or empyema.[2]",
        "Treat confirmed or strongly suspected influenza with oseltamivir in hospitalized CAP regardless of symptom duration, while recognizing that influenza can coexist with bacterial pneumonia. A positive viral assay should not reflexively terminate bacterial evaluation in a sick inpatient.[1,2,6]",
        "ATS 2025 conditionally recommends 3 to 5 total days, with at least 3 days of therapy, for outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP who achieve clinical stability. Stability requires improving vital signs and oxygenation, normal mentation, and ability to eat; bacteremia, empyema, abscess, unusual pathogens, or instability requires individualized longer therapy.[1,5]",
        "ATS 2025 conditionally suggests systemic corticosteroids for severe CAP, excluding influenza pneumonia, with low-quality evidence. CAPE COD used early IV hydrocortisone in selected ICU patients and reduced 28-day mortality from 11.9% to 6.2%; this does not justify routine steroids for non-severe CAP.[1,4]",
        "Support physiology while antibiotics reduce microbial burden: titrate oxygen, use cautious isotonic crystalloid for hypoperfusion, drain an infected pleural space, and escalate to high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation when respiratory effort or gas exchange is failing."
      ],
      "mechanism": "Beta-lactams inhibit bacterial cell-wall cross-linking, while macrolides inhibit the 50S ribosomal subunit and add atypical coverage. Early active therapy lowers microbial burden and pathogen-associated signaling; source control is required when an avascular, loculated pleural space prevents antibiotics and immune cells from clearing infection.",
      "teaching_pearl": "The 2025 steroid recommendation is a narrow severe-CAP recommendation, not permission to give corticosteroids to every admitted patient. Exclude influenza and consider hyperglycemia, GI bleeding, delirium, and secondary infection risk.[1,4]",
      "board_tip": "The major 2025 changes are conditional steroids for severe non-influenza CAP and, after stability, a possible 3- to 5-day course. IDSA declined endorsement because it rejected the two ATS recommendations concerning antibiotics in viral-test-positive CAP, so there is no longer a single fully endorsed ATS/IDSA consensus.[1,6]"
    },
    {
      "heading": "4. Outcomes & Prognosis",
      "minutes": "1-2 min",
      "points": [
        "The original PSI cohort demonstrated mortality rising from approximately 0.1% to 0.9% in risk classes I-III to 9.3% in class IV and 27.0% in class V, illustrating why age, comorbidity, vital-sign abnormalities, hypoxemia, azotemia, acidosis, and altered mentation matter prognostically.[3]",
        "Early complications include acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, ARDS, septic shock, acute kidney injury (AKI), parapneumonic effusion or empyema, lung abscess, arrhythmia, myocardial injury, and decompensation of underlying HF or COPD.",
        "Failure to reach stability by roughly 72 hours should trigger a structured reassessment: wrong pathogen or resistance, inadequate adherence or absorption, empyema or abscess needing drainage, airway obstruction, immunosuppression, or a mimic such as PE, HF, organizing pneumonia, alveolar hemorrhage, or malignancy.",
        "At discharge, verify oral tolerance, oxygen needs, mobility, follow-up, smoking cessation, and vaccination status. Repeat imaging is not routine after complete clinical resolution but is reasonable when symptoms persist or malignancy risk is substantial."

talk.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
talk.subtitle: From alveolar host defense and shunt physiology to severity-based antibiotics and the contested ATS 2025 update
guideline_sources: ATS 2025 Community-Acquired Pneumonia Clinical Practice Guideline; IDSA declined endorsement because of disagreement with the viral-positive antibiotic recommendations
ATS/IDSA 2019 Community-Acquired Pneumonia Guideline
summary_points: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) causes neutrophil-rich alveolar exudate, surfactant dysfunction, reduced compliance, and low-ventilation/perfused lung units; true intrapulmonary shunt explains why severe hypoxemia may respond incompletely to supplemental oxygen.

Diagnose CAP by a compatible acute syndrome plus a new infiltrate on chest imaging. Use the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) to support disposition, then use the ATS major/minor criteria to identify severe CAP requiring ICU-level assessment.[2,3]

Guideline-recommended empiric therapy remains amoxicillin or doxycycline for otherwise healthy outpatients and a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone for most hospitalized adults. Add methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or Pseudomonas coverage only for validated individual risk factors.[1,2]

ATS 2025 conditionally suggests systemic corticosteroids for severe CAP, except influenza pneumonia, with low-quality evidence—a reversal from ATS/IDSA 2019. The CAPE COD trial found lower 28-day mortality with early hydrocortisone in selected ICU patients with severe CAP.[1,4]

ATS 2025 conditionally permits a 3- to 5-day course, with a minimum of 3 days, for clinically stable outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP. A positive viral assay does not automatically exclude bacterial coinfection, and IDSA did not endorse the ATS 2025 viral-positive antibiotic recommendations.[1,5,6]

sections.heading: 1. Physiology First: Why an Alveolar Infection Causes Hypoxemia
points: Normal distal airways use mucociliary clearance, cough, secretory immunoglobulin, antimicrobial peptides, surfactant proteins, alveolar macrophages, and recruited neutrophils to keep the alveolar space nearly sterile. CAP develops when inoculum and microbial virulence overwhelm these defenses or when aspiration, impaired consciousness, smoking, age, or chronic cardiopulmonary disease weakens them.

Alveolar macrophages recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns through Toll-like and NOD-like receptors. Nuclear factor-kappa B and inflammasome activation release tumor necrosis factor, IL-1, IL-6, and neutrophil chemokines; systemic IL-1 and IL-6 produce fever and acute-phase responses, while tumor necrosis factor contributes to vasodilation, capillary leak, and shock in severe infection.

Endothelial and epithelial permeability rises, allowing protein-rich fluid, fibrin, erythrocytes, and neutrophils to fill alveoli. This exudate produces air bronchograms and lobar or multifocal opacities; neutrophil enzymes, reactive oxygen species, and microbial toxins may injure type I pneumocytes and the alveolar-capillary barrier.

Type II pneumocyte dysfunction reduces surfactant, increasing surface tension and promoting dependent alveolar collapse. Consolidated and atelectatic units become stiff, so lung compliance falls and the work of breathing rises, producing tachypnea and pleuritic splinting.

Perfusion continues through poorly ventilated or nonventilated alveoli, creating low ventilation/perfusion ratios and true intrapulmonary shunt. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction partly redirects blood, but inflammation blunts this compensation; severe shunt therefore responds less completely to oxygen than simple ventilation/perfusion mismatch.

Early tachypnea usually lowers PaCO2 and produces respiratory alkalosis. A normalizing or rising PaCO2 in a severely tachypneic patient may indicate respiratory muscle fatigue, worsening dead space, or impending ventilatory failure rather than improvement.
sections.mechanism: Innate immune signaling is necessary for microbial clearance but also fills the gas-exchanging unit with inflammatory exudate. The resulting shunt, surfactant loss, and low compliance connect the molecular response directly to hypoxemia, crackles, tachypnea, and respiratory failure.
sections.teaching_pearl: Oxygen corrects low ventilation/perfusion mismatch better than true shunt; persistent hypoxemia despite increasing oxygen should trigger reassessment for extensive consolidation, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), empyema, or another diagnosis.
sections.board_tip: Pneumonia classically produces an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, whereas pure hypoventilation produces hypoxemia with a relatively normal gradient.

sections.heading: 2. Recognition, Severity, and a Question-Driven Workup
points: Establish the syndrome: acute cough, sputum, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, fever or hypothermia, tachypnea, focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, or hypoxemia plus a new infiltrate. Older adults may instead present with delirium, falls, anorexia, or functional decline.

Confirm parenchymal disease with a chest X-ray (CXR). Lung ultrasound can rapidly identify subpleural consolidation, dynamic air bronchograms, or a parapneumonic effusion and is addressed as a diagnostic modality in ATS 2025; CT is useful when suspicion remains high despite nondiagnostic initial imaging or when obstruction, abscess, embolism, or another mimic is plausible.[1]

Ask whether the patient can go home: ATS/IDSA 2019 prefers the validated PSI over unstructured judgment or CURB-65, but disposition must also account for oxygen requirement, hemodynamics, oral intake, cognition, mobility, adherence, and home support.[2,3]

Identify severe CAP using either one major criterion—vasopressor-dependent shock or invasive mechanical ventilation—or at least three minor criteria: respiratory rate at least 30/min, PaO2/FiO2 at most 250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN at least 20 mg/dL, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, or hypotension requiring aggressive fluids.[2]

For uncomplicated outpatient CAP, routine cultures are low yield. Obtain blood cultures and a high-quality lower respiratory specimen in severe CAP or when empirically covering MRSA or Pseudomonas because microbiology can justify narrowing or stopping that coverage.[2]

Order influenza and other respiratory viral nucleic acid amplification testing when circulating or epidemiologically plausible. Legionella urinary antigen is most useful in severe CAP or an outbreak/travel exposure; pneumococcal urinary antigen can assist selected severe cases.[2]

Do not use a low procalcitonin level to withhold initial antibiotics when the clinical and radiographic diagnosis of CAP is established: early or localized bacterial infection may not generate a high value. Serial trends may support de-escalation only when integrated with clinical improvement and microbiology.[2]

If hypotension, altered mentation, oliguria, or marked hypoxemia suggests sepsis, obtain CBC, CMP, lactate, blood cultures, and an ABG or venous blood gas as appropriate. Each test should answer a question: organ dysfunction, perfusion failure, pathogen identification, or ventilatory reserve.
sections.mechanism: Severity tools quantify the consequences of failed pulmonary and systemic compensation: shunt causes hypoxemia, inflammation causes confusion and cytopenias, renal hypoperfusion raises BUN, and vasoplegia produces hypotension.
sections.teaching_pearl: The PSI estimates mortality and supports admission decisions, whereas the ATS severe-CAP criteria ask a different question: who needs ICU-level monitoring or organ support.[2,3]
sections.board_tip: Healthcare-associated pneumonia is no longer a treatment category. Prior healthcare exposure alone does not justify vancomycin or antipseudomonal therapy; look for validated, patient-specific resistance risks.[2]

sections.heading: 3. Treatment: Match Spectrum and Duration to Risk
points: Otherwise healthy outpatient without resistant-pathogen risk: guideline-recommended options are amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily. Azithromycin monotherapy is acceptable only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%.[1,2]

Outpatient with comorbid heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease; diabetes; alcoholism; malignancy; or asplenia: use amoxicillin-clavulanate or an oral cephalosporin plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy with levofloxacin or moxifloxacin after weighing adverse effects.[1,2]

Non-severe inpatient CAP: use a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Severe CAP: use a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a beta-lactam plus levofloxacin or moxifloxacin; avoid beta-lactam monotherapy.[1,2]

Add MRSA coverage with vancomycin or linezolid when there is prior respiratory isolation of MRSA or locally validated risk, particularly recent hospitalization with parenteral antibiotics. Add antipseudomonal therapy such as cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem for analogous Pseudomonas risk, then de-escalate promptly if cultures and rapid tests are negative.[2]
Do not routinely add anaerobic coverage for suspected aspiration pneumonia. Anaerobes become a treatment target when aspiration is complicated by lung abscess, necrotizing infection, or empyema.[2]

Treat confirmed or strongly suspected influenza with oseltamivir in hospitalized CAP regardless of symptom duration, while recognizing that influenza can coexist with bacterial pneumonia. A positive viral assay should not reflexively terminate bacterial evaluation in a sick inpatient.[1,2,6]

ATS 2025 conditionally recommends 3 to 5 total days, with at least 3 days of therapy, for outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP who achieve clinical stability. Stability requires improving vital signs and oxygenation, normal mentation, and ability to eat; bacteremia, empyema, abscess, unusual pathogens, or instability requires individualized longer therapy.[1,5]

ATS 2025 conditionally suggests systemic corticosteroids for severe CAP, excluding influenza pneumonia, with low-quality evidence. CAPE COD used early IV hydrocortisone in selected ICU patients and reduced 28-day mortality from 11.9% to 6.2%; this does not justify routine steroids for non-severe CAP.[1,4]

Support physiology while antibiotics reduce microbial burden: titrate oxygen, use cautious isotonic crystalloid for hypoperfusion, drain an infected pleural space, and escalate to high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation when respiratory effort or gas exchange is failing.
sections.mechanism: Beta-lactams inhibit bacterial cell-wall cross-linking, while macrolides inhibit the 50S ribosomal subunit and add atypical coverage. Early active therapy lowers microbial burden and pathogen-associated signaling; source control is required when an avascular, loculated pleural space prevents antibiotics and immune cells from clearing infection.
sections.teaching_pearl: The 2025 steroid recommendation is a narrow severe-CAP recommendation, not permission to give corticosteroids to every admitted patient. Exclude influenza and consider hyperglycemia, GI bleeding, delirium, and secondary infection risk.[1,4]
sections.board_tip: The major 2025 changes are conditional steroids for severe non-influenza CAP and, after stability, a possible 3- to 5-day course. IDSA declined endorsement because it rejected the two ATS recommendations concerning antibiotics in viral-test-positive CAP, so there is no longer a single fully endorsed ATS/IDSA consensus.[1,6]

sections.heading: 4. Outcomes & Prognosis
points: The original PSI cohort demonstrated mortality rising from approximately 0.1% to 0.9% in risk classes I-III to 9.3% in class IV and 27.0% in class V, illustrating why age, comorbidity, vital-sign abnormalities, hypoxemia, azotemia, acidosis, and altered mentation matter prognostically.[3]

Early complications include acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, ARDS, septic shock, acute kidney injury (AKI), parapneumonic effusion or empyema, lung abscess, arrhythmia, myocardial injury, and decompensation of underlying HF or COPD.

Failure to reach stability by roughly 72 hours should trigger a structured reassessment: wrong pathogen or resistance, inadequate adherence or absorption, empyema or abscess needing drainage, airway obstruction, immunosuppression, or a mimic such as PE, HF, organizing pneumonia, alveolar hemorrhage, or malignancy.

At discharge, verify oral tolerance, oxygen needs, mobility, follow-up, smoking cessation, and vaccination status. Repeat imaging is not routine after complete clinical resolution but is reasonable when symptoms persist or malignancy risk is substantial.
sections.mechanism: Prognosis worsens when local alveolar infection becomes diffuse barrier injury or systemic endothelial dysfunction. Persistent infection, inadequate source control, and limited cardiopulmonary reserve determine whether compensation progresses to respiratory, circulatory, or multiorgan failure.
sections.teaching_pearl: A patient who is not improving does not automatically need broader antibiotics; first ask whether the diagnosis is wrong or whether an anatomic complication requires drainage.
sections.board_tip: Clinical stability—not disappearance of the radiographic infiltrate—determines antibiotic duration. Radiographic clearing often lags symptomatic recovery by weeks.

talk.subtitle: Why CAP hypoxemia is shunt, and why ATS and IDSA no longer agree on steroids and duration

summary_points: CAP hypoxemia is a shunt problem: alveoli fill with exudate, are perfused but not ventilated, so hypoxemia is relatively refractory to supplemental oxygen — a rising FiO2 requirement means more consolidation, not just 'more oxygen needed'.

Site of care, not the pathogen, is the first decision. CURB-65 plus the ATS minor criteria drive outpatient vs ward vs ICU; the HCAP category is dead — assess individual MRSA and Pseudomonas risk (prior respiratory isolation, recent IV antibiotics plus hospitalization) instead [1].

Outpatient CAP with comorbidities and all inpatient non-severe CAP get a beta-lactam plus macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone; healthy outpatients get amoxicillin or doxycycline (macrolide monotherapy only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low) [1].

The highest-yield 2025 change: ATS now SUGGESTS corticosteroids in severe CAP (conditional, low-certainty), except in influenza pneumonia — a reversal of 2019. IDSA declined to endorse the ATS 2025 document over its viral-assay antibiotic recommendations, so there is no single consensus guideline right now [2].

Duration is shrinking: ATS 2025 conditionally recommends 3–5 days (minimum 3) for outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP who reach clinical stability — do not extend therapy for a persistent infiltrate on CXR [2].

Mortality is stratified, not uniform: roughly ≤1% outpatient, ~6–10% ward, and ~20–30%+ for ICU/severe CAP; prognosis is driven by host physiology (age, comorbidity, hypotension, hypoxemia, uremia) far more than by the organism.
