sections.heading: Physiology: Why a Lobe Fills, and Why Oxygen Stops Working
points: Normal alveolar sterility is maintained by a layered defense: mucociliary clearance, secretory IgA, surfactant proteins A and D that opsonize bacteria, and resident alveolar macrophages that phagocytose small inocula silently, without inflammation. CAP begins when inoculum size or virulence exceeds this quiet clearance capacity — most often by microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, not inhalation.

Streptococcus pneumoniae capsular polysaccharide resists complement-mediated opsonophagocytosis; its cell wall lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan are sensed by TLR2, and pneumolysin plus bacterial DNA/RNA engage TLR4 and cytosolic NLRP3. Macrophage and epithelial NF-kB activation releases TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, and CXCL1/2.

Those chemokines do two things simultaneously: they recruit neutrophils across the alveolar-capillary membrane and they loosen endothelial and epithelial tight junctions. Protein-rich edema fluid plus neutrophils plus fibrin fills the alveolus — this is the classic red hepatization/gray hepatization sequence, and it is the physiologic definition of consolidation.

Consolidation creates INTRAPULMONARY SHUNT: the alveolus is perfused but not ventilated, so blood leaves with mixed venous oxygen content. Because that blood never contacts gas, raising FiO2 cannot fix it — this is why the CAP patient on 6 L nasal cannula with a SpO2 of 88% is telling you the consolidated fraction is growing, and why a widening A-a gradient tracks disease extent.

Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction partially diverts flow away from the consolidated lobe, limiting the shunt fraction — which is exactly why vasodilators and, in the septic patient, pathologic loss of HPV worsen oxygenation. Tachypnea driven by juxtacapillary J-receptors and hypoxemia produces a respiratory alkalosis early; a NORMAL or rising PaCO2 in a tachypneic CAP patient is impending fatigue, not reassurance.

When the cytokine response spills systemically, you get sepsis physiology: IL-1/TNF-driven inducible nitric oxide synthase causes vasodilatory hypotension, tissue factor expression plus endothelial glycocalyx shedding drive microthrombosis and capillary leak, and mitochondrial dysfunction raises lactate even with adequate delivery. Severe CAP is the single most common cause of sepsis in the medical ICU [7].

Radiographic clearing lags the biology by weeks — macrophage-mediated clearance of fibrin and apoptotic neutrophils is slow. Clinical stability (afebrile, normalizing vitals, tolerating oral intake) precedes CXR resolution, and treating the film instead of the patient is the commonest source of antibiotic overuse [2].
sections.mechanism: Alveolar TLR2/TLR4/NLRP3 signaling converts a bacterial inoculum into a neutrophil-rich, protein-rich alveolar exudate. The exudate abolishes ventilation to a still-perfused unit, so gas exchange failure in CAP is shunt physiology — refractory to supplemental oxygen and only reversible by resolving the exudate.
sections.teaching_pearl: If the hypoxemia corrects easily with a small bump in FiO2, question consolidation — V/Q mismatch (mucus plugging, atelectasis, PE) responds to oxygen; true shunt does not. The FiO2-responsiveness of your patient's saturation is a bedside shunt test.
sections.board_tip: Classic exam trap: CAP patient with respiratory rate 34 and PaCO2 of 41. That is NOT normal — with that minute ventilation the PaCO2 should be in the twenties. A 'normal' PaCO2 in a tachypneic pneumonia patient is a pre-arrest finding and an indication for higher-acuity care.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and Site of Care: The Decision That Determines Everything Else
points: CAP requires a compatible clinical syndrome (fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, focal exam findings) PLUS a radiographic infiltrate. CXR remains the standard first study; CT is far more sensitive and reclassifies a meaningful minority of 'negative CXR' patients. ATS 2025 formally addresses LUNG ULTRASOUND as a diagnostic modality — sonographic consolidation with dynamic air bronchograms and focal B-lines is highly useful at the bedside, particularly when CXR is equivocal [2].

Do NOT get routine sputum and blood cultures in outpatient or non-severe inpatient CAP. DO obtain sputum Gram stain/culture and blood cultures in SEVERE CAP, in patients being empirically treated for MRSA or Pseudomonas, in prior MRSA/Pseudomonas colonization, and in those hospitalized with recent parenteral antibiotics [1].

Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens are not recommended routinely in non-severe CAP; Legionella testing is indicated in severe CAP and in outbreak or travel-associated settings [1]. Test for influenza (and SARS-CoV-2) when circulating — it changes therapy (oseltamivir) and, per ATS 2025, changes the steroid decision.

Site of care: use CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90/≤60, age ≥65) or the more discriminating Pneumonia Severity Index to identify who can go home; PSI is preferred by the guideline because it more reliably identifies low-risk patients [1,4]. These scores tell you who is LOW risk — clinical judgment, hypoxemia, and social factors override them upward.

ICU/severe CAP definition = one MAJOR criterion (mechanical ventilation or vasopressor-requiring shock) or ≥3 MINOR criteria (RR ≥30, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring aggressive fluids) [1].

HCAP IS GONE. Do not empirically cover MRSA and Pseudomonas because a patient came from a nursing home. Cover them based on validated individual risk: prior respiratory isolation of the organism, or hospitalization WITH parenteral antibiotics in the prior 90 days, plus locally validated risk factors — and obtain cultures so you can de-escalate [1].
sections.teaching_pearl: CURB-65 and PSI are decision-support for the LOW end. A 30-year-old with PSI class I who cannot keep fluids down or has a SpO2 of 89% is admitted regardless of the score — the score has no field for the things that actually kill outpatients.
sections.board_tip: 'Nursing home resident with pneumonia' is a distractor. The 2019 guideline eliminated HCAP; the answer is standard CAP therapy unless there is prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics [1].

sections.heading: Treatment: Antibiotics, Duration, and the 2025 Steroid Reversal
points: Healthy outpatient, no comorbidities: amoxicillin 1 g TID or doxycycline; a macrolide is acceptable ONLY where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25% — in most of the US it is not [1]. Outpatient with comorbidities (COPD, HF, CKD, liver disease, diabetes, malignancy, alcohol use): beta-lactam plus macrolide/doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) [1].

Inpatient non-severe CAP: ceftriaxone (or ampicillin-sulbactam/cefotaxime) PLUS azithromycin, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone. Severe CAP: beta-lactam PLUS macrolide, or beta-lactam PLUS fluoroquinolone — do not use fluoroquinolone monotherapy for severe CAP [1]. In septic shock from CAP, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour after drawing blood cultures, with balanced crystalloid and norepinephrine first-line for fluid-refractory hypotension [7].
Anaerobic coverage is NOT routinely added for suspected aspiration pneumonia unless there is lung abscess or empyema — this is a change many still get wrong [1].

CORTICOSTEROIDS — the highest-yield update. IDSA/ATS 2019 recommended AGAINST routine steroids in CAP [1]. ATS 2025 now SUGGESTS corticosteroids in SEVERE CAP, EXCEPT influenza pneumonia — a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence, driven largely by CAPE COD, in which hydrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality in ICU-level severe CAP [2,3]. State the strength when you teach it: this is conditional and low-certainty, not a strong recommendation, and it does not apply to non-severe CAP.

DURATION — ATS 2025 conditionally recommends 3 to 5 days (minimum 3 days) for outpatients with comorbidities and for inpatients with non-severe CAP who have reached clinical stability, shorter than the 'at least 5 days' of 2019 [1,2]. This is supported by randomized data: Uranga showed non-inferiority of a stability-guided ~5-day strategy, and the PTC trial showed 3 days of beta-lactam was non-inferior to 8 days in ward patients who were stable at day 3 [5,6]. Extend duration for complications — empyema, abscess, bacteremic S. aureus, Legionella with slow response — not for a lingering infiltrate.

TEACH THE SOCIETY SPLIT HONESTLY: there is no longer one consensus CAP guideline. IDSA accepted 8 of 10 ATS 2025 recommendations but DECLINED TO ENDORSE the document, rejecting the two recommendations regarding antibiotic use in patients with a positive viral assay [2]. When you cite CAP management, say which society you are quoting.

Prevention closes the loop: ACIP 2025 recommends pneumococcal conjugate vaccination (PCV21, PCV20, or PCV15) starting at age 50, plus annual influenza, COVID-19, and RSV per age/risk — vaccination is the only intervention that lowers CAP incidence rather than its case fatality [8]. Smoking cessation is part of the discharge order set.
sections.mechanism: Beta-lactams kill pneumococcus by irreversibly acylating transpeptidase (PBP) active sites, collapsing peptidoglycan cross-linking; the added macrolide or fluoroquinolone covers atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella), which lack a cell wall or live intracellularly and are therefore beta-lactam-unreachable — macrolides bind the 50S ribosome and fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV, both achieving high intracellular concentrations. Corticosteroids do not touch the organism: they suppress NF-kB-driven transcription of TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-8, attenuating the neutrophilic alveolar exudate and vasodilatory shock — which is why they help in the hyperinflammatory severe phenotype and plausibly harm in influenza, where blunting antiviral immunity increases viral replication.
sections.teaching_pearl: Macrolides in severe CAP may earn their place twice: as atypical coverage and as immunomodulators (reduced neutrophil chemotaxis and cytokine release), which is the leading explanation for why beta-lactam plus macrolide outperforms fluoroquinolone monotherapy in the sickest patients.
sections.board_tip: Two board-relevant flips: (1) steroids in SEVERE CAP went from 'recommended against' (IDSA/ATS 2019) to 'suggested, conditional/low-certainty, except influenza' (ATS 2025) [1,2,3]; (2) do not add anaerobic coverage for simple aspiration pneumonia without abscess or empyema [1].

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: Mortality is steeply stratified by site of care: roughly ≤1% for outpatients, approximately 6–10% for ward-admitted patients, and on the order of 20–30% or higher for ICU-level severe CAP — CAP remains a leading infectious cause of death in adults.

CURB-65 illustrates the gradient it was derived to show: 30-day mortality rises from well under 2% at a score of 0–1 to roughly 8–9% at a score of 2 and above 20% at scores of 4–5 [4]. PSI stratifies similarly across classes I–V and is better at confirming who is genuinely low risk [1].

What drives prognosis is host physiology, not microbiology: age, comorbid burden (HF, COPD, CKD, cirrhosis, immunosuppression), hypotension, hypoxemia/PaO2:FiO2, uremia, altered mental status, and multilobar involvement. Organism matters mainly at the extremes — S. aureus (especially MRSA), gram-negative bacilli, and Legionella carry higher mortality than pneumococcus in most series.

Key complications to anticipate: parapneumonic effusion and empyema (drain complicated effusions — antibiotics alone will not resolve loculated pus), lung abscess, ARDS, septic shock, and acute cardiovascular events. MI, new AFib, and HF decompensation cluster in the weeks after CAP, driven by inflammation-mediated plaque instability and increased myocardial demand.

Mortality risk does not end at discharge: post-CAP 1-year mortality substantially exceeds the index admission mortality, especially in older adults, reflecting unmasked frailty and comorbidity. Discharge planning should include follow-up, functional assessment, vaccination, and smoking cessation rather than only an antibiotic end date [8].

Failure to improve by 48–72 hours should trigger re-evaluation, not automatic escalation: consider empyema, obstruction (endobronchial lesion), resistant or unexpected organism (MRSA, Pseudomonas, TB, fungal), and non-infectious mimics — organizing pneumonia, PE with infarct, vasculitis, or HF.
sections.teaching_pearl: A patient who defervesces then re-spikes on day 4 with a growing effusion has a complicated parapneumonic process, not antibiotic failure. Send the fluid: pH <7.20, glucose <60, or positive Gram stain/culture means it needs a chest tube.
sections.board_tip: When a stem describes CAP that is not improving at 72 hours, the highest-yield next steps are imaging for empyema/abscess and reconsideration of the diagnosis — broadening antibiotics without a source-control assessment is the wrong answer.

gemini_errors: No clear factual errors identified; minor citation-attribution slippage in attributing 2019 IDSA/ATS empiric antibiotic regimens and the <25% macrolide-resistance threshold jointly to the ATS 2025 document [1] as well as [2].
claude_errors: Overstates shunt physiology: 'Because that blood never contacts gas, raising FiO2 cannot fix it' — CAP hypoxemia is usually a mixture of true shunt and low V/Q units, so it is typically partially, not absolutely, FiO2-unresponsive (the artifact hedges elsewhere but states it absolutely here).
Presents the beta-lactam+macrolide advantage over fluoroquinolone monotherapy in severe CAP as established ('outperforms'); the supporting data are observational/subgroup, not randomized.

Citation problem rather than physiology error: cites a 'Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 (SCCM/ESICM)' guideline and a specific '8 of 10 recommendations accepted by IDSA' figure — both unverifiable/anachronistic as written, and the 1-hour antibiotic target should be attributed to septic shock specifically (which it does, but sourced to a likely nonexistent document).
judge.why: Both artifacts are medically sound, correctly state that the corticosteroid recommendation for severe CAP is conditional/low-certainty and excludes influenza, correctly retire the HCAP category, correctly reproduce the 2019 major/minor severe-CAP criteria, and honestly disclose the IDSA non-endorsement of the ATS 2025 document. B is the more disciplined artifact: accurate CAPE COD absolute numbers (6.2% vs 11.9%), correct PSI validation-cohort mortality (9.3% class IV, 27.0% class V), a correct procalcitonin caveat, and correct 'oseltamivir regardless of symptom duration in hospitalized patients,' with no fabricated sources. A, however, delivers materially more teaching value for an IM resident — CURB-65 components and mortality gradient, the shortened-duration RCT evidence base (Uranga, PTC), an excellent pearl on 'normal' PaCO2 in a tachypneic patient, parapneumonic effusion drainage thresholds (pH <7.20, glucose <60), post-CAP cardiovascular events and 1-year mortality, and ACIP 2025 pneumococcal vaccination from age 50 — and its content is nearly all accurate. A loses points for one likely fabricated citation (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026), an unverifiable '8 of 10' claim, and an over-absolute shunt statement; B loses points for narrower scope (no prevention/vaccination, no CURB-65 detail, thinner complication teaching). On balance the breadth and depth of accurate, guideline-anchored teaching gives A the edge despite B's cleaner sourcing.

board_pearls: Severe pulmonary inflammation can produce alveolar-capillary injury and hypoxemia; corticosteroids attenuate this dysregulated inflammatory response.

Unlike nonsevere CAP, this patient has at least three ATS/IDSA minor severity criteria: RR ≥30/min, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, and BUN ≥20 mg/dL. [1,2]
The CAPE COD trial found lower 28-day mortality with early hydrocortisone in ICU patients with severe CAP, supporting the guideline change. [3]

The common trap is following the 2019 recommendation against routine corticosteroids without recognizing the 2025 ATS reversal for severe CAP; steroids remain inappropriate routinely in nonsevere or influenza pneumonia. [1,2]

Adjunctive corticosteroids do not replace prompt guideline-concordant antibacterial therapy.
Diabetes is not an absolute contraindication to corticosteroids, but glucose should be monitored and treated during therapy.

question.stem:
A 67-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department for 3 days of fever, productive cough, and progressive dyspnea. He has T2DM and HTN but no chronic lung disease. He has not been hospitalized or received antibiotics during the past 90 days and has no prior MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are started after blood and sputum cultures are obtained.

Temperature is 39.1 C, BP 112/68 mm Hg, HR 116/min, RR 34/min, and SpO2 91% on high-flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.50. He is alert. Bilateral crackles are present without wheezing.

ABG shows PaO2 68 mm Hg. BUN is 29 mg/dL and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Chest radiography shows bilateral multilobar infiltrates. Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 PCR tests are negative.

Which of the following is the most appropriate adjunctive medication?
question.explanation:
The 2025 ATS CAP guideline states that systemic corticosteroids are suggested for hospitalized adults with severe CAP, except those with influenza pneumonia; this is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. IDSA declined to endorse the overall 2025 update, creating a society-level split, although its objections centered on antibiotic discontinuation in viral pneumonia rather than this steroid recommendation. [1]

This patient has severe CAP based on at least four ATS/IDSA minor criteria: RR ≥30/min, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250 (68/0.50 = 136), multilobar infiltrates, and BUN ≥20 mg/dL. He does not need shock or invasive ventilation to qualify. Influenza PCR is negative, so the guideline’s influenza exclusion does not apply. Hydrocortisone should therefore be added to, not substituted for, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.

This recommendation reverses the 2019 ATS/IDSA position against routine corticosteroids in CAP except refractory septic shock. [2] The change was informed partly by CAPE COD, in which early hydrocortisone reduced 28-day mortality among ICU patients with severe CAP. [3] Hyperglycemia should be monitored, particularly given this patient’s T2DM.

wrong_explanations.why: Withholding corticosteroids reflects the 2019 guideline. The 2025 ATS update conditionally suggests them because this patient meets severe CAP criteria and does not have influenza. [1,2]
Oseltamivir is indicated for suspected or confirmed influenza pneumonia. Influenza PCR is negative, and no epidemiologic feature creates a compelling reason for empiric antiviral treatment.
Tocilizumab may be used in selected patients with severe inflammatory COVID-19, not routine bacterial CAP. SARS-CoV-2 PCR is negative.
Vancomycin is reserved for CAP with validated MRSA risk factors, such as prior respiratory MRSA isolation or recent hospitalization with parenteral antibiotics. Neither is present.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must calculate hypoxemic severity, identify multiple ATS/IDSA minor criteria, exclude influenza, and apply the conditional 2025 ATS corticosteroid recommendation rather than outdated 2019 guidance.
reasoning_steps: Recognize CAP and confirm that appropriate beta-lactam–macrolide therapy has already been initiated.
Calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio as 136 and combine it with tachypnea, multilobar infiltrates, and elevated BUN.
Classify the illness as severe CAP based on at least three ATS/IDSA minor criteria despite the absence of shock or invasive ventilation.
Exclude influenza pneumonia and apply the 2025 ATS conditional recommendation for adjunctive systemic corticosteroids.

talk.title: Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Adjunctive Corticosteroids
talk.subtitle: The 2025 ATS reversal, the influenza exception, and why IDSA only partly signed on
guideline_sources: ATS 2025 CAP Update (IDSA declined to endorse 2 of 10 recommendations)
IDSA/ATS 2019 Community-Acquired Pneumonia Guideline
CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023)
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026
talk.key_point: In severe CAP without influenza, add IV hydrocortisone (about 200 mg/day) early — a conditional, low-certainty ATS 2025 recommendation that reverses the 2019 advice against routine steroids.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Severe community-acquired pneumonia: adjunctive corticosteroids and the influenza exception

board_pearls: Adjunctive corticosteroids blunt the dysregulated cytokine response driving alveolar injury and vasodilatory shock in severe CAP; benefit appears when given EARLY (within 24 h of severe-CAP criteria), not as salvage on day 5. [3]

ATS 2025 CAP update: corticosteroids are SUGGESTED in severe CAP (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence) — an explicit reversal of the IDSA/ATS 2019 recommendation against routine steroids. [1,2]

The single discriminator that turns steroids from helpful to harmful is a positive influenza assay: ATS 2025 excludes influenza pneumonia, where steroids are associated with prolonged viral shedding and worse outcomes. This patient's influenza PCR is negative. [1]

CAPE COD (NEJM 2023) randomized 800 patients with severe CAP to hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV versus placebo and showed lower 28-day mortality; ESCAPe was neutral but enrolled later and in a different population. [3]

Classic trap: escalating antibiotics. HCAP is dead — MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage requires individual risk factors (prior respiratory isolation, recent IV antibiotics plus hospitalization), not merely ICU-level illness. [2]
teaching_points: Site-of-care and severity: severe CAP = 1 major criterion (mechanical ventilation, vasopressors) or ≥3 ATS minor criteria (RR ≥30, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN ≥20 mg/dL, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension needing fluids).

Empiric inpatient therapy remains a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone; adding MRSA or antipseudomonal coverage is risk-factor driven and should be de-escalated if cultures are negative. [2]

Know the society split: IDSA accepted 8 of 10 ATS 2025 recommendations but declined to endorse the two concerning antibiotic management in patients with positive viral assays — teach the disagreement rather than pretending consensus exists. [1]

Duration is shrinking: ATS 2025 conditionally supports 3-5 days (minimum 3) for outpatients with comorbidities and inpatients with non-severe CAP who reach clinical stability — but severe CAP is not the population for a 3-day course. [1]
summary_points: Severe CAP + influenza-negative → add IV hydrocortisone early, alongside standard beta-lactam plus macrolide therapy. [1,3]
The steroid recommendation is conditional and based on low-certainty evidence; monitor hyperglycemia and do not extend it to influenza pneumonia. [1]
Do not treat severity alone as an indication to broaden antibiotics or to check procalcitonin at the moment of clinical decompensation.

question.stem:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated in the ICU for worsening hypoxemia 10 hours after admission for pneumonia. He reports 4 days of fever, productive cough, and progressive dyspnea. He has HTN and T2DM. He has had no hospitalization or intravenous antibiotics in the past year and no prior MRSA or Pseudomonas isolation. Blood and sputum cultures were obtained and ceftriaxone plus azithromycin were started in the emergency department 8 hours ago. Nasopharyngeal PCR for influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2 is negative.

Temperature 38.9 C, BP 114/70 mm Hg without vasopressors, HR 106/min, RR 32/min, SpO2 91% on high-flow nasal cannula at 50 L/min with FiO2 0.60. He is alert. There are diffuse crackles in both lower lung fields.

WBC 16,800/uL, BUN 27 mg/dL, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, glucose 186 mg/dL, procalcitonin 4.2 ng/mL, PaO2 62 mm Hg (PaO2/FiO2 103). CXR shows bilateral multilobar infiltrates.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: This patient meets severe CAP criteria (≥3 ATS minor criteria: RR ≥30/min, PaO2/FiO2 ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, BUN ≥20 mg/dL) while receiving guideline-concordant beta-lactam plus macrolide therapy. The ATS 2025 CAP update SUGGESTS adjunctive corticosteroids for patients with severe CAP (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence), explicitly EXCEPT when influenza pneumonia is present — a deliberate reversal of the IDSA/ATS 2019 statement recommending against routine corticosteroids. This recommendation is anchored to CAPE COD (NEJM 2023), in which hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV begun within 24 hours of meeting severe-CAP criteria reduced 28-day mortality. His influenza and SARS-CoV-2 PCR are negative, so the exception does not apply, and he is early in his course — the window in which benefit was demonstrated. Note the society split worth knowing: IDSA endorsed 8 of 10 ATS 2025 recommendations but declined the two concerning antibiotics in patients with positive viral assays; the corticosteroid recommendation was not the point of contention. Practical caveats: anticipate hyperglycemia in T2DM and avoid steroids if there is concurrent influenza or an untreated fungal/mycobacterial process. Escalating antimicrobial coverage is not indicated here — the ATS/IDSA framework eliminated the HCAP category and requires individual MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, which he lacks.

wrong_explanations.why: Empiric MRSA coverage requires individual risk factors — prior MRSA respiratory isolation, or recent hospitalization plus IV antibiotics (and locally validated risk). Severity alone is not an indication; the HCAP category was eliminated in 2019, and reflexive vancomycin adds nephrotoxicity without benefit.

Oseltamivir is indicated for suspected or confirmed influenza, but nasopharyngeal PCR for influenza A/B is negative in a patient presenting 4 days into a bacterial-appearing illness with procalcitonin 4.2 ng/mL. Empiric antivirals do not address his need for adjunctive anti-inflammatory therapy.

Procalcitonin may support de-escalation or shortening of therapy later, but it must never be used to withhold or delay treatment in severe CAP. Serial measurement now changes nothing about the immediate decision and delays a mortality-reducing intervention.

Beta-lactam plus macrolide and respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy are equivalent inpatient options; switching between them in a deteriorating patient already on appropriate coverage offers no benefit and forfeits the possible immunomodulatory effect of the macrolide.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must classify severity by ATS minor criteria, recognize that current antibiotics are already guideline-concordant, apply a recently reversed 2025 recommendation, and confirm the single exclusion criterion (negative influenza assay) before choosing among four plausible escalation strategies.
reasoning_steps: Tally ATS minor criteria (RR 32, PaO2/FiO2 103, multilobar infiltrates, BUN 27) to establish severe CAP.
Confirm current therapy — ceftriaxone plus azithromycin — is already guideline-concordant, so antibiotic escalation is not the gap.
Exclude MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors (no prior isolation, no recent hospitalization or IV antibiotics), eliminating vancomycin.
Apply the ATS 2025 conditional recommendation for adjunctive corticosteroids in severe CAP, and verify the influenza exception does not apply (negative influenza PCR).
Recognize the therapeutic window: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV started early (CAPE COD) rather than diagnostic temporizing with procalcitonin.

gemini_errors: States flatly that 'IDSA did not endorse the overall update.' The 2025 ATS document was published with IDSA declining only specific recommendations (chiefly those on stopping antibacterials when a viral assay is positive); framing it as a wholesale non-endorsement overstates the society split, and A's own explanation contradicts itself by then saying IDSA's objections were narrow.

Minor imprecision: pearl says 'at least three' minor criteria while the explanation says 'at least four' — the vignette in fact supplies four (RR, P/F, multilobar, BUN); not wrong, but internally inconsistent.
claude_errors: 'Beta-lactam plus macrolide and respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy are equivalent inpatient options' (and the parallel teaching point) is incorrect in the severe CAP population being taught: the 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline recommends combination therapy (beta-lactam + macrolide or beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone) for severe CAP and does not endorse fluoroquinolone monotherapy there.
ABIM blueprint weight for Pulmonary Disease is listed as 10%; the ABIM IM blueprint assigns 9% (A has this right).
Lists 'Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines … 2026 (SCCM/ESICM)' as a guideline source — a future-dated/unpublished citation that supports no claim in the text (citation padding).
'IDSA accepted 8 of 10 ATS 2025 recommendations' is stated with a precision that may not be verifiable; asserting an exact count risks over-specification.
judge.why: Both artifacts get the core teaching right: severe CAP by ≥3 ATS/IDSA minor criteria, correctly computed P/F ratios, correct labeling of the 2025 ATS corticosteroid recommendation as conditional/low-certainty with the influenza exclusion, and correct attribution to CAPE COD. Neither overstates the strength of the recommendation. A is cleaner on citation discipline (no phantom sources, correct blueprint weight) but is thinner and mischaracterizes the IDSA position as a blanket non-endorsement while simultaneously narrowing it. B adds materially more accurate, board-relevant substance — hydrocortisone 200 mg/day, the early (<24 h) therapeutic window, the ESCAPe contrast and why it was neutral, the death of HCAP and risk-factor-driven MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage, and the misuse of procalcitonin — all of which are correct and high-yield for an IM resident. B's defects (fluoroquinolone monotherapy framing in a severe CAP case, a future-dated Surviving Sepsis citation that anchors no claim, and an off-by-one blueprint percentage) are peripheral rather than central to the clinical message. On balance the greater teaching value and more precise trial-level detail outweigh those blemishes, so B wins narrowly.

Physiology: Why Insulin Deficiency Produces DKA","minutes":"3 min","points":["Insulin normally activates adipocyte phosphodiesterase and suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase, limiting release of free fatty acids (FFAs). In DKA, low effective insulin and increased glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and GH activate lipolysis and deliver FFAs to the liver.","Hepatic β-oxidation converts FFAs to acetyl-CoA. Low insulin and high glucagon inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase, lowering malonyl-CoA and releasing carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 from inhibition; FFAs therefore enter mitochondria and generate large amounts of acetyl-CoA.","Oxaloacetate is diverted toward gluconeogenesis, limiting acetyl-CoA entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Excess acetyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate; dissociation of these ketoacids consumes bicarbonate and produces an anion-gap metabolic acidosis.","A high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio favors conversion of acetoacetate to β-hydroxybutyrate, making β-hydroxybutyrate the predominant ketone in severe DKA. The urine nitroprusside test detects acetoacetate but not β-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate initial severity.","Insulin deficiency and counterregulatory hormones also increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis while decreasing peripheral glucose uptake. Hyperglycemia and ketonuria create osmotic diuresis, causing water, Na⁺, K⁺, phosphate, and Mg²⁺ losses.","Total-body K⁺ is depleted, but serum K⁺ may initially be normal or high because insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality, and acidemia shift K⁺ out of cells. Fluid and insulin therapy reverse these shifts and can rapidly uncover profound hypokalemia."],"mechanism":"The central lesion is failure of insulin signaling in adipose tissue and liver. Fluids restore perfusion and renal substrate clearance, while insulin directly suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis and restores cellular glucose and K⁺ uptake.","teaching_pearl":"DKA is fundamentally a disorder of uncontrolled ketogenesis, not simply severe hyperglycemia; SGLT2 inhibitor-associated DKA may therefore occur with glucose <200 mg/dL.[1]","board_tip":"Kussmaul respirations are compensatory alveolar hyperventilation. Using Winter's formula, expected PCO₂ ≈ 1.5 × serum bicarbonate + 8 ± 2; a higher PCO₂ indicates superimposed respiratory acidosis."},{"heading":"2. Recognition, Diagnostic Criteria, and Trigger Search","minutes":"2 min","points":["Per the 2024 international consensus, diagnose DKA only when all three are present: diabetes or glucose ≥200 mg/dL; β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+; and venous pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.[1]","Initial testing: bedside glucose, BMP, venous blood gas, serum or capillary β-hydroxybutyrate, CBC, Mg²⁺, phosphate, urinalysis, EKG, and calculated anion gap. A venous blood gas is generally adequate because treatment is driven by acid-base status rather than arterial oxygenation.","Prefer quantitative β-hydroxybutyrate over urine ketones for diagnosis and serial assessment. Urine ketones may lag behind physiology and can transiently increase during recovery as β-hydroxybutyrate is oxidized back to acetoacetate.[1]","Classify severity using ketonemia, pH or bicarbonate, mental status, and overall clinical condition. Severe DKA—especially β-hydroxybutyrate >6 mmol/L, pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10 mmol/L, or stupor/coma—generally requires intensive care.[1]","Search for the precipitant: missed or inaccessible insulin, infection, new diabetes, MI, stroke, pancreatitis, glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics, pregnancy, insulin-pump failure, or SGLT2 inhibitor exposure. Obtain cultures and imaging when clinically indicated rather than reflexively.","Consider euglycemic DKA in a patient with nausea, abdominal pain, tachypnea, or anion-gap acidosis despite modest glucose, particularly with SGLT2 inhibitor use, pregnancy, prolonged fasting, or recent insulin reduction."],"mechanism":"The workup first proves ketone-driven acidosis, then identifies the physiologic stressor increasing insulin requirements or interrupting insulin delivery. Direct β-hydroxybutyrate measurement tracks the dominant ketoacid rather than a downstream surrogate.","teaching_pearl":"Abdominal pain can result from acidosis and impaired splanchnic perfusion; if it persists after metabolic improvement, investigate pancreatitis, ischemia, infection, or another surgical process.","board_tip":"A normal or mildly elevated glucose does not exclude DKA. The 2024 consensus permits a prior history of diabetes to satisfy the glycemic component when ketonemia and acidosis are present.[1]"},{"heading":"3. Acute Treatment: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Dextrose","minutes":"3 min","points":["Consensus-recommended fluid therapy: in adults without cardiac or renal compromise, begin isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500–1,000 mL/h for the first 2–4 hours, then individualize according to hemodynamics, Na⁺, urine output, and fluid balance.[1]","Use smaller boluses, such as 250 mL with frequent reassessment, in older adults and patients with HF, advanced CKD, or dialysis dependence. The goal is restoration of perfusion without provoking pulmonary edema.[1]","Balanced crystalloids are acceptable and may shorten DKA resolution while reducing hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis compared with saline; this is supported by a subgroup analysis of the SALT-ED and SMART pragmatic trials rather than a dedicated definitive DKA trial.[1,3]","If K⁺ is <3.5 mmol/L, hold insulin and begin K⁺ replacement until K⁺ is >3.5 mmol/L. If K⁺ is <5.0 mmol/L with adequate urine output, generally add 20–30 mmol K⁺ per liter of IV fluid to maintain K⁺ around 4–5 mmol/L.[1]","Once K⁺ is safe, give continuous IV short-acting insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h. In uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA, scheduled subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogues every 1–2 hours are a consensus-supported alternative when close monitoring is available.[1]","When glucose falls below 250 mg/dL, add 5–10% dextrose and reduce the IV insulin rate to approximately 0.05 units/kg/h. Continue insulin because suppression of lipolysis and ketogenesis—not glucose normalization—is the therapeutic endpoint.[1]","Do not routinely give bicarbonate. Consider it only for severe acidemia with pH <7.0; the consensus regimen is 100 mmol sodium bicarbonate in 400 mL sterile water, repeated every 2 hours until pH is >7.0.[1]","Do not routinely replace phosphate. Consider replacement when phosphate is <1.0 mmol/L with respiratory weakness, cardiac dysfunction, or other clinically important muscle weakness; monitor for hypocalcemia.[1]"],"mechanism":"Volume expansion improves renal perfusion and clearance of glucose and ketones. Do not use urine ketones because acetoacetate may remain detectable or increase during recovery.[1]","Administer scheduled subcutaneous basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping IV insulin to prevent an insulin-free interval and rebound ketogenesis. Preventing recurrence requires addressing these structural and behavioral causes, not merely adjusting the insulin dose.[1]"],"mechanism":"Overlapping basal insulin maintains continuous suppression of lipolysis as IV insulin disappears within minutes. Durable prevention requires preserving uninterrupted insulin exposure and reducing the stressors that repeatedly raise counterregulatory hormones.","teaching_pearl":"A patient can have normal glucose yet remain ketoacidotic, or have persistent low bicarbonate from saline-induced hyperchloremia after ketones have cleared; direct β-hydroxybutyrate resolves this ambiguity.","board_tip":"The transition error tested most often is stopping IV insulin before basal insulin has taken effect. summary_points: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is caused by inadequate effective insulin plus excess counterregulatory hormones, producing uncontrolled lipolysis, hepatic ketogenesis, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and osmotic diuresis.

Diagnosis requires all three components: diabetes or glucose ≥200 mg/dL, significant ketonemia, and metabolic acidosis. Measure serum or capillary β-hydroxybutyrate directly because urine nitroprusside testing does not measure the predominant early ketone.[1]
Give isotonic fluid, but never start insulin when K⁺ is <3.5 mmol/L. Insulin reverses ketogenesis but also shifts K⁺ intracellularly, potentially precipitating lethal hypokalemia.[1]
Once glucose is <250 mg/dL, add dextrose and continue insulin until ketonemia and acidosis resolve; glucose normalization alone does not mean DKA has resolved.[1]

The common pitfall is using the anion gap or urine ketones to determine resolution. Hyperchloremic acidosis can keep the gap abnormal, while β-hydroxybutyrate conversion to acetoacetate can make urine ketones appear worse during recovery.[1]

sections.heading: 1. Physiology: Why Insulin Deficiency Produces DKA
points: Insulin normally activates adipocyte phosphodiesterase and suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase, limiting release of free fatty acids (FFAs). In DKA, low effective insulin and increased glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and GH activate lipolysis and deliver FFAs to the liver.

Hepatic β-oxidation converts FFAs to acetyl-CoA. Low insulin and high glucagon inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase, lowering malonyl-CoA and releasing carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 from inhibition; FFAs therefore enter mitochondria and generate large amounts of acetyl-CoA.

Oxaloacetate is diverted toward gluconeogenesis, limiting acetyl-CoA entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Excess acetyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate; dissociation of these ketoacids consumes bicarbonate and produces an anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

A high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio favors conversion of acetoacetate to β-hydroxybutyrate, making β-hydroxybutyrate the predominant ketone in severe DKA. The urine nitroprusside test detects acetoacetate but not β-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate initial severity.

Insulin deficiency and counterregulatory hormones also increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis while decreasing peripheral glucose uptake. Hyperglycemia and ketonuria create osmotic diuresis, causing water, Na⁺, K⁺, phosphate, and Mg²⁺ losses.

Total-body K⁺ is depleted, but serum K⁺ may initially be normal or high because insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality, and acidemia shift K⁺ out of cells. Fluid and insulin therapy reverse these shifts and can rapidly uncover profound hypokalemia.
sections.mechanism: The central lesion is failure of insulin signaling in adipose tissue and liver. Fluids restore perfusion and renal substrate clearance, while insulin directly suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis and restores cellular glucose and K⁺ uptake.
sections.teaching_pearl: DKA is fundamentally a disorder of uncontrolled ketogenesis, not simply severe hyperglycemia; SGLT2 inhibitor-associated DKA may therefore occur with glucose <200 mg/dL.[1]
sections.board_tip: Kussmaul respirations are compensatory alveolar hyperventilation. Using Winter's formula, expected PCO₂ ≈ 1.5 × serum bicarbonate + 8 ± 2; a higher PCO₂ indicates superimposed respiratory acidosis.

sections.heading: 2. Recognition, Diagnostic Criteria, and Trigger Search
points: Per the 2024 international consensus, diagnose DKA only when all three are present: diabetes or glucose ≥200 mg/dL; β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+; and venous pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.[1]

Initial testing: bedside glucose, BMP, venous blood gas, serum or capillary β-hydroxybutyrate, CBC, Mg²⁺, phosphate, urinalysis, EKG, and calculated anion gap. A venous blood gas is generally adequate because treatment is driven by acid-base status rather than arterial oxygenation.

Prefer quantitative β-hydroxybutyrate over urine ketones for diagnosis and serial assessment. Urine ketones may lag behind physiology and can transiently increase during recovery as β-hydroxybutyrate is oxidized back to acetoacetate.[1]

Classify severity using ketonemia, pH or bicarbonate, mental status, and overall clinical condition. Severe DKA—especially β-hydroxybutyrate >6 mmol/L, pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10 mmol/L, or stupor/coma—generally requires intensive care.[1]

Search for the precipitant: missed or inaccessible insulin, infection, new diabetes, MI, stroke, pancreatitis, glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics, pregnancy, insulin-pump failure, or SGLT2 inhibitor exposure. Obtain cultures and imaging when clinically indicated rather than reflexively.

Consider euglycemic DKA in a patient with nausea, abdominal pain, tachypnea, or anion-gap acidosis despite modest glucose, particularly with SGLT2 inhibitor use, pregnancy, prolonged fasting, or recent insulin reduction.
sections.mechanism: The workup first proves ketone-driven acidosis, then identifies the physiologic stressor increasing insulin requirements or interrupting insulin delivery. Direct β-hydroxybutyrate measurement tracks the dominant ketoacid rather than a downstream surrogate.
sections.teaching_pearl: Abdominal pain can result from acidosis and impaired splanchnic perfusion; if it persists after metabolic improvement, investigate pancreatitis, ischemia, infection, or another surgical process.
sections.board_tip: A normal or mildly elevated glucose does not exclude DKA. The 2024 consensus permits a prior history of diabetes to satisfy the glycemic component when ketonemia and acidosis are present.[1]

sections.heading: 3. Acute Treatment: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Dextrose
points: Consensus-recommended fluid therapy: in adults without cardiac or renal compromise, begin isotonic saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500–1,000 mL/h for the first 2–4 hours, then individualize according to hemodynamics, Na⁺, urine output, and fluid balance.[1]

Use smaller boluses, such as 250 mL with frequent reassessment, in older adults and patients with HF, advanced CKD, or dialysis dependence. The goal is restoration of perfusion without provoking pulmonary edema.[1]

Balanced crystalloids are acceptable and may shorten DKA resolution while reducing hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis compared with saline; this is supported by a subgroup analysis of the SALT-ED and SMART pragmatic trials rather than a dedicated definitive DKA trial.[1,3]

If K⁺ is <3.5 mmol/L, hold insulin and begin K⁺ replacement until K⁺ is >3.5 mmol/L. If K⁺ is <5.0 mmol/L with adequate urine output, generally add 20–30 mmol K⁺ per liter of IV fluid to maintain K⁺ around 4–5 mmol/L.[1]

Once K⁺ is safe, give continuous IV short-acting insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h. In uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA, scheduled subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogues every 1–2 hours are a consensus-supported alternative when close monitoring is available.[1]

When glucose falls below 250 mg/dL, add 5–10% dextrose and reduce the IV insulin rate to approximately 0.05 units/kg/h. Continue insulin because suppression of lipolysis and ketogenesis—not glucose normalization—is the therapeutic endpoint.[1]

Do not routinely give bicarbonate. Consider it only for severe acidemia with pH <7.0; the consensus regimen is 100 mmol sodium bicarbonate in 400 mL sterile water, repeated every 2 hours until pH is >7.0.[1]

Do not routinely replace phosphate. Consider replacement when phosphate is <1.0 mmol/L with respiratory weakness, cardiac dysfunction, or other clinically important muscle weakness; monitor for hypocalcemia.[1]
sections.mechanism: Volume expansion improves renal perfusion and clearance of glucose and ketones. Insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, lowers hepatic FFA delivery, shuts down ketogenesis, and shifts K⁺ intracellularly; dextrose permits continued insulin after glucose falls so ketone metabolism can finish safely.
sections.teaching_pearl: The sequence is fluid and potassium assessment before insulin. Starting insulin in severe hypokalemia can abruptly shift K⁺ intracellularly and precipitate weakness, respiratory failure, ventricular arrhythmia, or death.
sections.board_tip: Do not stop insulin merely because glucose reaches 200–250 mg/dL. Add dextrose, reduce—not stop—the insulin infusion, and continue until ketonemia and acidosis resolve.[1]

sections.heading: 4. Resolution, Transition, Outcomes & Prognosis
points: DKA is resolved when plasma β-hydroxybutyrate is <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH is ≥7.3 or bicarbonate is ≥18 mmol/L; glucose should ideally also be <200 mg/dL.[1]

Do not use the anion gap alone to define resolution because chloride-rich resuscitation may produce a persistent normal-anion-gap hyperchloremic acidosis. Do not use urine ketones because acetoacetate may remain detectable or increase during recovery.[1]

Administer scheduled subcutaneous basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping IV insulin to prevent an insulin-free interval and rebound ketogenesis. Calculate the regimen from preadmission needs, weight, or recent IV requirements while accounting for nutrition and hypoglycemia risk.[1]

Before discharge, identify why DKA occurred, reconcile and supply insulin, confirm injection or pump technique, provide glucose and ketone monitoring supplies, review sick-day rules, and arrange close follow-up. Patients should not stop basal insulin during illness solely because oral intake is poor.[1,2]

Modern treated DKA has an in-hospital mortality below 1%, but risk rises with older age, severe comorbidity, sepsis, MI, delayed presentation, profound acidemia, hypokalemia, and altered mental status.[1]

Recurrent DKA is commonly driven by insulin omission, cost or access barriers, psychiatric illness, substance use, and inadequate diabetes education. Preventing recurrence requires addressing these structural and behavioral causes, not merely adjusting the insulin dose.[1]
sections.mechanism: Overlapping basal insulin maintains continuous suppression of lipolysis as IV insulin disappears within minutes. Durable prevention requires preserving uninterrupted insulin exposure and reducing the stressors that repeatedly raise counterregulatory hormones.
sections.teaching_pearl: A patient can have normal glucose yet remain ketoacidotic, or have persistent low bicarbonate from saline-induced hyperchloremia after ketones have cleared; direct β-hydroxybutyrate resolves this ambiguity.
sections.board_tip: The transition error tested most often is stopping IV insulin before basal insulin has taken effect. Overlap subcutaneous basal insulin by 1–2 hours.[1]

talk.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: From Malonyl-CoA to the Insulin Drip
talk.subtitle: A mechanism-first chalk talk anchored to the 2024 ADA/EASD hyperglycemic crises consensus and ADA Standards of Care 2025
guideline_sources: ADA/EASD Consensus Report: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults with Diabetes (2024)
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2025 (Diabetes Care 48:Suppl 1)
Society of Critical Care Medicine / general critical care fluid literature (SMART, SCOPE-DKA)
summary_points: DKA is a two-hormone disease: absolute or relative insulin deficiency PLUS counterregulatory excess (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, GH). Insulin deficiency alone raises glucose; it takes glucagon-driven fall in hepatic malonyl-CoA and disinhibition of CPT-1 to generate ketoacids.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is the diagnostic and monitoring analyte. The 2024 ADA/EASD consensus defines DKA as glucose >=200 mg/dL (or known diabetes), BHB >=3.0 mmol/L (or ketonuria >=2+), and pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L — anion gap is a fallback only when BHB is unavailable.

Urine nitroprusside dipsticks detect acetoacetate, not BHB. During successful treatment BHB is oxidized back to acetoacetate, so urine ketones can look worse while the patient is improving — never titrate therapy to urine ketones.

Treat with volume first, then insulin: isotonic balanced crystalloid (preferred over 0.9% NaCl in the 2024 consensus), IV regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/h without a bolus, add dextrose once glucose <250 mg/dL, hold insulin if K <3.3 mEq/L, and reserve bicarbonate for pH <7.0.

The two commonest pitfalls: stopping the insulin infusion before overlapping subcutaneous basal insulin by 1-2 hours (rebound ketoacidosis), and missing euglycemic DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor because the glucose is 180 mg/dL.
Adult DKA mortality is now <1% in well-resourced systems; deaths are driven by the precipitant (sepsis, MI) and by iatrogenic hypokalemia/hypoglycemia, not by the acidosis itself.

sections.heading: The Physiology: Why Ketones Form at All
points: Start with the ratio, not the hormone. Portal insulin-to-glucagon ratio is the master switch. In DKA insulin falls (absolute in type 1, relative in type 2 under stress) AND glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and GH rise — you need BOTH limbs. Insulin deficiency alone gives hyperglycemia; the counterregulatory surge is what turns on ketogenesis.

Liver, arm 1 — glucose overproduction: low insulin/high glucagon induces PEPCK and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and activates glycogen phosphorylase, so gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis run unopposed while peripheral GLUT4 translocation stalls. Glucose rises from both ends.

Adipose — substrate delivery: insulin normally activates phosphodiesterase-3B, dropping cAMP and keeping hormone-sensitive lipase and ATGL dephosphorylated/inactive. Remove insulin and add catecholamines, and cAMP-PKA phosphorylates HSL — unrestrained lipolysis floods the portal vein with free fatty acids.

Liver, arm 2 — the ketogenic switch: glucagon suppresses acetyl-CoA carboxylase, so malonyl-CoA falls. Malonyl-CoA is the physiologic brake on carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1); release that brake and fatty acyl-CoA pours into the mitochondrion for beta-oxidation. Acetyl-CoA generation now exceeds TCA capacity because oxaloacetate has been siphoned into gluconeogenesis — the overflow is routed through HMG-CoA synthase to acetoacetate, then reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) in proportion to the mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio.

Why this is an acidosis and not just a ketosis: BHB and acetoacetate have a pKa near 3.6, so at physiologic pH they are fully dissociated strong-acid anions. Each one titrates a bicarbonate and leaves an unmeasured anion behind — that is your high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Acetone (from spontaneous acetoacetate decarboxylation) is non-acidic and merely smells fruity.

Why the patient is dry: once plasma glucose exceeds the proximal tubular reabsorptive maximum (~180-200 mg/dL), glucosuria creates an osmotic diuresis that drags water, Na, K, Mg, phosphate, and the ketoanions with it. Typical deficits are ~100 mL/kg of water and 3-5 mEq/kg of potassium.

The potassium paradox: serum K is often normal or high while total body K is profoundly depleted. Insulin deficiency reduces Na-K-ATPase-mediated cellular uptake, and hyperosmolarity plus acidosis shifts K out of cells. Give insulin and that gradient reverses within minutes — this is why K must be watched hourly.
sections.mechanism: Every therapy in DKA reverses one of these steps: fluid corrects the osmotic-diuresis deficit and improves renal ketoanion clearance; insulin reactivates PDE3B to shut off lipolysis (its most important effect, at doses far lower than needed for glucose control), restores malonyl-CoA to re-brake CPT-1, and drives K back intracellularly.
sections.teaching_pearl: Ketogenesis is a CPT-1 gating problem, not a fatty-acid supply problem. That is why very low-dose insulin (0.1 U/kg/h) closes the gap — the antilipolytic and anti-ketogenic IC50 for insulin is far below the dose needed to normalize glucose.
sections.board_tip: An anion-gap acidosis with a normal or near-normal glucose in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor is euglycemic DKA: the drug removes glucose in the urine while simultaneously raising glucagon and lowering insulin secretion, so ketogenesis proceeds unmasked. Check BHB, not glucose.

sections.heading: Diagnosis: The 2024 Criteria and Where People Get Fooled
points: The 2024 ADA/EASD consensus defines DKA by a triad: glucose >=200 mg/dL (or a prior diagnosis of diabetes), ketonemia with BHB >=3.0 mmol/L (or urine ketones >=2+), and metabolic acidosis with pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L [1].
Anion gap has been demoted. It remains an acceptable surrogate ONLY where point-of-care BHB is unavailable; capillary or serum BHB is now the preferred analyte for both diagnosis and monitoring [1].

Severity is graded by acid-base, not mentation: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarb 15-18), moderate (pH 7.00-<7.25, bicarb 10-<15), severe (pH <7.00, bicarb <10). The 2024 consensus removed mental status from the severity grading because it correlates better with effective osmolality than with pH [1].

Nitroprusside dipsticks react with acetoacetate and acetone but NOT with BHB. Since BHB is the dominant ketone at presentation and is oxidized back to acetoacetate as you treat, urine ketones can paradoxically intensify during recovery.
Venous blood gas is sufficient — venous pH runs ~0.03 lower than arterial and tracks it reliably. There is no reason to repeatedly puncture an artery.

Send the workup that explains WHY: CBC with differential, BMP with calculated effective osmolality (2[Na] + glucose/18), magnesium, phosphate, ECG and troponin in anyone over 40 or with chest symptoms, lipase if abdominal pain, blood/urine cultures and CXR if febrile, urine or serum drug screen, and a pregnancy test. Insulin nonadherence and infection account for most adult episodes.

Overlap syndromes are common. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (glucose >600 mg/dL, effective osm >300, minimal ketosis) coexists with DKA in roughly a third of severe presentations — grade both axes and treat the sicker one [1].

Mimics to keep honest: alcoholic ketoacidosis (low/normal glucose, heavy drinking, thiamine first), starvation ketosis (BHB rarely >3, bicarb rarely <18), lactic acidosis, toxic alcohols (osmolar gap), and salicylate toxicity.
sections.teaching_pearl: Leukocytosis of 10-15 K is a catecholamine and stress-hormone response to DKA itself. A left shift with bands >10%, or a WBC >25 K, argues for a real infection — do not hand-wave it.
sections.board_tip: Pseudonormonatremia: correct sodium by ~2 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL of glucose above 100. A 'normal' measured Na of 140 with glucose 800 means a corrected Na of ~154 — free water depletion that will bite you as the glucose falls.

sections.heading: Management: Fluid, Insulin, Potassium — In That Order
points: FLUID FIRST. Isotonic crystalloid 500-1000 mL/h (or 10-15 mL/kg/h) for the first 1-2 hours, then taper to 250-500 mL/h. The 2024 ADA/EASD consensus now prefers a BALANCED crystalloid (lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) over 0.9% NaCl for both resuscitation and maintenance in DKA [1]. Mechanism: normal saline has a strong ion difference of zero and reliably produces a superimposed hyperchloremic acidosis that delays bicarbonate recovery, whereas the organic anions in balanced fluids are metabolized to bicarbonate.

Evidence status for balanced fluids: this is a guideline preference built on the SMART trial DKA subgroup and the small cluster-crossover SCOPE-DKA trial, which showed faster DKA resolution at 24-48 h without a mortality signal — reasonable-certainty physiologic evidence, not a large mortality RCT [1,3,4]. Once corrected Na is high and glucose is falling, switch to a dextrose-containing hypotonic or half-isotonic fluid to replace the free water deficit.

INSULIN: continuous IV regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/h. The consensus states an initial bolus is NOT required if a weight-based infusion is started; skipping it avoids abrupt osmotic shifts and hypokalemia [1]. Target a glucose fall of 50-75 mg/dL/h and a BHB fall of ~0.5 mmol/L/h.

When glucose reaches ~250 mg/dL, ADD dextrose (D5 or D10) and continue insulin at the same or slightly reduced rate. You are treating ketosis, not glycemia — stopping insulin at a normal glucose is the single most common error and reopens the CPT-1 gate [1,2].

POTASSIUM before insulin if K <3.3 mEq/L: hold the insulin, replace at 20-30 mEq/h, and only then start the drip. For K 3.3-5.2, add 20-30 mEq per liter of fluid to keep K 4-5. For K >5.2, no supplement — recheck in 2 hours [1].

Mild-to-moderate uncomplicated DKA can be managed with subcutaneous rapid-acting analog protocols (e.g., lispro or aspart 0.2 U/kg then 0.1 U/kg q1-2h) outside the ICU — equivalent resolution time with lower cost and less ICU use in randomized trials, and this is explicitly endorsed for non-severe DKA [1,5]. Severe DKA (pH <7.0), altered mentation, hemodynamic instability, or pregnancy belongs on an IV drip in a monitored bed.

BICARBONATE: no demonstrated benefit and real harms (paradoxical CNS acidosis, hypokalemia, delayed ketone clearance, left-shifted oxyhemoglobin curve). The 2024 consensus does not recommend routine use and permits consideration only at pH <7.0 — low-certainty, expert-opinion territory [1].

PHOSPHATE: routine replacement does not improve outcomes. Replace only if phosphate <1.0 mg/dL with cardiac dysfunction, respiratory depression, or hemolysis — and watch for iatrogenic hypocalcemia [1].

RESOLUTION and the handoff: BHB <0.6 mmol/L plus pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >18, with the patient eating. Give subcutaneous basal insulin (glargine/degludec) 1-2 HOURS BEFORE stopping the infusion — the IV half-life of insulin is minutes, and an unbridged gap reliably produces rebound ketoacidosis [1,2]. Restart the home regimen if it was adequate; for insulin-naive patients start 0.5-0.6 U/kg/day total split basal/bolus.

Before discharge: identify and document the precipitant, provide sick-day rules (never stop basal insulin, check ketones when glucose >250 or when ill), ensure a home ketone meter, address insulin access and cost, and arrange follow-up within 2-4 weeks — cost-related insulin rationing is a leading driver of recurrent DKA in the US [2].
sections.mechanism: Fluid alone lowers glucose 35-70 mg/dL/h by dilution, restored renal perfusion, and glucosuria, and it dampens the counterregulatory surge — which is why volume precedes insulin. Insulin then works primarily by re-activating PDE3B to shut off adipocyte lipolysis and by restoring hepatic malonyl-CoA to re-inhibit CPT-1; glucose lowering is a side effect of the same signal. Potassium must be given because insulin drives K intracellularly via Na-K-ATPase into a body that is already 3-5 mEq/kg depleted.
sections.teaching_pearl: The gap closes before the bicarbonate normalizes. Renal ketoanion loss during the osmotic diuresis means you have excreted potential bicarbonate; combined with chloride loading, you get a residual hyperchloremic non-gap acidosis that resolves over 24-48 h without any intervention. Do not chase it with more insulin.
sections.board_tip: An SGLT2 inhibitor should be stopped at admission and held for at least 24 hours after resolution; its glucosuric effect persists for days, so these patients often need dextrose-containing fluids plus insulin to clear ketones while looking euglycemic [1].

sections.heading: Outcomes & Prognosis
points: In-hospital mortality for adult DKA in well-resourced systems is now under 1%, and the deaths are usually attributable to the precipitant — sepsis, MI, mesenteric ischemia — or to iatrogenic hypokalemia and hypoglycemia rather than to the acidosis itself [1].

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state carries a substantially higher mortality (roughly 5-20% in reported series), reflecting older age, greater comorbidity, and profound volume depletion; mixed DKA-HHS presentations track with the HHS end of the spectrum [1].
Prognosis worsens with age >65-70, hypotension or shock at presentation, coma, elevated BUN/creatinine, severe hypokalemia, and comorbid cardiovascular or malignant disease.

Cerebral edema is the feared complication but is overwhelmingly pediatric (~0.3-1% of pediatric episodes, with high mortality/neurologic morbidity); risk relates to severity of dehydration and rate of osmolar change. It is rare in adults, which is why adult protocols tolerate faster glucose correction.

Hypoglycemia and hypokalemia are the two most frequent treatment-related complications and are almost entirely preventable by adding dextrose at glucose ~250 mg/dL and checking potassium every 2-4 hours [1,2].

Recurrent DKA — driven by insulin nonadherence, insulin cost, eating disorders, and psychosocial instability — is the strongest predictor of long-term mortality in type 1 diabetes. A readmission is a prescription-and-social problem, not a physiology problem, and should trigger diabetes education, mental health screening, and cost mitigation [2].
sections.teaching_pearl: The most important prognostic intervention you make in DKA happens at discharge, not on the drip. Structured education, sick-day ketone rules, and eliminating cost barriers to insulin reduce recurrence far more than any change in your fluid choice.
sections.board_tip: An adult who dies of DKA almost always died of the trigger. If the acidosis is not resolving as predicted, stop titrating insulin and go looking for occult infection, ischemia, thrombosis, or a missed second toxic alcohol/lactate source.

talk.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis With Hypokalemia
talk.subtitle: Potassium replacement before insulin therapy
guideline_sources: 2024 ADA/EASD/AACE/JBDS/DTS Consensus Report: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes
talk.key_point: In DKA with serum potassium below 3.5 mEq/L, replace potassium and defer insulin until potassium exceeds 3.5 mEq/L. [1]

abim_classification.specific_topic: Diabetic ketoacidosis: potassium-guided initial management

board_pearls: DKA causes profound total-body potassium depletion through osmotic diuresis and vomiting, even when the initial serum potassium is normal or elevated.

The 2024 international hyperglycemic-crisis consensus recommends potassium replacement at approximately 10 mmol/h and delaying insulin when potassium is below 3.5 mEq/L; no formal GRADE strength was assigned. [1]
The discriminator from routine IV insulin initiation is potassium 2.9 mEq/L with U waves; insulin would worsen hypokalemia through intracellular potassium shifting.
The 2024 consensus DKA diagnostic triad comprises diabetes or hyperglycemia, elevated ketones, and metabolic acidosis; this patient fulfills all three components. [1]
A common trap is giving bicarbonate because the bicarbonate concentration is markedly reduced; routine bicarbonate is not recommended unless the pH is below 7.0. [1]
teaching_points: Measure serum potassium before starting insulin in DKA and monitor it frequently during treatment because insulin and correction of acidosis rapidly lower extracellular potassium. [1]
Once potassium exceeds 3.5 mEq/L, insulin can be started while potassium replacement continues to maintain a target concentration of approximately 4–5 mEq/L. [1]

Balanced crystalloids are appropriate for initial volume replacement, but additional rapid boluses do not supersede urgent potassium correction in a hemodynamically stable patient with severe hypokalemia. [1]
summary_points: In hypokalemic DKA, immediate insulin can precipitate life-threatening arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness; potassium replacement must come first. [1]

question.stem:
A 24-year-old woman with T1DM is evaluated in the emergency department for 18 hours of nausea, vomiting, polyuria, and diffuse abdominal pain. She stopped taking basal and prandial insulin 2 days ago because she was unable to eat. She has received 1 L of balanced crystalloid while awaiting laboratory results.

Temperature 37.2 C, BP 112/68 mm Hg, HR 108/min, RR 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air. She has dry mucous membranes and deep respirations. Her abdomen is mildly tender without guarding. Urine output is present.

Glucose is 468 mg/dL, sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, chloride 95 mEq/L, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, BUN 30 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Venous pH is 7.12, and beta-hydroxybutyrate is 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with U waves.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation:
The 2024 ADA/EASD/AACE/JBDS/DTS hyperglycemic-crisis consensus report recommends beginning potassium replacement at approximately 10 mmol/h and delaying insulin when serum potassium is below 3.5 mEq/L until it rises above that threshold. This consensus recommendation was not assigned a formal GRADE strength or certainty.

This patient has DKA based on hyperglycemia, beta-hydroxybutyrate elevation, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Her potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and ECG U waves indicate clinically important hypokalemia. Despite the low serum value, her total-body potassium deficit is even greater because osmotic diuresis and vomiting have caused potassium losses. Insulin would shift potassium intracellularly and could precipitate malignant arrhythmias or respiratory muscle weakness.

IV potassium replacement is therefore the immediate priority. Insulin should begin only after potassium exceeds 3.5 mEq/L, with continued potassium supplementation and close monitoring. Ongoing maintenance crystalloid remains appropriate, but another rapid bolus is not the key next intervention because she is no longer hypotensive and has urine output. Bicarbonate is not routinely indicated at a pH of 7.12; the consensus limits its consideration to severe acidosis with pH below 7.0.

wrong_explanations.why: Volume replacement should continue, but she has already received initial crystalloid and is hemodynamically stable. Severe hypokalemia with ECG changes requires immediate potassium replacement before insulin.
Routine bicarbonate does not improve DKA outcomes and may worsen hypokalemia. It is generally reserved for severe acidosis with pH below 7.0.
IV insulin is standard for severe DKA, but potassium below 3.5 mEq/L requires delaying insulin because intracellular potassium shifting could provoke life-threatening hypokalemia.
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin may be used in selected uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA, but no insulin route is appropriate until this patient's severe hypokalemia is corrected.

question.difficulty_rationale: The solver must diagnose DKA, recognize total-body potassium depletion, interpret hypokalemic ECG findings, and apply the potassium threshold that temporarily overrides routine insulin initiation.
reasoning_steps: Confirm DKA from hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
Recognize that osmotic diuresis and vomiting produce substantial total-body potassium depletion.
Identify potassium 2.9 mEq/L with U waves as a contraindication to immediate insulin administration.
Replace potassium first, then begin insulin after the potassium concentration exceeds 3.5 mEq/L.

board_pearls: Insulin, not fluid alone, shuts off lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis; hyperglycemia corrects faster than beta-hydroxybutyrate clears, so glucose normalization is a substrate problem, not a signal to stop insulin. [1]

The 2024 ADA/EASD/AACE/DTS/JBDS consensus report on hyperglycemic crises directs clinicians to add dextrose-containing fluid (5%-10%) once glucose approaches 250 mg/dL in DKA and continue insulin until ketoacidosis resolves. [1]

Resolution of DKA is defined by ketone and acid-base criteria—beta-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L with venous pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >=18 mEq/L—not by a glucose value; this is what separates continuing the infusion from transitioning to subcutaneous insulin. [1]

The older 2009 ADA criteria (glucose <200 mg/dL plus two of: bicarbonate >=15 mEq/L, pH >7.30, anion gap <=12) have been superseded by direct beta-hydroxybutyrate-based criteria in the 2024 consensus report. [1,3]

The classic trap is stopping or halving insulin when glucose normalizes: this predictably causes rebound ketoacidosis, and if dextrose is not running concurrently it causes iatrogenic hypoglycemia. [1]
teaching_points: Two independent endpoints must be tracked in DKA: glucose (hours) and ketoacidosis (often 12-24 hours). Dextrose is the tool that lets you keep treating the second after the first has corrected.

Transition to subcutaneous insulin requires BOTH biochemical resolution of ketoacidosis AND the ability to eat; basal insulin should overlap the infusion by 1-2 hours before the drip is stopped to prevent rebound ketosis. [1]
IV bicarbonate has no demonstrated benefit in DKA and is at most considered at pH <7.0; it may worsen hypokalemia, delay ketone clearance, and paradoxically lower CSF pH. [1]
Potassium must be maintained at 4-5 mEq/L during insulin therapy, and insulin should be withheld if serum potassium is <3.3 mEq/L until repletion begins. [1,3]
summary_points: Persisting beta-hydroxybutyrate elevation with a normalizing glucose means the insulin infusion continues—with dextrose added. [1]
Use ketone/acid-base criteria, not glucose, to declare DKA resolved and to time the subcutaneous insulin transition. [1]

visual_memory_card.top_right: Insulin suppresses ketogenesis; glucose corrects first
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: Add dextrose, keep insulin until ketones clear
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: Stopping insulin at normoglycemia causes rebound ketosis

question.stem:
A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is being treated in the ICU for diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by viral gastroenteritis. On arrival, glucose was 528 mg/dL, venous pH 7.05, bicarbonate 7 mEq/L, anion gap 29, and potassium 4.9 mEq/L. Over 6 hours she has received 3 L of isotonic saline, IV regular insulin at 0.1 U/kg/h, and KCl 20 mEq/L in her fluids. She remains nauseated and has not tolerated oral intake.

Temperature 37.1 C, BP 116/72 mm Hg, HR 92/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Mucous membranes are moist, urine output is 80 mL/h, and mental status is normal.

Repeat labs: glucose 208 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 111 mEq/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, anion gap 15, beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.6 mmol/L, venous pH 7.25, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Discontinue insulin and start subcutaneous glargine
Give an additional 1-L isotonic saline bolus
Reduce the insulin infusion without adding dextrose
Start dextrose 5% infusion and continue insulin

question.explanation: Her hyperglycemia has largely corrected, but ketoacidosis has not: beta-hydroxybutyrate is 3.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, anion gap 15, pH 7.25. The 2024 ADA/EASD/AACE/DTS/JBDS consensus report on hyperglycemic crises states that once plasma glucose approaches 250 mg/dL in DKA, dextrose-containing fluid (5%-10%) should be added so that the insulin infusion can be CONTINUED until ketoacidosis resolves, defined as beta-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L with venous pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >=18 mEq/L. Physiologically, insulin—not fluid—suppresses lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, and glucose normalizes several hours before ketone clearance is complete. Dextrose is therefore the substrate that permits ongoing insulin delivery without iatrogenic hypoglycemia. Starting 5% dextrose (and continuing insulin, with the rate adjusted to keep glucose roughly 150-200 mg/dL) is the guideline-concordant next step. Additional supportive elements are already satisfied: potassium is 4.1 mEq/L (insulin can safely continue; insulin is withheld only if K <3.3 mEq/L), she is euvolemic with good urine output, and pH is well above the threshold at which bicarbonate is even considered.

wrong_explanations.why: Bicarbonate has no proven benefit in DKA and is at most considered at pH <7.0; her pH is 7.25 and rising. It may worsen hypokalemia, delay ketone clearance, and lower CSF pH. [1]

Transition requires resolved ketoacidosis (beta-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3 or bicarbonate >=18) and ability to eat—neither is met. Stopping the infusion now predictably causes rebound ketoacidosis. [1]

She is already volume-repleted after 3 L: normal BP, moist mucous membranes, urine output 80 mL/h, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Extra saline will not clear ketones and risks hyperchloremic acidosis, already suggested by chloride 111 mEq/L.

Lowering the insulin rate without dextrose slows ketone clearance and still allows glucose to fall toward hypoglycemia. Rate reduction (to about 0.05 U/kg/h) is appropriate only once dextrose-containing fluid is running. [1]

question.difficulty_rationale: The item requires recognizing that glucose and ketoacidosis resolve on different timelines and then selecting the one intervention that permits continued ketone clearance, with each distractor encoding a distinct error (bicarbonate threshold, transition criteria, volume status, hypoglycemia risk).
reasoning_steps: Interpret the repeat labs: beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, anion gap 15, pH 7.25 — ketoacidosis is improving but unresolved.
Recognize that glucose has fallen below the ~250 mg/dL threshold while ketosis persists, because hyperglycemia corrects faster than ketone clearance.
Apply the mechanism: only continued insulin suppresses lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, so the infusion must not be stopped or under-dosed.
Conclude that dextrose-containing fluid must be started to allow continued insulin without hypoglycemia, per the 2024 hyperglycemic crises consensus report.
Exclude competing options: pH >7.0 (no bicarbonate), euvolemic (no bolus), resolution and oral intake criteria unmet (no subcutaneous transition).

claude_errors: States insulin should be withheld only if serum K <3.3 mEq/L and attributes this to the 2024 ADA/EASD/AACE/DTS/JBDS consensus report [1]; the 2024 consensus raised the threshold to <3.5 mmol/L (with KCl ~10 mmol/h) — 3.3 is the superseded 2009 figure, so the citation to [1] does not support the claim
Ironically cites the 2009 criteria as 'superseded' elsewhere while still applying the 2009 potassium threshold as current practice
judge.why: Both items are high-yield, internally consistent, and use the correct primary source (2024 hyperglycemic crises consensus report, Diabetes Care). A is medically flawless: DKA triad, K threshold >3.5 mEq/L with 10 mmol/h repletion, target K 4-5, bicarbonate only considered at pH <7.0, and—notably—explicit citation honesty in stating that the consensus assigned no formal GRADE strength. Lab values are internally coherent (AG 29). B teaches an arguably more clinically nuanced point (dextrose addition and ketone-based resolution criteria rather than glucose) with accurate resolution thresholds (BHB <0.6, pH >7.3 or HCO3 >=18), correct AG arithmetic, and well-constructed distractors, but it commits a guideline-fidelity error by attributing the outdated 3.3 mEq/L insulin-withholding threshold to the 2024 report and repeating it as current in the answer explanation. Since accuracy and guideline fidelity are weighted most heavily, A edges out B despite B's broader teaching content.

talk.title: Occult GI Evaluation in Iron Deficiency Anemia
talk.subtitle: Why negative stool testing does not end the evaluation
guideline_sources: AGA Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Gastrointestinal Evaluation of Iron Deficiency Anemia, 2020
talk.key_point: Men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency anemia should undergo bidirectional endoscopy even without GI symptoms or overt bleeding. [1]

abim_classification.specific_topic: Iron deficiency anemia: GI evaluation

board_pearls: Chronic occult GI blood loss depletes iron stores before producing overt bleeding or GI symptoms.
The 2020 AGA guideline strongly recommends bidirectional endoscopy in asymptomatic men with iron deficiency anemia, based on moderate-certainty evidence. [1]
Colonoscopy alone is inadequate because peptic ulcer disease and upper GI malignancy remain possible, particularly with NSAID exposure.
The AGA recommends a ferritin cutoff below 45 ng/mL when diagnosing iron deficiency in patients with anemia; this patient's ferritin is 8 ng/mL. [1]
A negative fecal immunochemical test does not exclude the GI lesions responsible for iron deficiency anemia and should not delay endoscopy.
teaching_points: Iron deficiency anemia is established by microcytosis, increased RDW, low ferritin, low serum iron, and low transferrin saturation.
Guideline-recommended evaluation in men and postmenopausal women examines both the upper and lower GI tracts, preferably during the same session. [1]
Iron replacement may begin during the evaluation, but treatment alone is insufficient because it does not identify a potential bleeding lesion or malignancy.
summary_points: Confirmed iron deficiency anemia in an older man warrants EGD and colonoscopy regardless of absent GI symptoms, NSAID use, or negative stool blood testing. [1]

visual_memory_card.top_right: Occult GI loss depletes iron stores
